- Published
The European Union is to remove sanctions on two oligarchs imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to reports, prompting anger in Ukraine.
France had campaigned for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be taken off the list, citing "national security concerns". Luxembourg called for the removal of Russian-Israeli businessman Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets.
Latvia initially opposed the deal but agreed to a compromise, part of which involved extending sanctions on nearly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years.
Ukrainian officials said the move was "unacceptable" and sent the wrong signal to Moscow.
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X.
He urged all EU member states to instead announce national sanctions on the two individuals. Latvia has already said it would do so.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov earlier welcomed the prospect of the two oligarchs being taken off the list, claiming the EU's sanctions were illegal and all Russians should be removed.
Usmanov founded USM Holding company, an investment group that owns iron, steel and copper suppliers, and the Megafon telecommunications company. He has in the past had ties with the English Premier League clubs Arsenal and Everton.
The EU froze his assets in 2022, describing him as "a pro-Kremlin oligarch with particularly close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin". Usmanov said the decision was "unfair".
It has been reported that France's initiative was linked to a prospective prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan.
Fridman, a Russian-Israeli citizen born in Ukraine, is the founder of the Alfa Group investment conglomerate, with key interests in energy and banking. The EU has described him as a top Russian financier and enabler of Putin's inner circle.
Fridman himself said at the time of Russia's full-scale invasion that the conflict should end as soon as possible, but avoided outright condemnation of President Putin.
His Russian-Latvian business partner Pyotr Aven was stripped of Latvia's highest civilian honour in 2022 for failing to condemn the invasion of Ukraine.
This may have influenced Latvia's opposition to the move, vetoing it in a vote by EU ambassadors on Monday.
However, on Tuesday it changed its vote to an abstention as a compromise was reached. The new deal involved extending sanctions on some remaining 2,600 individuals and entities to three years. Until now, sanctions had to be renewed every six months.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also announced that France had agreed to start talks with Latvia about joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative and strengthen its military presence in Latvia.

c12aaf7da729.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russia-and-ukraine-trade-strikes-ahead-of-zelenskyys-meeting-with-trump Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russia and Ukraine trade strikes ahead of Zelenskyy's meeting with Trump World Sep 22, 2026 3:02 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian missiles and drones struck at least four Ukrainian regions overnight, killing five people, officials said Tuesday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country's forces had damaged two more Russian oil refineries in their latest long-range strikes. The continuing exchange of aerial attacks, even as front-line positions remain largely unchanged, provided the backdrop for Zelenskyy's visit to the United States. U.S. President Donald Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are contributing to global shortages and higher prices. The supply crunch has also been aggravated by reduced oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz following the outbreak of the Iran war. Kyiv began targeting Russian refineries after Moscow repeatedly attacked Ukraine's power grid. Zelenskyy has offered to halt Ukraine's strikes if Russia ends its attacks on energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy was scheduled to meet Trump and other world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly in New York. He is seeking their help to end Russia's more than 4½-year-old full-scale invasion. Russia's President Vladimir Putin is not due to attend the annual event. The war, which Western officials say has killed more than 500,000 Russian troops, has had global repercussions. Western analysts estimate that Ukraine has recorded more than 500,000 military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths. Zelenskyy also wants help to ensure the flow of Ukrainian grain and other farm products to world markets through the Black Sea. Russian attacks on cargo vessels have severely disrupted Kyiv's exports, hurting its economy and threatening global supplies. Russia and Ukraine have in recent years accounted for around 30% of the world's wheat exports and 12% of corn exports, most of it shipped through the Black Sea. But last month, attacks slashed both countries' agricultural exports by two-thirds, Thomas de Waal of the Brussels-based think tank Carnegie Europe said in a report Tuesday. "The lack of that grain in world markets puts several African countries at risk of famine, while world cereal prices, already pushed up by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, could rise even higher," he said. Zelenskyy takes de-escalation proposals to New York French President Emmanuel Macron said on Tuesday that France would provide Ukraine with additional radar systems to help protect its power grid. Macron said in a social media post that he had discussed with Trump a possible truce between Moscow and Kyiv that would halt strikes on energy infrastructure, as well as a "moratorium" on attacks in the Black Sea. Zelenskyy began his visit to New York by meeting with U.S. senators. He thanked them for what he described as strong bipartisan support for Ukraine and for backing a tougher sanctions bill against Russia that Trump signed into law. Peace and security would be closer once the legislation was fully implemented, Zelenskyy said. He said on social media that he had briefed senators on de-escalation proposals he planned to discuss with Trump later Tuesday. READ MORE: Ukraine fires over 1,000 drones at Russia, including 'largest ever' attack on Moscow In Kyiv, Iryna Panina awoke around 2 a.m. on Tuesday as a jet-powered Russian drone approached her home. The blast shattered a window and left her apartment covered in debris. Panina, 36, said she had lost hope in international efforts to secure peace. "As an ordinary person just trying to live and survive each day, I find it hard to believe they fully understand what's actually happening, how hard it is, and how much ordinary people are suffering," she told The Associated Press. Zelenskyy also planned to press Trump for more U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems, which Kyiv says it urgently needs to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. Ukraine hits a Russian oil refinery Zelenskyy said that Ukrainian special forces struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, southeast of Moscow, and another refinery in the neighboring Bashkortostan region in overnight attacks. One person was killed and four others were wounded in the Samara attack, regional Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. He said that "the enemy targeted industrial facilities," but didn't specify which ones. The Russian Defense Ministry on Tuesday said that its forces downed 297 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula. Russia says it struck missile plant and ammunition factory Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine included anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and more than 200 drones, Ukraine's air force said. The strikes killed four people in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration. A drone also killed a woman in the northern Sumy region, local police said. The strikes across Ukrainian regions damaged homes, businesses and storage facilities, wounding at least five people, authorities said. Five people were wounded in the capital, Kyiv, according to officials. The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces struck metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as port infrastructure facilities in four regions of Ukraine. They included a Fire Point plant in Kyiv producing components for long-range cruise missiles and a tobacco factory in the central Poltava region used to make small arms ammunition, it said. Barr

President Donald Trump has told the United Nations General Assembly he faces a "big decision" on whether to strike Iran again or pursue a peace deal.
Members of Iran's delegation walked out during the president's speech in New York, in which he said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved.
Before a standing-room-only audience, Trump also targeted "global government", vowed to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine and ensure the US wins the artificial intelligence race.
His tone contrasted with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General AntÃ³nio Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples.
Trump's speech on Tuesday came ahead of a day of high-level diplomacy at the United Nations. He is meeting more than a dozen world leaders as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine test his foreign policy agenda.
He began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime, in remarks that sounded more pitched to voters in November's US midterm elections than the diplomats in Manhattan.
He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran, which has spiked global oil prices while dragging down his approval ratings since the US and Israel launched the military action in February.
Trump argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - rather than deal-making or compromise.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
He also once again predicted his diplomacy would end Russia's war in Ukraine, which has shown little sign of letting up as the two sides trade tit-for-tat missile and drone strikes deep into each other's territory.
"We're working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," Trump said. "It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand."
Trump also played down fears about AI, vowing that the US would not surrender its lead to China because of alarmism or what he described as a "globalist scheme" to control the technology.
The US president argued artificial intelligence should instead be known as "super intelligence".
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful."
On the sidelines of the general assembly on Tuesday, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to beef up US military presence on the North Atlantic island.
The deal reaffirms the sovereignty of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, but grants the US broad access to the island's airspace and territory.
Trump is also meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and leaders from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman.
Earlier, Guterres gave his farewell speech as UN secretary general, urging unnamed superpowers to recognise "that their power isn't so super".
"The fault lines in our world are widening," Guterres said, citing geopolitical rivalries, wars, climate change and artificial intelligence.
By contrast, Trump criticised international institutions, accusing the UN of a "far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected".
The US president instead emphasised national sovereignty and "unmatched" American military power.
"There is no global government," he said.
He also warned that the US would not allow threats to establish themselves anywhere in the Western hemisphere.
"If necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said.
Trump accused Cuba's communist government of cultivating ties to left-wing groups in the US, including the Communist Party USA, Antifa and the Democratic Socialists of America.
The Cuban delegation also appeared to walk out of the assembly chamber as Trump turned his sights on them, referring to the island as a "failed state".

- Published
The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over it.
At a signing ceremony at the UN General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said "we will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations".
Danish PM Mette Frederiksen said the deal was "good for the US, Denmark and Greenland" and also for Europe and Nato, while Greenland's PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it was a "win-win-win".
The three leaders then inked the deal, seemingly ending more than a year of tension over the Arctic territory.
Trump had threatened to "take" the semi-autonomous Arctic territory over what he said were national security concerns, citing its strategic defence location and its mineral wealth.
His rhetoric prompted outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders who issued a joint statement saying his words "undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral".
The deal signed on Tuesday amends and updates a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US.
The new agreement says the US "shall be allowed to establish an additional Defence Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig" - referring to locations in Greenland's south and east.
Narsarsuaq has deep-water access and a large runway which US military engineers were surveying last week, according to Danish media.
The Mestersvig outpost is remote, far less developed, and used by a Danish naval dog sled unit.
The "modalities and technical details" of the bases are yet to be confirmed, and according to the deal, must be mutually agreed by all parties.
Washington currently operates its Pituffik Space Base in Greenland's north-west, and the new deal allows the US to "modernise and expand its activities" there.
It also says that "no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland".
Speaking at the signing ceremony, Trump said: "We going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship."
"This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States, for everybody, and for Greenland it's going to be incredible."
Meanwhile, Frederiksen described the signing of the deal as a "milestone in our long-standing co-operation".
"Seventy-five years ago we entered into an agreement about the defence of Greenland. Today, we're signing an even bigger and better agreement - a deal that can last forever."
The Danish prime minister stressed that the agreement "respects sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland's right to self-determination".
Jens-Frederik Nielsen said that "for Greenland, it is not only an agreement about us, it is [an] agreement with us.
"It takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods and the development of our country.
"Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security," he said, adding that the Nato had a key role to play in the North Atlantic in a changing security situation.
The agreement also confirmed Greenland would remain in Nato if it were to gain independence from Denmark.
The 1951 agreement already allowed the US to send as many troops as it wanted to Greenland. Washington already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base.
Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex Greenland, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.
He argued the Arctic island was an essential piece of his plan to build a futuristic "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US against missile attacks.
However the deal only mentions the project once, and contains no concrete proposal.
The island has vast - and largely untapped - reserves of rare earth minerals, many of which are crucial for technologies including mobile phones and electric vehicles.
Trump said last week that the new deal came with "no cost to the United States".
A Nato spokesperson said shortly afterwards that the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".

6a5d8b787402.text: By — Jacqueline Ganun, Associated Press Jacqueline Ganun, Associated Press By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/abdul-el-sayed-says-kamala-harris-visit-for-his-michigan-u-s-senate-race-is-about-democratic-unity Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Senate candidate El-Sayed and former VP Harris speak at Black maternal health roundtable Politics Sep 22, 2026 4:04 PM EDT DETROIT (AP) — Michigan U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said Tuesday that he wants Kamala Harris' midterm campaign stop in Detroit to unify Democrats in the key swing state where their party's factions were on full display in a hotly contested primary earlier this year — and in Harris' 2024 presidential defeat. "We're building an electoral coalition here," El-Sayed said, speaking about the economy hours ahead of a planned appearance with the former vice president. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. An unapologetic progressive, El-Sayed downplayed his differences with Harris over the Biden administration's support for U.S. military aid to Israel. El-Sayed has called Israel's military actions in Gaza a genocide against Palestinians. Israel rejects that position, but it aligns El-Sayed with many voters in Michigan's large Arab American community and with progressives who withheld their votes from Harris in 2024, when the state tipped narrowly to Republican Donald Trump. That election "ended where it did because we could not find the places of agreement to be able to bring people together or move in the direction that we need to move," El-Sayed said, emphasizing that he and Harris both want to help voters who are struggling economically. Harris, the first Black vice president, remains popular among Black voters who anchor the Democratic base in Detroit and who leaned in favor of El-Sayed's primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, in the August primary. El-Sayed said Harris, who will attend a roundtable on Black maternal health with him and separately join an event hosted by the Detroit chapter of the NAACP, is a critical advocate in helping him close ranks as he tries to defeat Republican Mike Rogers. "Her presence here speaking to communities that were really empowered by her voice throughout her political career, I think will help us to continue to bring our coalition together," El-Sayed said. El-Sayed vs. Rogers is a critical contest for Senate control The Democrat's matchup against Rogers, a former congressman, will help determine control of the Senate for the final two years of Trump's presidency. If Democrats hold the seat, which was opened by Sen. Gary Peters' announced retirement, they'd still need to win at least four more currently held by Republicans to flip the chamber. A Rogers victory would narrow Democrats' path to a majority. Rogers' campaign framed Harris' visit as a sign of weakness for both Democrats. "Abdul is so desperate that he's parachuting Kamala Harris into Michigan to save his flailing campaign," said Alyssa Brouillet, Rogers' spokesperson. Rogers has been campaigning in Detroit, a predominantly Black city where his campaign is optimistic he can pick up support from voters hesitant to support El-Sayed. Black voters could prove especially critical as El-Sayed also faces pressure among white Jewish voters who typically back Democrats. READ MORE: How Abdul El-Sayed rose from political oblivion to progressive breakthrough in Michigan "Jews in Michigan are currently scared" by their Senate options, said Barry Goodman, a Democratic National Committee member and major Michigan fundraiser in the party. Goodman backed Stevens in the primary. The race is also seen as another referendum on progressives' viability in battleground races. El-Sayed is running to the left of the Democratic Party establishment, including advocating for universal healthcare. Goodman described himself and many other Jewish Democrats as "holding our noses and voting for Abdul" because they "believe in the Democratic ticket and they believe that one man can help win the Senate but can't destroy the Senate." Other moderates, Goodman said, are still deciding whether to back Rogers or sit out the Senate race. El-Sayed has attempted to soften his approach on Israel and Gaza. He has apologized for some past controversial comments and said he is committed to Jewish safety. Michigan will also be a key state for the 2028 Democratic presidential primary For Harris, the trip comes as questions swirl about her intentions to run for president again. Under the Democratic National Committee's recently revised nominating calendar, Michigan now will hold the fifth presidential preference primary in 2028. It's unclear whether Harris will use the trip to restate or recalibrate her past statements on Israel. But campaigning with El-Sayed is notable, nonetheless, given her past tensions with Democrats' left flank. "She probably figures she won't lose her establishment folks, so maybe she makes gains to her left," Goodman said. Harris has said she's in no rush to announce whether she will run in 2028. But ahead of Election Day this November, she also has campaign stops planned in Nevada and Georgia, two other important states on the political map. GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues. Barrow reported from Atlanta. AI agents are here. Will internet gatekeepers let them in the door? Amazon banned Metaâs Muse assistant, while Shopify welcomed it in, the first sign of battle lines being drawn in the way we spend money online.
As they sharpen, expect a rough sorting. On one side will be retailers like Amazon, which want to keep control of human eyeballs that can be sold to advertisers and pitched on add-on purchases. On the other will be e-commerce enablers like Shopify, whose primary relationship is with merchants, and which makes money from licensing storefront software, fulfillment services, and financing.
Less obvious is how companies that care a lot about customer loyalty but donât depend on impulse purchases, like airlines, will treat bots. (My efforts to rebook a Delta flight via Muse this weekend ran into a bot-blocker.)

Kalshi will let users juice their bets with borrowed money â but only some, showing where the prediction-markets platform thinks its future lies. Kalshi asked the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to let it extend margin loans to customers, but is excluding sports, mentions, and culture bets from the product. That leaves the categories most attractive to institutional investors looking to wager on, or protect themselves from, big global events like elections and commodity prices.
Kalshi and Polymarket need to decide whether they want to be key players in the financial markets or degen OTBs. They are worth far more, I wrote this spring, as the place where Meta locks in AI compute pricing, Home Depot hedges its lumber risk, and investment firms manage the effect of a midterms surprise on their portfolios than as a betting parlor for US black-op nighttime raids. In that light, todayâs announcement carries risks â leverage always does â but suggests Kalshi has made its choice. Polymarket, meanwhile, has some growing-up to do.

Lizâs view
âThis is the beginning of a bankless world,â proclaimed a 2016 ad for SoFi, which embodied the sneering disdain its generation of fintech startups had for the banks they were out to dethrone.
SoFi is now a bank, the 46th biggest in America. So are Klarna and PayPal. Chime is the latest to bite the bullet, announcing the acquisition of a bank earlier this month. Revolut, whose CEO was once quoted saying âI just donât like banks,â has also applied for a license. Block, which got a skinny banking license in 2021, wants another one.
Contempt for banks was hard-coded into these companiesâ DNA. Now they all want to be one. Why?
First, the real money to be made in financial services is in lending, especially as the young tech-savvy customers they courted through YOLO brokerage, crypto trading, and money transfers grow up and want to buy a house. In the lending business, controlling your funding is important, and thereâs no cheaper funding in the world than savings accounts. Relying on bank partners to fund the loans you want to make is risky, as LendingClub found out the hard way, which is why it bought a bank in 2020 and is now a full-fledged bank called Happen.
These companiesâ pivots are also an acknowledgement that their hypergrowth stage is over. Regulators donât like banks growing too quickly because they tend to screw up when they do, which is why Robinhood abandoned its pursuit of a license in 2019. A reminder: We had âRobinhood becomes a bankâ on our 2026 Semafor Business bingo card. We might be early, but I donât think weâre wrong.

SoftBankâs energy business and nuclear company Holtec put off their listings after investors balked, The New York Times reported. At the same time, SoftBankâs junk-bond offering, which will fund its investment in OpenAI, appears to have healthy demand.
The first-order AI trades â frontier labs and chipmakers â are holding up, but a fragility is emerging further down the chain among smaller deals. Whoâs going to pay attention to this stuff when they have to make big decisions on this enormous capital?â

f4f4a162b3f4.text: By — Nayara Batschke, Associated Press Nayara Batschke, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/brazils-lula-warns-against-foreign-interference-in-elections-urges-leaders-to-respond-to-global-conflicts Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Brazil's Lula warns against foreign interference in elections, urges leaders to respond to global conflicts World Sep 22, 2026 3:35 PM EDT Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Tuesday warned that countries shouldn't interfere in the internal affairs of other nations, while also urging world leaders to take stronger action in response to intensifying global conflicts. The mixed messages came as Lula spoke to the United Nations General Assembly, just before U.S. President Donald Trump addressed the group. Lula criticized external interference in Brazil's internal affairs, only weeks ahead of his country's elections. WATCH: Day 1 of the 2026 United Nations General Assembly "We will not allow the enemies of democracy, whether domestic or foreign, to undermine popular will. Brazilian democracy belongs to Brazilians. Brazil will continue to be a sovereign country," Lula said. "Nobody will turn us away from this path." Lula's speech comes amid escalating tensions between the U.S. and Brazil. Last year, the U.S. imposed an initial round of tariffs, citing what Trump called a "witch hunt" trial against the country's former president, Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest following his conviction for an attempted coup. Since then, relations between the two countries have become further strained, amid growing allegations of foreign interference in October's elections in Brazil, in which Lula is seeking a fourth, nonconsecutive presidential term. His main political rival is Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, one of the sons of the former president. The Trump administration has publicly backed Bolsonaro. Recently, Trump designated two Brazilian criminal groups, the First Command of the Capital, or PCC, and the Red Command, or CV, as foreign terrorist organizations. Lula rejected the decision, and some analysts and politicians have argued that the move could be intended to interfere in the country's election by portraying Lula as soft on organized crime. Speaking to the U.N., Lula said Brazil's electoral system is "modern and robust" and warned against disinformation campaigns seeking to distort public debate during the campaign, noting that "democracy is once again in jeopardy." "Brazil is nobody's backyard," he said. "We are once again witnessing external interference in electoral processes." Lula said Brazil does not underestimate the challenge of organized crime but "will not outsource the responsibility of defending" its own borders. His remarks Tuesday follow the unveiling last Friday of a pilot plan to expand the federal government's role in fighting gang violence in Rio de Janeiro. During his speech, Lula also addressed the Brazilian economy, saying that despite the massive tariffs, the country will break a new export record this year. He says UN's credibility at all-time low Lula started his speech railing against what he called weakness in the U.N.'s actions on wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and called for reform of the U.N. Security Council, saying that in 2025 alone the world "will see the highest number of armed conflicts since World War II" with "trillions of dollars financing a new arms race." "The U.N. is failing in one of its highest missions: to save humanity from the scourge of war," Lula said. "Its credibility has never been lower." Lula said the U.N. must recover its capacity for dialogue and mediation and that it is time to choose between multilateralism or global fragmentation. "Concessions to the law of the stronger have surpassed all limits. This is not idealism, but pure realism," he said. "War is not the continuation of politics by other means; it's the complete breakdown of politics." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. The head of the Inter-American Development Bank said Tuesday the lender is weighing a return to Venezuela after nearly a decade away, but did not say whether Caracasâ unpaid debts would be forgiven.
âAs a development bank, we need to look at Venezuela and look at the Venezuelan people and see if thereâs an opportunity for us to engage,â IDB President Ilan Goldfajn said at Semaforâs The Next 3 Billion, adding that talks on a formal engagement plan are already underway.
Asked about whether the IDB would seek repayment of Venezuelaâs doubts, Goldfajn said only that it was âpart of the conversation.â
The bank halted new loans in 2018 after Venezuela fell behind on its payments, leaving roughly $2 billion outstanding; a planned re-engagement would focus on electricity and social protection, according to Reuters.
The future governance of Venezuela was thrown into doubt after US forces captured President NicolÃ¡s Maduro in Caracas in January. His former vice president, Delcy RodrÃguez, has since taken over as acting president. Ella Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas has overtaken Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history.
Released last October, the bittersweet song details Langley's suspicions that her boyfriend is about to run off with another woman.
It topped the US Billboard chart for the first time in February, and has now spent 23 weeks at number one., external
Choosin' Texas also rose to pole position on the UK singles chart at the start of September, where it replaced Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In.
That song had also spent 23 weeks at number one, making it the UK's longest-running chart-topper.
The immovability of both songs has raised questions about stagnation in the charts, and whether streaming services are doing enough to promote new music.
Langley's song was written at a writing retreat in 2024, with assistance from country star Miranda Lambert.
Unexpectedly, it started with a discussion about a pet kangaroo Lambert had once owned.
"She told me the story about how she got pulled over [by the police] with a kangaroo in the passenger seat and a dog in the back," Langley explained.
The officer was so surprised that she didn't issue a ticket.
Langley responded to Lambert, saying the cop must have known she was from Texas, given the chaos unfolding in the car.
That prompted the lyric, "She's from Texas, I can tell."
Over the next 30 minutes, the writers (who also included Luke Dick and Joybeth Taylor) cooked up a story about a woman in Tennessee, who realises her partner's heart still belongs to Texas... and to another girl.
First previewed on stage in February 2025, Langley said she instantly knew it would become the first single from her sophomore album, Dandelion.
"We loved that song, but I don't think I could ever have imagined what's happening with it right now," the singer told Billboard magazine.
"Every day I wake up and it's doing something that I didn't even know was a goal I could have had. It's crazy, it's nuts."
Its success helped the 27-year-old, who is actually from Alabama, sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May.
She won in all seven categories in which she was nominated, including female artist of the year, artist songwriter of the year, and both single and song of the year, for Choosin' Texas.
Records tumble
It is now one of only two songs to surpass 20 weeks at number one on the US charts - with the other being Mariah Carey's perennial Christmas smash All I Want for Christmas Is You.
But the records for long-running hits have been tumbling ever since streaming became a mainstream phenomenon.
For 23 years, Carey's own One Sweet Day, a duet with Boyz II Men, held the title, notching up 16 weeks at number one.
Daddy Yankee and Luis Fonsi's Despacito remix, featuring Justin Bieber, tied the record in 2017; then Lil Nas X's Old Town Road surpassed it the following year, eventually spending 19 weeks at the top.
All I Want for Christmas Is You eventually overtook that, thanks to its habit of returning to the charts every December.
But critics say that streaming services are increasingly encouraging listeners to play the same playlists of familiar songs over and over again, creating a bottleneck that makes it harder for new music to break through.
In 2022, a report by the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, external found that more than 60% of streams were of music recorded by only the top 0.4% of artists.

A US judge has temporarily blocked the deportation of a Venezuelan man who was shot by immigration agents in Texas, his lawyer says.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, is being held in a detention centre with a bullet in his back, according to his lawyer. Judge Orlando Garcia, a Clinton appointee, scheduled a hearing for Garces Perez to appear in court in person next week.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has said it is investigating the shooting of an illegal migrant in the Texan capital, but have not confirmed he was shot in the back.
It comes months after a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man in Houston.
Garces Perez's immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, has filed a federal lawsuit for a temporary restraining order to prevent his removal from the country.
Since the judge ordered that her client appear in person on 30 September, he cannot be deported before then, she said.
"For now, we have secured a temporary block on his deportation while his case moves forward," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on social media.
"This is an important step, but our work is not over," she wrote. "Wilber still needs appropriate medical care, and we will continue fighting to protect his rights."
The gunshot fractured his clavicle and he is wearing a sling while having "significant swelling and pain," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
The cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced has not yet been determined, she said.
A spokesperson for US Attorney's Office in Texas declined to comment on the case.
Lincoln-Goldfinch previously told the BBC that after being unable to move his arm in the detention facility, Garces Perez was taken back to hospital on Monday evening. He was treated there and has since been returned to the detention facility.
He said he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during his transfer, despite his injury, she said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch added that detention personnel had revoked his communication privileges and moved him from an infirmary into an isolated room with a flat, non-adjustable bed.
The BBC has contacted DHS for comment.
Texas lawmaker Joaquin Castro, a Democrat, on Tuesday demanded the Venezuelan national's release from detention.
Local and state officials have pushed for an independent investigation into the shooting, which occurred just before on Sunday afternoon.
Hours later, dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave the city.
The man's lawyer told US media he was making a DoorDash delivery when an unmarked black truck sideswiped his car.
He did not know the truck was an ICE vehicle and made a U-turn, she said. His car was hit again before agents got out and shot him, according to the attorney.

Amazonâs chief sustainability officer said Tuesday the company needed to âdo betterâ on communicating the environmental impact of its vast data center buildout, amid growing opposition to the projects in the US and Europe.
âThere is a lot of debate, backlash against data centers in this country right now, and one of the things that weâre doing is taking a look at what have we done well and where have we fallen down and what do we need to do better,â Kara Hurst told Semaforâs The Next Three Billion event in New York.
âAnd so, weâre revising a number of our practices. Weâre calling for a lot more transparency and accountability because thatâs what people in these communities deserve. Weâre saying, âhold us accountable for our practices,ââ Hurst said.
Amazonâs carbon footprint grew for the second year in a row in 2025, as the tech giant accelerated its data center buildout, investing $220 billion in capital expenditure in 2026 alone.
But local opposition threatens to hinder tech giantsâ race to build, with data center projects worth some $68 billion delayed or blocked because of local opposition between April and June this year, according to Data Center Watch.
Amazon is looking to publish more metrics tracking its environmental footprint such as the effectiveness of energy and water usage at sites, Hurst said, part of a wider effort to address concerns from environmentalists and communities.
Communities where data centers are built should also get a âreturn on that investment,â Hurst said. âThey should get workforce development, they should get upskilling, they should get economic development.â
Know More
There is currently no national framework in the US requiring hyperscalers to report data centersâ environmental impact.
But Hurst said that voluntary reporting has an advantage over mandated disclosure: It lets companies put data out, have scientists test whether the metrics hold up, and revise the methodology if they donât, rather than locking in a potentially flawed standard.
âWhat we need is to publish data, information thatâs science-led, and to publish it quickly and to put it out there and say, âIs this the right methodology?ââ she said.
The data center race has posed a dilemma for sustainability goals globally. An S&P Global assessment of data center companies globally found that just 15 of the 50 firms surveyed received a passing grade signaling that they would be low-carbon and climate-resilient by 2030.
Amazon has set a goal to be net-zero carbon by 2040, but Hurst said the firm will likely see emissions rise in the near term as the data center buildout heats up.
âWeâve said all along this is not going to be linear,â Hurst said.

Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.
"I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.
The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.
Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.
Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."
Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.
The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.
Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.
"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.

This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.

US President Donald Trump has said he would back proposals to halt American diesel exports in a bid to ease prices for drivers at the pumps.
His comments come after Republicans lawmakers put pressure on the president ahead of November's mid-term elections to curb exports, as diesel prices soar to record highs in the US.
Speaking on the sidelines at the United Nations General Assembly, Trump suggested keeping domestic supplies inside the US could also ease broader petrol prices.
"I've called for that too. I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel. That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline," he said .
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed officials were assessing "whether a full or partial ban would work" without disrupting refinery capabilities.
National average diesel prices surpassed $6.50 (Â£4.87) a gallon on Tuesday according to AAA data, a new high.
The conflict in the Middle East has constrained global oil supplies, putting pressure on pump prices.
The surge in the cost of diesel has sparked political urgency ahead of crucial mid-term elections on 3 November, with several Republicans pressing the administration to restrict the fuel's export to ease financial strain on voters.
US Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for Senate in Iowa, said on Monday that the state's consumers were "being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump."
In Alaska on Tuesday, Senator Dan Sullivan similarly urged for a "temporary pause of American diesel and exports" to rebuild domestic reserves.
Adding to the global market volatility, Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy facilities has knocked out the country's refining capacity.
"It is a serious hit on the Russians," Trump said during a meeting with Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday. "It's also a serious hit on the price of diesel."
Trump confirmed he would discuss the strikes with the Ukrainian president, alongside broader efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict. "I think it's going to happen," he said.
Kyiv has intensified drone attacks on Russian processing plants in recent months to choke off the Kremlin's primary source of war funding.
Because Russia ranks among the world's leading diesel suppliers, reduced refining capacity â combined with Moscow's own strict export bans â has severely squeezed global reserves.
While restricting US exports could offer short-term relief for American drivers, a ban may risk pushing up prices internationally.
The US exports roughly 1.3 million barrels of diesel per day â nearly a quarter of its refining output.
Cutting these shipments could put pressure on supplies for Western allies, including the UK and the Netherlands, which have relied on American fuel to cover deficits left by sanctions on Russian energy.

US President Donald Trump returned to the stage at the United Nations on Tuesday, where he touted his administration's policies in front of world leaders and issued pointed threats to some of those gathered in the room.
The lengthy speech was wide-ranging, covering the war in Iran, AI, Cuba and the role of America's military.
The BBC's correspondents who covered the address have picked five key moments that stood out.
1. Trump pushes message of American power
By Sarah Smith, North America editor in the room
The US president has no great respect for the United Nations â he accused it of imposing a far-left agenda â but he does relish the global platform it gives him.
He used Tuesday's speech to tout his achievements, and claim the mantle of a peacemaker, at the same time as he issued a number of pointed threats.
Iran might be annihilated, lethal strikes on small boats suspected of drug smuggling will continue and the Cuban regime may even be toppled.
The clear message was: America is still prepared to use its military might wherever Trump thinks it might be required to secure its national interests.
Trump said he was "reasserting American power" and flexed what he called the country's "unmatched military might".
"The United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere," he said.
Once again, Trump has made the full-throated assertion to the world of "America First".
2. Cubans walk out as Trump calls nation 'failed state'
By Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter in the room
Trump took aim at one of the US's closest neighbours, Cuba, calling it "an absolutely failed state" and saying his administration has been pursuing "a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba".
"It will fall," he said.
The Cuban delegation walked out of the hall as Trump continued his remarks.
Over the last year, the US president become more vocal in criticising Cuba's communist government. On Tuesday, he said it was under "enormous pressure" and "failing like never before".
The US has not, however, provided a detailed picture of what it believes change will look like in Cuba.
Cuba's foreign minister reacted angrily to Trump's comments and accused the US president of spreading "falsehoods".
"The US government is incapable of accepting that Cuba is and has the right to be a full sovereign and independent country," Bruno Rodriguez wrote on X.
3. A direct threat to 'annihilate' Iran
By Khashayar Joneidi, BBC Persian correspondent in Washington
Trump presented Iran with a stark choice at the UN General Assembly: reach an agreement with Washington and rebuild the country, or face the rapid "annihilation" of the Islamic Republic.
He then again predicted that a deal to end the war would probably follow the US midterm elections in November.
His remarks illustrated Trump's familiar strategy of coercive diplomacy - keeping negotiations open while also threatening overwhelming force.
But his language blurred the distinction between destroying the political system and threatening Iran itself.
International law experts have previously expressed concern at what they called "alarming rhetoric" used by US officials, including Trump himself, who has posted that the US might "obliterate" Iran's power plants.
References on Tuesday to leaving "no chance of survival" and "no hope" for future generations will likely have stoked similar alarm. There is also an irony in delivering this warning at the United Nations, an organisation founded to save future generations from war.
Yet the speech was not a declaration that diplomacy has failed.
It was an attempt to define the terms of possible negotiations: the US remains prepared to make a deal, but only under the shadow of an existential threat.
4. Trump hails new Greenland security deal
By Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter in the room
Trump also praised a new deal with Greenland under which he said the US would build two military bases in the Arctic territory.
"We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe," he said of the deal, which he first announced on Friday.
He added that it "very much enhances" the defence alliance Nato.
The US, Denmark and Greenland held a joint signing ceremony at the UN shortly after Trump's address.
Although Greenland is a semi-autonomous territory, it is part of the Kingdom of Denmark which primarily handles its foreign policy.
Trump administration officials are already hailing the agreement as enhancing US security at minimal cost - and with relationships intact.
Denmark and Greenland's governments, however, will be hoping it ends the long-simmering disagreement that began when Trump threatened to take Greenland by force.
That threat shook the Nato alliance and sorely tested the US-Danish relationship.
Few clear details about the nature of the deal have been confirmed publicly, and given Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, some analysts are viewing it as a quiet win for diplomacy.
5. An attempted rebrand of AI
By Nada Tawfik, New York correspondent at the UN
Trump has a penchant for branding, and in his speech he gave Artificial Intelligence a new name: Super Intelligence.
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful."
"Welcome to the new world of Super Intelligence - SI," he added.
Trump has previously argued that the US must come out on top in the AI development race, saying last week: "Whoever wins AI, wins."
The president is firmly against government regulation or introducing new guardrails - and that puts him at odds with many of those gathered at the UN.
For those who are calling for regulation, the question is whether the slow pace of diplomacy can keep up with AI's rapid development.

3c25d6671800.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/air-traffic-control-calamity-disrupts-hundreds-of-u-s-flights-spotlighting-the-aging-system Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Air traffic control calamity disrupts hundreds of U.S. flights, spotlighting the aging system Nation Sep 22, 2026 5:49 PM EDT Communications failures that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast on Monday have put the spotlight back on the aging systems that air traffic controllers rely on in the U.S. Congress already handed the Federal Aviation Administration $12.5 billion last year to overhaul technology after the deadliest U.S. plane crash in more than two decades killed 67 people when an American Airlines flight collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter over the Potomac River and a series of radar outages later that spring led to widespread cancellations at Newark Liberty International Airport. WATCH: House approves aviation safety bill The same Philadelphia facility that had the radar outages in the spring of 2025 lost both its primary and backup data lines at the same time on Monday. But that regional air traffic control center isn't alone; similar communications outages have also disrupted flights in Minneapolis and Dallas over the past year. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy quickly turned Monday's disruption that hit every major airport in the New York area into the latest example of why he's asking Congress for $20 billion more to pay for the next phase of the air traffic control overhaul. Airlines were working to recover from the outage on Tuesday, but FlightAware.com showed nearly 100 flights had been canceled by midday because a number of planes and crews were out of position after Monday's cancellations. "I need new money to do a whole new design — a new architecture of telecom so it will never go down." The aviation industry's Modern Skies Coalition backed Duffy's plan again and urged Congress to approve the money because the latest disruptions "demonstrate how critical it is to replace the antiquated technology and outdated systems that underpin our nation's air traffic control infrastructure." Both the primary and backup lines failed on Monday A switch on the primary communications line at the regional FAA air traffic control facility in Philadelphia failed Monday morning, but when it turned to the backup fiber optic line authorities discovered that it had been inadvertently severed by railroad construction workers. More than 200 flights into and out of Philadelphia International Airport were also canceled, while disruptions hit LaGuardia and Kennedy airports in New York. Flights had resumed by Monday evening. Technical problems that affect Newark Liberty Airport tend to get outsized attention because it's a key hub for United Airlines. The Dallas outage last September disrupted American Airlines' key hub, and last month's communications failure at a regional air traffic control facility in Minneapolis halted flights across several Midwestern states and led to numerous diversions and delays. Problems at key regional control facilities affect flights nationwide Sheldon Jacobson, whose research contributed to the design of the TSA PreCheck system, said the FAA needs to make sure that its backup systems are independent of the primary line to reduce the chance that both will fail at the same time. And he said maybe the agency should look at adding a third line to have an additional backup system. He will also relay âthe gravity of the moment that weâre in, and a recognition that these models really are displaying capabilities that are strategically significant,â she added.
Know More
Bakerâs remarks came amid concerns that advanced AI models could be turned into potent hacking tools, capable of finding and exploiting unknown security flaws with little human direction.
OpenAI earlier this month launched Astra, its first model designated as being âcybercritical.â
Baker said there are no current plans to leverage the model to allow the US government to do offensive cybersecurity work, like proactive attacks on adversaries.
âWeâ¦ acknowledge that in the wrong hands it could be used for offensive cyber,â she said. âThat is not something that weâre provisioning models for right now.â

ae85eb3828e2.text: By — Caleb McCullough, PolitiFact Caleb McCullough, PolitiFact By — Louis Jacobson, PolitiFact Louis Jacobson, PolitiFact By — Loreben Tuquero, PolitiFact Loreben Tuquero, PolitiFact By — Samantha Putterman, PolitiFact Samantha Putterman, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/fact-checking-trumps-speech-to-the-2026-united-nations-general-assembly Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Fact-checking Trump's speech to the 2026 United Nations General Assembly Politics Sep 22, 2026 5:37 PM EDT This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. In his address to the United Nations General Assembly, President Donald Trump defended the United States' robust use of military force in Iran, Venezuela and elsewhere, saying the international community is incapable of handling threats from those countries. WATCH: Trump addresses 2026 United Nations General Assembly Undaunted by polls that show Americans tiring of the nearly-seven-month Iran war and its impact on fuel prices, Trump said in the Sept. 22 speech that the U.S. is "settling years of unfinished business. And we're doing it well." He also brushed off concerns that rapid advances in artificial intelligence could endanger humanity, saying the U.S. "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control artificial intelligence." Members of the Cuban and Iranian delegations walked out at points during Trump's speech. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was traveling to address the General Assembly on Sept. 23 — an unusual visit by a leader of a country at war with the U.S. Here are fact-checks of some of Trump's statements. Artificial intelligence "The very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming … These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all. … This is the group that came up with the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax, the Ukraine, Ukraine, Ukraine hoax, climate change, open borders." Although some anti-AI groups may have overlaps with advocates concerned about climate change, alarms over AI are not confined to one group of people. The loudest warnings of late have come from the top of the industry itself. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a Sept. 12 essay urging a slower pace of developing AI capability. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind Cofounder and Chair Demis Hassabis and xAI founder Elon Musk agreed with Amodei, a rare concurrence in the competitive tech industry. U.S. lawmakers from both parties have introduced legislation to regulate AI. On artificial intelligence, "We're leading now over China by a lot." The U.S. has a lead over China in model capability, but key AI industry leaders and experts have said China is only a few months behind. U.S. models have rapidly become more powerful, leading to multiple safety breaches, and AI leaders are calling for a slowdown. The gap between the U.S. and China could shrink if development proceeds more slowly in the U.S., but China continues apace. "From this point forward, all United States documents and hopefully the world's will be changed to use the much more accurate term 'super' as opposed to artificial. So it's superintelligence. In other words, welcome to the new world of superintelligence — SI." Superintelligence is a specific term in the field of AI, but those in the industry say it's not an accurate description of currently available AI systems. WATCH: Trump dismisses concerns about AI risks at UN, says he won't rein it in Superintelligence is generally understood by industry experts as an AI system that is far ahead of human intelligence at nearly all cognitive tasks, including scientific research and communications. A recent paper from Google's AI lab, Deepmind, defined artificial superintelligence, or ASI, as "an artificial general intelligence that has superhuman abilities across virtually all tasks and domains of human interest and activity." Current AI systems excel at coding, math, and a lot of complex cognitive tasks. But they have limitations that place them well behind superintelligence. A 2026 international AI safety report describes current AI's performance to be "jagged across tasks and contexts." U.S. involvement in wars, conflicts "The cowards and traitors would love to say the United States is low on munitions, but that's not true. We have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we're building them at levels that we have never done before." This is misleading. Several news and expert reports have found that U.S. weapons stockpiles are rapidly decreasing as the Iran war continues. A May analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a national security-focused think tank, projected that certain heavily-used munitions in the Iran war — such as the Tomahawk missile system and Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense interceptors that defend against missiles and drones — will take about three to four years to replenish. In July, NBC News reported that the U.S. military was rationing munitions and allowing some Iranian attacks because of the diminishing stockpile. Defense experts have said that aid to Ukraine under President Joe Biden's administration also reduced the United States' weapons reserve. The Biden administration started a process to expand production and replenish the stockpile, something the Trump administration has accelerated. "The United States has carried out dozens of strikes on cartel drug boats, destroying 97% of the drugs coming into the ocean and sea." False. Air and marine drug seizures have dropped since the strikes began in September 2025, but the administration hasn't provided a clear link. The Coast Guard, which oversees most drug seizures on water, recorded a 200% increase in seizures in fiscal year 2025 compared with other annual averages. Seizures show how many drugs are stopped from entering the U.S., not how many drugs are being sent to the U.

El Nino is part of a natural climate cycle of warming ocean temperatures, but this year's is expected to reach new extremes of drought, heat waves, flooding and other climate-related disruptions in South America, Africa and Asia. Southeast Asia is one of the world's most climate vulnerable regions. It's already beset by an energy crisis triggered by the war in Iran. El Nino is already fueling wildfires across farmland, depleting water supplies for major cities and hurting fish catches in the region. WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns Asian governments that have been drawing on their financial reserves to mitigate the war's ripple effects of higher energy costs and scarce fertilizer supplies have less capacity to cope with this year's intensifying El Nino, which is forecast to peak in December. The phenomenon may amplify other crises in Southeast Asia, according to Paul Teng, with Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, who said, "El Nino is only compounding all the other problems that we see." Extreme El Nino may threaten global food security During El Nino years, sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean are warmer than usual. This happens every few years and often alters global weather patterns. This year, the seas already are hotter than average, with global oceans hitting new temperature records in August as the climate warms, said Kareff Rafisura, chief of the Disaster Risk Reduction Division at the U.N. Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific. This intensifying El Nino may be the "strongest in living memory," according to the United Kingdom's national weather and climate service. Similarly, the U.S.' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said there is a 69% chance that this will be the strongest recorded El Nino since record-keeping began in 1950. El Nino's impact will be felt differently across regions, but it is expected to jeopardize food security worldwide. It could push at least 49 million more people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, according to the United Nations' World Food Program. The problem will be worst in parts of Central America and southern Africa, with significant effects also anticipated in eastern Africa and South and Southeast Asia, warned the food agency. "I would have rather not moved. There were plenty of livelihood opportunities here," said Hussen, who only uses one name, as he ferried people across the receding reservoir. This is just the beginning, said Erma Yulihastin with Indonesia's Research Center for Climate and Atmosphere, who warned El Nino has only just begun its "super phase." Southeast Asia's fisheries brace for drought Less rainfall and hotter temperatures are putting pressure on Southeast Asia's fisheries, an essential source of protein. It's a pressing problem along the Mekong, a river basin that flows through six nations and is being disrupted by mining and construction of hydropower dams. "It's one punch after another," said Zeb Hogan, with the University of Nevada, Reno, who runs the research and conservation project, Wonders of the Mekong. "If the river doesn't catch a break, we will reach a point where it's no longer going to sustain people in the way that it always has." Lower flows are especially hard on communities along the Mekong that depend on predictable water levels for fishing and farming, said Kongmeng Ly, with the Mekong River Commission, an intergovernmental group for Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. Rice and palm oil supplies are at risk Southeast Asia's wet season generally runs from June to October, when rains usually replenish reservoirs, cool overheated cities and supply water for irrigation ahead of the next planting season. Drought may force farmers to delay planting, reduce acreage or switch crops entirely, said Rafisura, with the U.N. "Agriculture is definitely on the front line," she said. Burnham 'gets it' says Trump, as the two leaders meet for first time
Andy Burnham and Donald Trump have been speaking to reporters at their first face-to-face meeting in New York.
The US president said he could do business with the UK prime minister, but criticised the "terrible" Chagos deal.

- Published
Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.
The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.
The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship".
"We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."
Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".
Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).
He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."
The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.
Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".
He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.
His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.
Torpedo exercise
For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history.
In advance of the meeting, the UK revealed that the UK and the US have, for the first time, fired an American torpedo from a British undersea drone in a military exercise.
The torpedo, described as "heavyweight" by UK officials, is "designed to sink ships and deep diving submarines", Downing Street said.
It was launched in UK waters last week from a 12-metre long undersea drone called Excalibur, made in Plymouth.
It is the first time either the UK or the US have launched a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, rather than a crewed submarine, and is seen as a breakthrough in attempts to protect vital infrastructure such as deep sea data cables.
"Our work together already shows what can be achieved when our two countries combine our expertise and innovation," the prime minister said.
Burnham was also asked by reporters about the UK government seeking to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.
It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.
Burnham spoke to the Mauritian prime minister, Navin Ramgoolam, on Monday.
He was asked by reporters to outline what he had told Ramgoolam, whether he supported the deal and if he had a plan to convince Trump to back it.
Burnham replied: "I said that we remain determined to secure the long-term operation of the base, which is crucial to our security and that of our allies.
"The assurance I gave was I will work towards a resolution, at the moment we don't have that, but I gave an assurance that I would commit to working towards one."

The News
Republicans are running away from the Iran war and scrambling to curtail high gas prices as they try to keep hold of Congress â and even some who arenât up for reelection are breaking with the Trump administration in high-profile fashion.
Itâs a critical moment for the congressional GOP as the Senate prepares to empty out for election season as soon as this week, joining their House colleagues on the fall campaign trail. But as they do so, there are growing instances of daylight between President Donald Trump and the Republican Party he leads, a notable trend after so many months of muted criticism.
Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, is pushing for an investigation of Donald Trump Jr. over his business dealings while Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., reprimanded Trump for inviting Chinese leader Xi Jinping to Washington for a formal state visit this week. And looming over it all is the nearly seven-month Iran war, which is starting to generate public friction with swing state Republicans across the country. This week, Democrats are seeking to make the Senate vote on curtailing the conflict one last time before the election.
On Monday, Michigan Republican Senate candidate  Mike Rogers along with Iowa GOP Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, called for an end to the Iran war. They were joined by Rep. John James, a Republican running for governor of Michigan, and endangered Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio.
âItâs not popular. They are in tough elections. People understand the need to have a safe nation but we also understand the need to resolve this conflict,â retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, told Semafor of her Iowa colleagues. âThe administration hasnât been clear on how to end this and I think thatâs why people are moving.â
Ernst said sheâll âprobablyâ continue voting against the Democratic-led efforts to rein in the conflict, though she wants a âclear understandingâ of the path forward.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., another retiring swing state senator, said heâd seen enough. He said the war had âmeandered for too longâ and urged GOP candidates to take the same position if thatâs what their political predicaments demand.
âThere are so many headwinds now for these candidates that I hope that the administration gets the point that you can be 90% with the president and speak about the 10% youâre not. So I think youâre seeing that distance,â Tillis said. âYouâve got a lot of people out there that want to vote for Republicans, but theyâre a little uncomfortable with one issue or another, the presidentâs tone, whatever.â
Curtis and Wicker gave Republicans further cover to find that distance. Curtis asked the Senate Judiciary Committee to subpoena both Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden, declaring that reports on Trump Jr.âs wedding and business deals raise âlegitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting presidentâs family.â Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, declined to comment on that request.
Wicker didnât mince words about Xiâs visit, calling Xi a âbrutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directlyâ at the United States.
Know More
Most Senate Republicans in competitive races like Husted, Dan Sullivan of Alaska, and Roger Marshall of Kansas have backed the Iran war on the Senate floor. Sullivan also threw his support behind a diesel export ban â prompting Trump himself to back it. But a few, like Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, have voted to rein in Trumpâs conflict.
Miller-Meeks and Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa, both voted last week against the war. Both Rogers and James had sounded significantly more supportive of the war earlier this year but said they want to end it this week.
âWe all want it to end as quickly as possible. I think theyâre being bold and theyâre being direct,â said Sen. Ted Budd, R-N.C., of Republican candidates. âYou have to be in sync with people in your state to get elected â in an authentic way. I think people genuinely want the war to be over; that doesnât mean you quit, you bring it to a successful resolution.â
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he was hoping he could keep Republicans from splintering on Iran right before the election: âI would hope the team could hang together on this.â
The View From the white house
Trump has repeatedly threatened to escalate the conflict only to predict a deal is close at hand. He said during his speech at the UN General Assembly that he has a âbig decisionâ to make on Iran. He can either cut a deal that helps Iran rebuild and ends the war, or, Trump suggested, he could âannihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly.â
Burgessâs view
Republicans have wanted the war to end basically since it started, but are reluctant to cross the president publicly. Thatâs clearly starting to change, but itâs one thing to criticize the war and another to vote against it.
Thatâs what makes Miller-Meeks and Nunnâs votes so interesting. And if Senate Republicans with similar views really want to show voters they oppose the war, their best chance to do so is to vote against it.
