On a hot July afternoon this year, electricity generated from renewable energy briefly met over half of India's peak power demand - only the second time this happened. The first instance was around the same period a year ago.
While it was only briefly that power generated from solar, wind, hydro and nuclear sources collectively outstripped coal-based output, it was a milestone moment reflecting the astonishing growth of non-fossil fuels to the country's electricity mix over the last decade.
"It showed that renewable energy is no longer a marginal source sitting at the edge of the power system," Sumant Sinha, CEO of ReNew Power, one of India's largest Nasdaq-listed clean energy companies, told the BBC.
To be sure, coal-based power plants still continue to generate 70% of India's electricity on average because they run on a higher load factor, or for more hours than solar or wind. Yet, the country's push for clean energy appears to have reached a crucial inflection point.
A decade ago India's installed renewable energy capacity was barely 4GW. It now makes up 300GW or 54% of its total 552GW installed capacity, external - a target that's been achieved five years ahead of schedule.
For a nation long seen as the poster child for dirty coal dependence, this rapid transition points to a remarkable achievement in decarbonising its grid.
Yet, the gains are tempered by some serious challenges.
Foremost among them is a shortage of grid capacity. The renewables' build out has significantly outpaced transmission infrastructure, a point of major concern for policymakers.
"In the first quarter of 2026, transmission constraints accounted for nearly two-thirds of all renewable energy curtailment at 300 gigawatt-hours (GWh)," according to Ember, a global energy think-tank.
Put simply, that means a bulk of the clean energy that was produced in India was wasted because the country's transmission lines have been dogged by missed targets, with one out of four inter-state projects facing delays of over a year.
The difficulty lies in matching the speed of generation projects with the grid build-out, says Sinha.
"Generation projects can be constructed in 18-24 monthsâ¦ Transmission can take much longer because they involve right-of-way, land acquisition, approvals and coordination across many agencies. It is an execution issue that becomes more important as the system gets larger," he adds.
Vibhuti Garg of the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis also blames "poor planning" for the problem.
The grid was able to absorb new capacity as long as India was generating 10-15GW annually, she told the BBC. But that pace has dramatically increased, reaching a record 51GW last year, and the infrastructure is no longer able to cope.
The concentration of renewables projects in the north-western states of Gujarat and Rajasthan has also compounded the challenge of evacuating power in the face of such grid shortages.
Analysts at Ember now believe this growing mismatch between fast-moving generation projects and slower-moving transmission infrastructure, is the "most critical operational risk to the country's 2030 target of 500 gigawatts (GW) of non-fossil electricity".
A quick solution to addressing this gap would have been to build battery storage systems at renewable pooling stations to integrate the power into the grid.
"Had that been the case, India could have stored the energy and used it during evening hours rather than wasting it," says Garg.
But storage capacity has not grown because of a huge jump in the price of batteries, raw material shortages due to the war in the Middle East and a fall in the value of the Indian currency which has jacked up financing costs for Indian companies.
"Many storage projects that were meant to come up fell through as a result," Garg adds.
Yet, finance isn't a constraint merely for storage projects but an industry wide problem.
While ample global capital is available for green transition across the developed world, getting access to it remains a persistent struggle for Indian clean energy companies, despite the strides that the country has made in its renewables commitments.
Estimates suggest the country will require $400-$500bn to meet its 500GW renewables target by 2030, external. But currently, around 83% of India's finance for climate mitigation is sourced domestically, according to the government's economic survey. While the Paris Agreement clearly mandated developed countries to provide financial resources to the tune of $100bn annually up to 2025 to developing countries for their climate action, that money has been hard to get.
"Emerging and developing economies outside China receive only around 15% of global clean-energy investment, despite accounting for roughly two-thirds of the world's population," says Sinha.
According to him, while India does not necessarily need developed countries to finance its entire transition, help is needed in the form of cheaper loans, guarantees and protection against currency losses so that private investors are encouraged to put in more money into the space.
Plugging these critical gaps in finance, transmission infrastructure and storage will be critical given this transition is under way at a pivotal moment, say experts.
India is the world's third largest emitter of greenhouse gases and facing a sharp rise in electricity demand, which has grown at a compounded rate of over 7% every year. It is expected to further accelerate with the expansion of industries like data centres and chip manufacturing.
The International Energy Agency, external predicts India's electricity demand will increase by 80% by 2035, the sharpest jump among emerging economies. It also credits the country's robust expansion of its renewables as a major contributor for slowing emissions in the developed world this year, even as energy related CO2 emissions rose more strongly in advanced economies for the first time since the 1990s.

94749f9f7a2f.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/fall-has-officially-arrived-heres-what-to-know-about-the-autumnal-equinox Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Fall has officially arrived. Here's what to know about the autumnal equinox Science Sep 22, 2026 6:31 PM EDT The fall equinox is Tuesday, when light and darkness split the day evenly. It marks the beginning of fall for the Northern Hemisphere and the beginning of spring in the Southern Hemisphere. On the equator, the sun will be directly overhead at noon. Equinoxes are the only times when both the north and south poles are lit by sunshine at the same time. READ MORE: Worsening El Nino threatens Asia with severe drought, potentially threatening global food security Equinoxes have been marked and celebrated around the world for centuries. Japan marks public holidays during the equinoxes. At the Mayan site Chichen Itza in Mexico, people gather during the equinox to watch the sun create a shadow pattern that resembles a serpent descending a pyramid called El Castillo. Here's what to know about the Earth's orbit. What is the equinox? As the Earth travels around the sun, it does so at an angle, making the sun's warmth and light fall unequally on the northern and southern halves of the planet for most of the year. During the equinox, the Earth's tilt is neither toward the sun nor away from the sun, so both the Northern and Southern hemispheres get an equal amount of sunlight. The sun rises almost exactly due east, and it sets almost exactly due west. The word equinox comes from two Latin words meaning equal and night. That's because on the equinox, day and night last almost the same amount of time — though one may get a few extra minutes, depending on where you are on the planet. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Northern Hemisphere's fall — or autumnal — equinox can land between Sept. 21 and 24, depending on the year. This year it is Tuesday at 8:05 p.m. Eastern time. Its spring — or vernal — equinox can land between March 19 and 21. The exact time of the equinox is the moment the sun is directly overhead at the equator. What is the solstice? The solstices mark the times when the Earth is tipped most extremely either toward or away from the sun. This means the hemispheres are getting very different amounts of sunlight, and days and nights are at their most unequal. At the Northern Hemisphere's summer solstice, the Earth's upper half is leaning toward the sun, creating the longest day and shortest night of the year. The summer solstice falls between June 20 and 22. The opposite happens at the Northern Hemisphere's winter solstice: the Earth's upper half leans the furthest away from the sun, leading to the shortest day and longest night of the year. The winter solstice falls between Dec. 20 and 23. What's the difference between meteorological and astronomical seasons? These are just two different ways to carve up the year. While astronomical seasons depend on how the Earth moves around the sun, meteorological seasons are defined by the weather. Meteorologists break down the year into three-month seasons based on annual temperature cycles. By that calendar, spring starts on March 1, summer on June 1, fall on Sept. 1 and winter on Dec. 1. b23b5b42feeb.text: A notorious cybercrime group is claiming they stole more than 2 terabytes of data that includes detailed personal information about thousands of FBI employees and job applicants. Why it matters : Cybercriminals and state-sponsored attackers have penetrated U.S. IT systems for years, but stealing detailed and sensitive information about FBI employees is brazen, cyber experts told Axios. Cybercriminals are known to trade leaked information on the dark web, a prospect that would leave the data up for grabs from the highest bidder. Driving the news : ShinyHunters, a group that's broken into numerous institutions, said in a post on its dark-web site Tuesday that it stole "very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job." An FBI spokesperson said in a statement the bureau is "aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating." What to watch : Cynthia Kaiser, a former top official in the FBI's cyber division, told Axios that when a hacker targets the FBI, expect the bureau "to marshal additional resources to bring them more quickly to justice." The big picture : While the breach is likely to bring more law enforcement attention to ShinyHunters in the short term, the long tail impact is greater on the FBI employees and their families whose information was stolen, Allan Liska, a threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future, told Axios. "The data is out there and has likely been repeatedly downloaded and passed around to other threat actors," Liska said. Axios has not been able to corroborate that the data stolen is legitimate or recent, but cybersecurity researchers confirmed that the attack appears legitimate. 404 Media obtained a sample of the stolen data, which appears to include information about 5,000 alleged agents. Zoom in : ShinyHunters told Axios in an email that the stolen data includes names, FBI agent statuses, emails, phone numbers, home addresses and "sometimes even spouse information," including their Social Security numbers. The group also claims it broke into the FBI's criminal justice, HR and other services. ShinyHunters also said it seized and defaced the FBI's jobs webpage via a zero-day in Oracle's PeopleSoft platform. The site was still offline as of Tuesday afternoon. Screenshot: FBI career page on Sept. 22. Catch up quick : ShinyHunters says its hack is not financially motivated. Instead, the group is pushing the FBI to retract statements it made about how ShinyHunters operates. In a May advisory , the FBI warned the hackers "commonly use harassment strategies, sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members, and in some cases, swatting." ShinyHunters claims this isn't true and told Axios that it believes these claims have been tied to their group because "other low-skilled threat actors" have been using the group's name in their attacks. Threat level: Andrew Brandt, principal threat intelligence incident commander at Huntress, told Axios that a major concern is over whether ShinyHunters chooses to sell the data to other criminal or nation-state hackers. "It doesn't take much imagination to picture scenarios where employees or their families could be threatened or harmed by this kind of information being released," Brandt said.

1906702651d8.text: Congressional Republicans are increasingly breaking with an unpopular president on foreign policy and pocketbook issues as they try to stop their majorities from slipping away. Why it matters: They aren't engaged in a full-scale revolt against President Trump, but some Republicans are testing new ways to distance themselves from him — a sign of their election anxiety. Driving the news: Trump — facing a barrage of demands from Republican lawmakers to impose a ban on diesel exports — pulled a rare about-face Tuesday, saying on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York that he'll support a ban. Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), along with Iowa GOP Reps. Ashley Hinson and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, were among those calling for a ban to ease skyrocketing diesel costs for U.S. farmers and truckers. Sullivan and Hinson are in tight Senate races. Just on Tuesday: Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) railed on the Senate floor at Trump's decision to host Chinese President Xi Jinping this week for a state dinner. Wicker urged Trump to "keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly" at the U.S. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) called for the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. over his foreign business dealings and the hundreds of thousands of dollars he allegedly received from a Russian oligarch for his wedding. "If your family's involved in the [presidency], then you ought to be very transparent," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), a close Trump ally, told Axios last week when asked about the reporting on Trump Jr.'s wedding. On Iran: The Senate is expected to vote this week on a war powers resolution. Leadership can't guarantee it won't get the Republican votes needed to pass. "We're constantly, of course, checking," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said. "But I would hope that you know the team could hang together on this." The House passed a war powers resolution last week in a rebuke to Trump's military campaign against Tehran — with the most Republican support yet. Both Hinson and Michigan's Republican Senate candidate, former Rep. Mike Rogers, have called for the war to end. On the trail: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) told Trump his immigration crackdown has gone too far in a new campaign ad shot in front of the White House. "I think she's saying what a lot of my constituents are thinking," Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost his primary in May amid opposition from Trump, told Axios. In Iowa, Hinson recently skipped a rally put on by Vice President Vance. And Florida's GOP gubernatorial candidate, Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), deleted at least eight mentions of Trump from his campaign website, the Miami Herald reported. The bottom line: Trump's approval ratings have hit record lows at the worst possible time for Republicans — and that's reflected in lawmakers' willingness to publicly challenge him. "Members are generally reflecting their base. If they really feel that way, they should say so," retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) told reporters Tuesday of the GOP opposition to the Iran war. "And the administration should let these people be whoever they are to win the race."

Two divergent worldviews emerged from the first two national addresses on the opening day of the United Nations General Assembly’s 81st session in New York.
Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva called for decarbonizing economies, protecting forests and supporting the energy transition through technology transfer. U.S. President Donald Trump followed with a rejection of global climate and artificial intelligence regulations, dismissing warnings about global warming while presenting fossil fuel abundance and technological supremacy as foundations of national power.
This year’s General Assembly session is taking place against a slew of global challenges supercharged by geopolitical rivalries and rising planetary warming. June was the second-warmest on record globally and the hottest Western Europe ever measured. A potentially record-breaking El Niño is expected to peak around December, raising fears of drought, crop failures and global food-price shocks.
In the U.S., surging AI data center growth is triggering expensive fossil-fuel generation and grid upgrades, raising electricity bills. Meanwhile, the U.S.-Iran conflict has spread through the region, with clashes between Houthi and Saudi forces further roiling global oil markets already constrained by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
Lula framed climate policy, forest protection and technology regulation as necessary parts of a rule‑based, multilateral effort to reduce emissions and manage systemic risks. He said the planet is facing a shared, urgent climate emergency that demands decarbonization and environmental protection—not delay or denial. He called for nations to “resume the offensive and inflict a defeat on denialism,” and warned that “the glaciers in the Himalayas are melting” and “torrential rains and forest fires” are already here. The impacts, Lula said, “will hit the most vulnerable the hardest.”
He presented Brazil as proof that countries can “combine economic value with reduced emissions,” and pledged to “move forward by the roadmap for the decarbonization of the Brazilian economy.” In his view, forests and ecosystems are climate assets worth protecting and technology, including AI, must be governed and restrained, calling it an “unprecedented technological revolution with great risks and opportunities.” Lula insisted it would be an “unforgivable historical mission not to address the challenge of regulating the big techs and artificial intelligence” and criticized “technical oligarchies without rules or transparency” that bypass the U.N. and scientific oversight.
Trump presented an almost opposite worldview by downplaying climate change, celebrating fossil fuel expansion and attacking global climate regulation. He mocked those who warned about global warming as “the very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming, a name since reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead.”
Trump claimed his administration had stopped what he called an international “global carbon tax” on shipping, insisting “there is no global government, and while I’m president, there will be no global taxes.” Rather than talking about emissions or a just energy transition, he boasted that American energy is fueling the planet and claimed that the U.S. and Venezuela together hold “more than 60 percent of the oil in the world.” This alone, he said, will drive down energy costs.
On technology, he rejected any “globalist scheme to control” AI, rebranding it as “super-intelligence” and pledged his administration will “only encourage superintelligence.” On the whole, Trump’s roughly 35-minute speech treated carbon taxes, climate regulations and global tech governance as threats to sovereignty and growth, and presented fossil fuels and technological dominance as core tenets of national strength.
Environmental advocates, climate scientists and experts reacted sharply to those remarks and challenged Trump’s assertions on climate change and high energy costs.

“The science is clear: fossil fuel-driven climate change is already causing significant harm and these harms will only grow if we fail to sharply curtail heat-trapping emissions and invest in resilience,” Cleetus said.

So we're going to encourage it, not rein it in. 4fe2f9a32f90.text: As President Trump fights the press over coverage, the White House launched its own 24/7 streaming channel — Trump TV. Why it matters: Trump TV gives the president a White House-run video platform to reach the public without relying on traditional news organizations. So far, Trump TV resembles a round-the-clock presidential highlight reel more than a news network. Driving the news: Trump TV launched the same day major TV networks suspended White House pool coverage — a protest that left one Trump speech airing without sound. The White House had teased the channel through cryptic videos , and it went live on its YouTube account, WhiteHouse.gov and the official White House app. Reality check: Presidents have long used White House platforms to share speeches and events with the public. What we know about Trump TV How it works: The channel launched as "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station." "Trump TV is a 24/7 livestream of the Administration's greatest hits, unfiltered," Kaelan Dorr, deputy assistant to the president, wrote on X . So far, the channel has shown curated clips of past Trump speeches and executive actions, along with live events. Catch up quick: The initial programming included Trump's July 3 Mount Rushmore speech before shifting into footage of his 2025 inauguration, per multiple reports . The Daily Beast reports 8,500 viewers were watching the stream during its first hour. Around 1,200 people were watching Tuesday afternoon as the channel aired a Trump health care announcement from August, according to an Axios review of the stream. Zoom in: The stream can also carry live events. On Tuesday, the stream carried Vice President Vance's briefing on fraud claims. But while Trump addressed the United Nations General Assembly Tuesday morning, Trump TV was replaying an earlier speech from the National Prayer Breakfast. Unanswered questions about Trump TV What we're watching: So far, Trump TV has no anchors, news ticker or headline chyrons. The stream includes banners asking viewers to text White House officials. It's unclear who staffs the channel, makes programming decisions or sets its schedule. What they're saying: A White House official tells Axios that the channel's purpose is to replay Trump's "greatest hits that the media fails to cover fairly, oftentimes on purpose." The intrigue: The White House's revamped livestream page labels its regular feed "CH 45" and Trump TV "CH 47" — references to Trump serving as the 45th and 47th president. Trump's previous streaming ventures Flashback: Trump has experimented with direct-to-audience video before. In 2016, Trump's presidential campaign launched a nightly Facebook Live show called "Trump Tower Live" that was meant to deliver campaign messaging directly to the public. Trump Media's Truth+ offers 24/7 news streams and on-demand entertainment. It appears on Truth+ apps and remains a commercial streaming service rather than an official government stream. The service began rolling out in 2024. Its lineup has included broadcasts of Newsmax, OAN and Real America's Voice.

38d409c05c99.text:
'Super Intelligence': the president’s new term for AI, explained
A look at President Donald Trump’s relabel from artificial intelligence to ‘Super intelligence,’ and the phrase’s original meaning
President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced a rebranding of the term “artificial intelligence,” saying during the United Nations General Assembly that from now on, it will be called “super intelligence.”
“From this point forward, all of United States’ documents, and hopefully the world’s, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, ‘super,’ as opposed to ‘artificial’,” he said.
Though the rebrand may have been a surprise to many, superintelligence is already an established term in AI literature. It was popularized in philosopher Nick Bostrom’s 2014 bestseller Superintelligence, which defines the term as “any intellect that greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest.” Artificial superintelligence, or ASI, thus refers to future AI systems that could be much smarter than humans, and contrasts with the weaker forms of AI that exist today.
ASI is a step beyond AGI, or artificial general intelligence, which OpenAI defines as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.” By this definition, today’s AI isn’t AGI yet, much less ASI, since we can’t yet hire AI as a reliable virtual employee.
Some experts dislike the term superintelligence, or question whether it’s a coherent concept. In the influential 2025 paper “AI as Normal Technology,” authors Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan write, “We do not think there is a useful sense of the term ‘intelligence’ in which AI is more intelligent than people acting with the help of AI.”
But others say the possible renaming contributes to an ongoing conversation about AI’s growing abilities.
“‘Super’ does align well with the fact that AI is exceeding human capabilities in a growing range of tasks and by increasing margins, which can have distinct national security implications beyond simply matching human performance,” said Caleb Withers, a research associate for the Technology and Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
For example, in early September, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, one of the most important open problems in math.
As AI becomes more capable, it has grown increasingly central to the U.S.-China relationship. Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping are slated to meet this week to discuss trade and AI issues. Bostrom, who has warned of the dangers of fully superintelligent AI systems, said an all-out AI race increases the risk that the technology gets out of control. “If competitors are convinced that coming second [in the AI race] means the total loss of everything they care about, they will take whatever risk necessary to bypass their rivals,” he said.
Trump reportedly worries that an AI slowdown could cause a market crash, and sees “super intelligence” as a critical sector for America to stay ahead of China. “Whoever wins AI, you have to remember this, and now I say, whoever wins SI, whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins.”

Some 175,000 people in Indonesia have suffered from respiratory illness since August, its health ministry said, as it continues to battle wildfires that have raged for weeks.
More than 40,000 cases â which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia â involve toddlers.
Forest fires have blanketed parts of the country as well as neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore in toxic smog, pushing air quality indices into "unhealthy" territory.
Indonesia has deployed more than 54,000 officials and dozens of jets to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra for water bombing, but the vast territory and challenging peatland conditions make it hard to put out the fires, authorities say.
"From the air to the ground, all forces continue to move," Indonesia's Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said on Monday.
"Everything is being done to extinguish the fires, reduce the impact of the smoke, and, most importantly, protect the public from the threat of forest and land fires."
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during its annual dry season, which usually runs from July through October.
This year, however, the fires and haze have been turbocharged by a so-called "Godzilla" El Nino, which has fuelled extremely dry conditions.
The independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas has detected around 734,000 hotspots across the country as of Wednesday - a figure that is more than 30% higher than that of 2019, one of Indonesia's worst wildfire seasons.
Since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land â nearly six times the size of Greater London â have been burned.
The wildfires have led to school closures and a surge in hospital admissions across Indonesia.
The number of people suffering wildfire-related respiratory illnesses had more than doubled to 113,336 by 9 September, up from 50,891 on 1 September, according to figures from the health ministry.
The toxic smog has also taken a toll on wildlife, including critically endangered orangutans.
Late last month, an Indonesia-based wildlife foundation shared footage showing an orangutan writhing on the ground on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan, one of Indonesia's hardest-hit provinces. The great ape, which was discovered by a farmer, was rescued and given emergency treatment for hypoxia, but later died.
Indigenous and civil society groups in West Kalimantan filed a class action suit last week against the central government and local administrations, accusing them of deliberate negligence for failing to properly tackle the wildfires scorching the province.
"This is a disaster that occurs every year. This recurring pattern proves our view that the defendants knew about the potential haze disaster and the risks of disaster from forest and land fires," the group's lawyer Glorio Sanen said in a statement at the time.
Indonesia has carried out several rounds of cloud-seeding operations in recent weeks, some conducted together with members of Japan's Self-Defense Forces who arrived in Borneo earlier this month to help with firefighting efforts.
Cloud seeding involves manipulating existing clouds, such as by dropping salt crystals or silver iodide into them, to help produce more rain. Meteorologists, however, are divided over the effectiveness of the practice.
In the Malaysian state of Sarawak, one of the worst-affected areas outside Indonesia, authorities launched a five-day cloud-seeding operation earlier this month.
Apart from tackling the ongoing haze, this exercise was aimed at boosting declining water levels at several hydropower dams ahead of a severe dry spell forecast for October.
"October might be hotter and drier," Sarawak's Deputy Premier Douglas Uggah Embas told reporters. "We want to increase the water levels as much as possible while we still can."
The haze has reached as far as parts of the Philippines, where local officials have urged residents to stay indoors as much as possible, and Singapore, where authorities have begun issuing daily haze advisories.

A rare snail found in just one lake in the UK started laying eggs on its six-hour journey from Wales to Kent, as a zoo joined a nationwide effort to save the species.
Glutinous snails are no bigger than a fingertip and used to be widespread across UK water ways.
It is thought habitat disruption and environmental changes reduced their population to such an extent that they are only now found in Llyn Tegid, a lake in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia.
Wingham Wildlife Park near Canterbury has taken some of the wild population to breed and release into the wild. Samantha Eden, assistant curator, said the zoo started with six snails and recently started a new colony.
Despite their slow reputation, the breeding efforts are off to a flying start, Eden said.
"I brought 24 snails back from Wales at the start of July," she said.
"It was a six hour drive, and by the time I'd arrived back at the park I had about 12 egg pods in the carry containers that we were using. They'd laid eggs literally whilst we were driving.
"We started, with one of the ponds, with just six adult snails. We recently moved 130 babies out of that pond to start a new colony."
Hannah Ellins, head of reptiles and invertebrates, said: "We do a lot of work with exotics, but it's cool being able to help our animals here."
She added: "We'll keep breeding them and then hopefully we'll eventually then release them into the wild and help wild populations."
The scheme is part of a wider national effort to protect the very rare species.
Wingham Wildlife Park is joining Askham Bryan Wildlife Park in York and Longleat in Wiltshire, along with Dudley and Chester zoos, with the Freshwater Habitats Trust searching for suitable water bodies where the snails could eventually be released.

Top Iranian and US officials have held talks at the UN in New York on a day when the US leader said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved.
No breakthrough has been reported from the meeting mediated by Qatar and involving Iran's foreign minister and US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff - the first since a June ceasefire unravelled.
Witkoff said a round of discussions had been completed "that we hope will prove constructive and promising". Iran repeated its demand for the US to end its "acts of aggression".
The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of prices.
It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.
In his address at the annual meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime - remarks that sounded more pitched to voters the US midterms than the diplomats in the hall.
He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran - a huge contrast with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General AntÃ³nio Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples.
The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open.
Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly.
Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met Witkoff.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, quoted by state broadcaster IRNA, later said negotiations took part through a Qatari mediator who communicated Tehran's conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and to US "acts of aggression".
The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. Witkoff later confirmed on X that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day".
"They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff said. "The mediators will continue their work."
Since the ceasefire collapsed, both sides have intermittently exchanged fire.
Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.
The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast.
The US has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing a huge disruption to the Iranian economy.
In an effort to force Tehran to agree a deal to end the conflict, President Trump has also threatened sanctions against any country that continues trading with Iran. But so far, there has been no indication of a change of course in Iran, which insists the US and Israel end their war, including against the Iran-backed Shia group Hezbollah in Lebanon which Israel has been attacking.
Yemen's Houthis - also allied to Iran - have recently intesified attacks aimed at disrupting oil shipping from Saudi Arabia, promting an escalation of the conflict with the kingdom.

At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.
Gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township late on Tuesday and opened fire on 14 people. Ten were killed at the scene and four were taken to hospital, where one later died from their injuries, police said.
Police said some of the victims were on their watch in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched".
While the motive of the shooting has not yet confirmed, the police said they could not rule out a "feud between rival groupings".
"Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the police said in a statement. The woman is among those who died.
A local TV reporter from the eNCA channel at the scene said the gunmen had set fire to a vehicle belonging to one of the victims before fleeing, with footage showing the burnt-out car.
The police say they have launched a manhunt for the suspects.
South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with police data showing a murder rate equivalent to more than 60 deaths a day.
In recent weeks, the gruesome discovery of at least nine murdered women, with some of the bodies dumped by the roadside, has heightened fears in the country.
Last year, nine people were killed in a mass shooting at a tavern in Johannesburg.
Rivalry among criminal gangs amid turf wars, drug trafficking and illegal mining is common in the country, often driving violence within communities.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa said organised crime was "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development", as he announced that he would be deploying the army to support the police.

The US Justice Department has filed documents that accuse three media outlets banned from the White House of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods" and reporting which "threatened national security" as it prepared to defend the move in court.
Last week, President Donald Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news".
After their reporters had their passes confiscated and were denied access to the building, the three outlets jointly launched legal action, calling the move unconstitutional.
On Wednesday, a judge is set to decide whether to issue an order temporarily lifting the ban, pending a full hearing.
According to a court filing by the Justice Department in a District of Columbia court, the three outlets were issued with a list of "reporting incidents" by the White House ahead of the ban.
The filing cites a number of stories about construction at the White House - including about a security bunker and the building of a new ballroom, as well as a report on an internal information leak investigation.
It goes on to say that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right".
The three media organisations have argued that the ban breaches their rights under the First Amendment, which forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press.
In a joint statement confirming legal action against the government, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
Major TV networks have withdrawn from a media-sharing arrangement of video and images of the president, known as the pool, in protest over the ban.
Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president.

The UK will grow by less than expected next year amid the ongoing US-Israel war in Iran, an international agency has said.
It is one of many countries whose economic prospects are facing a hit due to the prolonged conflict, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said.
The downgrade to the UK's economic growth outlook is moderate, according to the OECD, which predicted it will grow by 1% in 2027, against an earlier forecast of 1.1%.
The agency also upgraded the UK's growth outlook for 2026, from an expected 0.9% to 1.1% for the year.
The prediction comes as Chancellor John Healey prepares to deliver his first Budget at the end of October.
In the short-term, UK growth in 2026 is expected to be higher than the OECD predicted in June after "solid domestic demand growth".
But it will be lower than predicted in 2027 as higher fuel prices eat into growth. The effects of this depend on how long supply disruptions last, it said.
Risks to the global economy include the war in the middle east and climate-change related supply shocks, the OECD said.
Next year, global growth is expected to also be 0.1% lower, with countries affected including Australia, Canada, and the Euro-area.
Conflict in the Middle East has contributed to higher oil and gas prices globally, pushing up inflation in countries including the UK.
Weather-related shocks, including from a strong El Nino, could hit farmers and help push up food prices, it added.

111e3881c6c1.text: President Trump's Board of Peace will unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza at a meeting of its members on Wednesday. Why it matters: The 66-project proposal offers one of the most comprehensive roadmaps yet for what the early months of post-war reconstruction and governance in Gaza would look like. The plan is a result of a year of work by dozens of people both on the Board of Peace, which includes 28 member countries, and in the Palestinian technocratic government. It includes projected spending for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force, according to a copy of the plan obtained by Axios. "The plan shows how to stand up a government from nothing, an economy from shambles and a territory from disaster," a Board of Peace official said. Yes, but: For the plan to move forward, the Board of Peace needs Israel and Hamas to cooperate. While the Netanyahu government has agreed in principle to aspects of the plan that have been previously discussed, it refused to start implementing it , mainly for domestic political reasons ahead of the elections. And while Hamas agreed in principle to disarm , it hasn't been tested yet, partly because Israel won't implement a 14-day ceasefire before the demilitarization process starts. The Board of Peace hopes that after the Israeli elections on Oct. 27 and the formation of a new Israeli government, the Gaza recovery process can finally start. But the election is unlikely to yield a clear winner, resulting in a caretaker government and a political stalemate. That could further undermine implementation of the Gaza proposal. The big picture: The plan estimates physical damage in Gaza at $35.2 billion and says full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4 billion over the next decade. Zoom in: The plan divides the 66 projects into six areas: infrastructure development, human development, economic acceleration, digital transformation, legal affairs, and peace and security: Infrastructure accounts for the largest share, at roughly $1 billion, including about $400 million for temporary shelters, $275 million for rubble and unexploded ordnance clearance, $50 million for hospital rehabilitation and $30 million to repair Gaza's badly damaged road network. The plan also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar-power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects. Security-related projects account for roughly $885 million, making them another major component of the proposal. The plan allocates about $275 million for a permanent hardened site in Rafah capable of supporting 5,000 personnel from the International Stabilization Force (ISF) and another $140 million to recruit, train, equip and deploy a multinational security contingent. Another $120 million would go toward mobilizing Palestinian police. While thousands of Palestinians from Gaza have been selected and vetted to serve in the new Gaza police force, Israel has blocked them from leaving Gaza for training in Egypt. $20 million would fund a weapons buy-back program offering incentives for weapons and ammunition to be surrendered by Hamas and members of other armed groups and safely disposed of. According to the plan, the Palestinian technocratic government would also eventually take over management of Gaza's border crossings with Israel and Egypt for both goods and passengers. What to watch: One of the most immediate priorities is moving Palestinians out of tents. Roughly $400 million is earmarked for insulated caravans for displaced Palestinians currently living in tents. Separately, the UAE would fund a pilot "Emirati Neighborhood" in the Rafah area designed to house 50,000 people currently living in tents, with independent utilities. The plan also allocates roughly $300 million for health, education and welfare programs. Between the lines: The proposal isn't limited to emergency relief. It is also intended to establish the infrastructure of a functioning Palestinian administration and restart Gaza's private sector. Projects include a digital ID system, digital payments, 4G connectivity, electronic health and education systems, grants to restart small businesses and a new Gaza investment fund. The Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic government say recovery should be Palestinian-led and based on "Palestinian ownership." What's next: A key challenge is funding. At the moment, the Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic government haven't secured the entire $2.45 billion. But Board of Peace officials say they don't need the entire sum immediately when the new Palestinian technocratic government enters Gaza. The officials expressed confidence that once the political hurdles are cleared, donor countries will step up to fund the various projects. Representatives from 35 countries are expected to attend the Board of Peace briefing on Wednesday morning, including from the EU and several of its member states who are not part of the board. Trump's senior adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner, who spearheaded the administration's Gaza effort, and White House envoy Steve Witkoff will speak at the event. Board of Peace High Representative Nickolay Mladenov, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, the head of the Palestinian technocratic government Ali Shaath, ISF Commander Gen. Jasper Jeffers and Board of Peace advisers Yakir Gabay, Liran Tancman, Aryeh Lightstone and Josh Gruenbaum will also brief the participants.

9d72cf2a0915.text:
Washington canât stop talking about AI doom scenarios and the public backlash to data centers â but around the world, sentiment toward the fast-moving technology is much more nuanced.
In 34 out of 37 countries polled by Gallup, more adults express positive feelings about AI than do negative ones.
In 25 of those countries, majorities of adults who are aware of AI say it will improve their daily lives, rather than negatively affect them; majorities in 18 countries say they believe the technology will have a positive impact on their countries overall.
Optimism is high in countries like China, where 93% of adults familiar with AI think it will help people, versus 36% of US adults.
Wealthy Western countries tend to be most anxious about AI, per Gallup, though the more people in these countries use the technology, the less it worries them.

5320fa55636f.text: Data: Charles F. Kettering Foundation and Gallup; Note: Values shown may not total 100% due to rounding and exclusion of "don't know" responses; Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios Visuals A majority of Americans say the rule of law in the U.S. is weaker now than a decade ago, when Donald Trump was first elected president, according to a massive new survey of more than 23,000 U.S. adults. Driving the news: 78% of those responding to the survey by Gallup and the Charles F. Kettering Foundation for its Democracy for All Project say government officials must always follow laws and the Constitution. But just 28% trust that political leaders will be held accountable if they don't. Zoom in: Throwing out incumbents was respondents' top choice (17%) when asked what one step could be taken to most improve U.S. democracy. That response reflects a prominent theme of a midterm campaign that's shadowed by widespread voter dissatisfaction. Other steps suggested by survey respondents included electoral reform and improved voting access (13%) and limiting executive power (9%). One stunning stat: Older Republicans (65+) appear significantly less trusting of election officials now than just a year ago, with 42% saying it's reasonable to assume that election officials acted improperly if election outcomes are surprising, up from 30%. By the numbers: The share of Americans who say the rule of law is weaker now than in 2016 is four times higher than the share who think it's stronger (56% compared with 14%), while 29% say it's unchanged. Democrats and independents were much likelier than Republicans to say it's weaker. The top reason respondents cited for getting involved in a social or political cause: Feeling an important right or freedom is being threatened (27%), followed by feeling you can make a difference (26%) and seeing officials abuse or misuse power (19%). 57% said they prefer candidates who challenge powerful or established interests, while 42% prefer candidates who work within the establishment. What we're watching : Two-thirds of Americans said democracy is the best form of government, the same as last year. But across several measures, the data show the public more pessimistic now than in 2025: 49% say they don't agree with the idea that U.S. leaders are committed to having a strong democracy, up from 44% a year ago. 47% say they're comfortable openly expressing opinions about government and laws, down from 52%. 56% say democracy is doing poorly, up from 51% the year before. That sense is largely being driven by rising concerns from Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, while Democrats and neutral independents already were highly critical. Respondents give the state of democracy higher marks at the local level than the national level. What they're saying: "People care about democracy, and that is something worth building on," said Derek Barker, senior program officer for research initiatives at Kettering. "Right now, it's a matter of getting through this period where people are really concerned about how it's performing and how leaders are acting in office." Methodology: The Gallup Poll conducted this survey for the Gallup-Kettering Foundation's Democracy for All Project. The survey was completed by 23,683 U.S. adults, aged 18 and older, including 10,800 respondents recruited for the study and 12,883 supplemental respondents from a third-party sample provider. 21,652 respondents completed the survey as a web survey April 24-May 21, 2026, and 2,031 respondents completed the survey as a mail survey April 24-June 10, 2026. For results based on this sample, the maximum margin of sampling error, which takes into account the design effect from weighting, is ±1 percentage point at the 95% confidence level.

3635eba7c21c.text: By — Matt Loffman Matt Loffman Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-dont-like-data-centers-they-really-dont-like-them-close-to-home Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters don't like data centers. They really don't like them close to home Politics Sep 23, 2026 5:00 AM EDT Voters share an opposition to data centers that scrambles usual party lines, according to the latest poll from PBS News, NPR and Marist. Public opposition especially hardens when people are asked about construction in their own communities. Fifty-eight percent of U.S. voters say the construction of new data centers by companies like Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI will mostly have a negative effect on the country. And 65% of voters oppose construction in their communities, including 43% who are strongly opposed. A quarter of voters say they support data center construction. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The opposition barely follows party or geography. It runs above 60% in big cities, suburbs, small towns and rural areas alike. More than 80% of Democrats oppose local construction. Republicans overall are close to evenly split, with 46% in favor and 44% opposed. The president's core supporters are an exception. More than half of self-identified MAGA supporters are in favor of data centers in their own communities, the only group that favors construction. MORE: Why communities are revolting against data centers The intense opposition to data centers has had far-reaching effects this year. At least 75 data center projects worth roughly $130 billion were blocked or delayed in the first three months of 2026, according to Data Center Watch, a research project tracking opposition efforts. The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in an August memo obtained by Axios that data centers had become a "sleeper issue" for the entire cycle. And candidates in both parties have featured ads on the issue. WATCH: How data centers became a major issue in the midterms What to do about data centers is another issue entirely as lawmakers scramble for solutions. Last week, the House overwhelmingly passed bipartisan legislation that would require state energy regulators to consider requiring data centers to pay for electrical upgrades in their communities. Trump, however, remains on the side of data centers. Communities that oppose construction will be "backwards and poor," he wrote on social media last month. "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement." The split leaves Republicans in districts with angry constituents choosing between them and him. "I understand the balancing act that Donald Trump is doing," despite public concern and rising energy costs, Republican strategist Melik Abdul said. "From Donald Trump's perspective, it should just be a wild, wild west because he doesn't want the regulations." Trump, Abdul argued, is worried that more government oversight would lead to a competitive advantage for China, which has fewer regulations. WATCH: Sen. Mark Warner says U.S. can strengthen AI safety without losing race to China Democratic strategist Joel Payne said the president is trying to pull his party along with him. "He is essentially trying to make it a litmus test for Republicans," he said. "I don't believe that has been met with the success that he intends for it to." The president is "out there on his own on this one," said Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion. He added that the anxiety increasingly runs through a broader fear of artificial intelligence. Neither party, Payne argued, can afford non-answers on this issue. "From a political standpoint, there is no nuance. The public has no nuance within how they think about AI and data centers." f46e28353012.text: By — Matt Loffman Matt Loffman Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-lead-in-new-poll-as-trump-looms-over-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrats lead in new poll as Trump looms over midterms Politics Sep 23, 2026 5:00 AM EDT President Donald Trump's efforts to make the midterm elections a referendum on his presidency appear to be backfiring as Democratic congressional candidates hold a significant lead over Republicans in the latest poll from PBS News, NPR and Marist. More than half of registered voters – 53% – say they would vote for Democratic candidates if the election were today, while 41% prefer Republicans. Independents, who often decide competitive races, favor Democrats by a margin of 25 points. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Driving this sentiment is a president who isn't on the ballot but has asked voters to pretend he is. About 7 in 10 voters acknowledge the president is a factor, one way or another, in their vote for Congress. Just 30% of voters say Trump isn't a factor in their vote. "The Democrats are sitting in a very good place," said Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion. "There's a lot of grumbling in the electorate and a lot of sentiment for changing things around." More than half of registered voters – 53% – say they would vote for Democratic candidates if the election were today, while 41% prefer Republicans. Graphic by Steff Staples/PBS News. Trump bragged of Republicans riding his electoral coattails during his speech to the party's midterm convention in Dallas this month, building his strategy on the premise that voters turn out for him and not for anyone else. His appeal is effective largely among self-identified MAGA supporters; 71% say in this poll that their vote for Congress is mostly a vote for the president. But with absentee and mail voting already underway in a handful of states, the poll suggests Trump's influence may have the opposite effect on other voters. Overall, 45% of registered voters and 54% of independents say their vote will be mostly to express their opposition to Trump. Eight in 10 Democrats are motivated to vote against Trump. Just 24% of voters and 12% of independents say they are voting to show support for the president. "That's devastating," Democratic strategist Joel Payne said. In this political environment, he added, it's expected that political partisans will line up behind their team, but when independents are strongly motivated to vote against one side, "that's significant." The president's own numbers have been frozen for most of the year, with 39% approving of his job performance and 59% disapproving in this latest poll. But that top line understates the asymmetry: More than half of voters – 53% – strongly disapprove of the job he's doing, the highest share recorded by Marist across either of his terms in office, and on par with high voter dissatisfaction with Trump in the aftermath of the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. Congressional Republicans have little room to run from Trump. "It's a nationalized election whether they like it or not," Miringoff said. The president's own numbers have been frozen for most of the year, with 39% approving of his job performance and 59% disapproving in the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist poll. Graphic by Dan Cooney/PBS News. Thirteen incumbents were defeated in their primaries this year, and dozens of members announced plans to retire or run for another office. Nearly one in five lawmakers who started this Congress will not return for the next one, according to an NPR analysis, driven by record-setting retirements and primary defeats. READ MORE: Rising gas prices frustrate voters. Trump says it's an 'inexpensive price to pay' for the Iran war With gas prices, the war in Iran and other national issues dominating, he said, "it'd be next to impossible" for a congressional candidate to ignore those and focus only on local issues. "It's not believable enough because [Trump's] such a dominant force." "These numbers are concerning to Republicans behind the scenes," Republican strategist Melik Abdul said. Abdul wondered whether the president's luck had run out. "It's almost like he's Icarus," the famous figure from Greek mythology, he said. The question is whether Trump's "gotten a bit too close to the sun this time." Republicans lag in enthusiasm The premise behind Trump's plea to pretend he's on the ballot points to a potential turnout problem among his base. The poll shows few signs that his appeal is closing the enthusiasm gap. Voters overall are highly engaged. Nearly 9 in 10 say they care a great deal or quite a bit about which party controls Congress, and 75% say they're following the midterm elections closely. But the passion tilts toward Democrats. Seventy-six percent of Democrats say they care a great deal who wins Congress, while 67% of Republicans say the same. Additionally, 42% of Democrats are following the election very closely compared to 34% of Republicans. Trump's most loyal supporters match Democrats' fervor. Three-quarters of MAGA supporters care a great deal about the outcome. But the rest of the Republican coalition that Trump is asking to show up is lagging behind. Independents are the least engaged of all, with 30% following the race very closely. Miringoff said that gap is the problem Trump's messaging is trying to solve. "When he's not on the ballot, it doesn't automatically transfer," he said. The calculation Republicans have had to make, he added, is that "the enthusiasm factor for their base is a little soft." 5629412a6ddb.text: By — Matt Loffman Matt Loffman Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-trust-local-election-officials-theyre-less-sure-about-the-mail Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters trust local election officials. They're less sure about the mail Politics Sep 23, 2026 5:00 AM EDT President Donald Trump's unfounded insistence that mail-in ballots lead to fraud appears to be persuading only his loyal coalition and almost no one else, a new PBS News/NPR/Marist poll finds ahead of midterm elections. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. With early and mail voting underway in a handful of states, many of those ballots that will help determine which party controls Congress are moving through a system that Trump has spent more than a year trying to reshape. In August 2025, Trump pledged to issue an executive order ending the use of mail-in ballots and voting machines before the midterms. The order he signed in March directed the U.S. Postal Service to build a system for blocking delivery of ballots to voters not on lists presubmitted by state officials, prompting lawsuits from 23 Democratic-led states and voting rights groups. Read more from this poll: Democrats lead in new poll as Trump looms over midterms Voters don't like data centers. They really don't like them close to home Last week, as this poll was in the field, the Supreme Court refused to clear the way for the president's plan. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that state and local officials lacked sufficient time to implement the rule before the elections. Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer at the National Association of Election Officials, told PBS News after the Supreme Court decision that election officials breathed a "sigh of relief." "It was almost an impossible ask to have election officials try and implement this rule in this late hour," she said, adding, "I think everyone is a little bit relieved that we don't have to do this for the November election, and they can focus on the tasks at hand and getting prepared for what is to come." READ MORE: Election officials get mail-in voting clarity after Supreme Court decision While the president has repeatedly insisted, without evidence, that elections and mail ballots in particular are rife with cheating, voter fraud is incredibly rare. The conservative Heritage Foundation lists roughly 1,500 cases over decades in its database, compared to hundreds of millions of votes cast. Even so, 41% of voters say there is a great deal or good amount of fraud when people can vote by mail. Seventy percent of Republicans and 75% of self-identified MAGA supporters say the same, compared with 18% of Democrats and 32% of independents. Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion, doubted the fraud argument would move many votes beyond the president's base. "He has image problems, he has turnout problems, he has issue problems," Miringoff said. The mail message, he added, is "not exactly telling the voter something he hasn't already told them." Seventy-five percent of voters trust their state or local government to run a fair and accurate election, according to the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist poll. Graphic by Dan Cooney/PBS News. More recently, the Trump administration has threatened to prosecute state election officials if they don't prevent noncitizen voting, which is already illegal and rare. When it comes to voter behavior, the consequences of Trump's repeated attacks on mail voting are visible in this poll. Nearly a quarter of voters plan to cast a mail ballot this year; 31% voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election. Democrats are nearly three times as likely as Republicans to say they'll vote by mail. Half of voters say they'll vote in person on Election Day. At the same time, 75% of voters trust their state or local government to run a fair and accurate election. Among Democrats, 86% say they are somewhat or very confident, while 66% of Republicans say the same. Miringoff said that trust is because voters feel differently about the election workers in their own communities. "They sort of know these people," he said. Confidence in the Postal Service, however, has dropped considerably. Fifty-eight percent of voters are confident USPS will deliver election mail on time this year, down 13 points since 2024. WATCH: Whistleblower's attorney details concerns over USPS mail-in ballot system On nearly every question about how Americans vote, Democrats and Republicans are on opposite sides, but this is one area where they agree. In both parties, around 4 in 10 voters have little to no confidence mail will arrive on time. Patrick said that means voters need to be more vigilant. She urged that anyone who does want to vote by mail both makes their request and returns their ballot early, either at a drop box or by mail, depending on what options are available in your state. PBS News, NPR and Marist Poll conducted a survey from Sept. 14 to 15, 2026, that polled 1,280 registered voters by phone, text and online with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points. For Democrats, the margin of error is 6.5 percentage points; Republicans, 6.8 percentage points; independents, 7.2 percentage points. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Thousands of farmers missed out on vital government funding after online applications for a Â£233m green scheme for the whole of England closed down in under six hours.
Farming and environmental groups condemned the race to secure the sustainable farming incentive (SFI) funding, with some comparing it to a "frantic" online scramble to secure Glastonbury or Oasis gig tickets.
The post-Brexit scheme, which replaced EU subsidies with payments for farmers to look after nature and provide "public goods", opened at 10:00 BST on Tuesday but had run out of budget by 15:48 BST.
The government said farmers had responded "in force" to the scheme and there would be further funding opportunities for 2027.
The National Farmers' Union (NFU) is calling for the government to explain why the scheme opened and closed so quickly, with so many farmers left out of pocket.
It said it wanted "clarity and urgency" from the government and added that it had made "repeated warnings of a lack of sufficient budget".
NFU vice-president Robyn Munt said: "The rapid uptake of the scheme comes as no surprise. Its closure in less than six hours shows the scale of demand there is from farmers to deliver for the environment and to invest in farm resilience.
"The current cashflow pressures facing farmers and growers only exacerbates that demand as they look for certainty and clarity for the year ahead."
Vicki Hird, agriculture lead at the Wildlife Trusts said "the scramble for green farming schemes was worse than the dash for Oasis tickets".
She added: "The budget has been inadequate for far too long and the Treasury must recognise this and allocate far greater funds to ensure climate resilience in farming in the next budget."
The SFI scheme is vital for many farmers who have turned large swathes of their land over to nature-friendly schemes, such as planting hedges, creating wildflower margins and protecting the soil.
When the scheme was suddenly closed without notice last year, there were concerns that some farmers might turn their backs on environmental work if they could not access the payments and demand for Tuesday's scheme was expected to be high.
'Race against time'
The Nature Friendly Farming Network (NFFN), which helps farmers to manage land in environmentally-friendly ways, criticised the "frantic scramble" and said farmers had "faced a desperate race against time" to secure their funding agreements.
Cambridgeshire arable farmer Martin Lines, who leads the NFFN, said: "This entire SFI system, with windows opening and closing within a few hours, isn't fit for purpose.
"We need to find a better way based on continuous, whole-farm agreements, not doors that slam shut on day one because the money has already gone."
He pointed out that after years of extreme weather, many farmers were relying on the funding to help adapt their farms to climate change and become more resilient.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it would provide further information on future opportunities for funding applications in 2027 "soon".
A Defra spokesperson said: "This year we ensured small farms and those new to SFI were prioritised - with an exclusive first window in the summer.
"In anticipation of high demand in the second window, ministers decided to allocate an additional Â£20m to the fund, on top the Â£50m announced by the prime minister in August, so that we could fund as many agreements as possible."
Farming Minister Stephen Morgan added that the SFI had been designed to be simpler to apply for and that farmers had "responded in force".
"This is a scheme that works for farmers, backs food production, and delivers practical, sustainable land management, supporting the aims of our farming roadmap, our long-term plan for English farming," he said.

fa8e5e38733e.text: The shift of the AI frontier toward more powerful, lower-cost models could pave the way for safely slowing development, experts say. Why it matters: Top U.S. startups including OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as other AI players, have to develop a financially viable path to allow them to slow development. Otherwise financial incentives will be too powerful . Driving the news : The health of the entire U.S. economy now rests in part on the AI boom. Yet the companies at the center of the race are burning far more cash than they take in, and will be for the foreseeable future. Their top executives have also shown unusual solidarity in expressing a desire to slow the pace of model development due to a troubling series of incidents in which rogue AI agents hacked outside companies. Between the lines : To enable a slowdown, in a financial sense, the companies have to find a way to build a value proposition to users that isn't solely rooted in the most mind-blowing intelligence imaginable. That's because remaining at the so-called frontier of capabilities requires a treadmill of never-ending — and mind-boggling spending — to keep up. Slowing the extent of that spending, some of which is used for the computing firepower needed to train new models, would help the companies generate better returns. That wouldn't necessarily threaten spending on computing, data centers and infrastructure such as upgrading the electric grid, according to some economists and AI pros. Those investments will still be needed in order to service demand for AI usage that continues to skyrocket. Catch up quick: Everybody gets a new model this week, and the one thing they all have in common is that they're cheaper than ever without forgoing top intelligence. OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX all emphasized the relatively low costs of their new models this week, as well as their ability to outperform some of their own top systems from only a few months ago. Chinese models including DeepSeek have done the same. DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash, released earlier this month, is now number one on OpenRouter's leaderboard with a 172% spike in usage this week. Reality check: The rationale for the price cuts also goes beyond safety. In a report sent to clients, Citadel Securities found that falling per-token costs are fueling enough additional usage to increase overall AI spending, meaning higher profits for labs even as they cut costs. This paradox is why the AI labs have a rich history of effectively cutting prices for models over time: it increases their customer base and their profits. The bottom line: The race to win on AI costs could be the very thing that allows the labs to enable the slowdown they are seeking.
