The more scientists look for chemicals that can increase breast cancer risk, the more they find.
Hundreds of potential breast carcinogens lurk in consumer goods, food, drinking water, pesticides, drugs and building materials, scientists reported in a peer-reviewed study published Wednesday in the journal Environmental Health Perspectives.
Exposure to these chemicals is ubiquitous, the authors warn, yet biomonitoring efforts are failing to measure people’s exposures to most chemicals or assess risks from compound exposures.
Chemicals found in and derived from fossil fuels accounted for some of the largest production volumes and environmental releases of potential breast carcinogens, said lead author Jennifer Kay, a research scientist at the Silent Spring Institute, which works to reduce toxic threats to women’s health. She called widespread use of petrochemicals, particularly to make plastic, “a huge problem.”
Bisphenols and phthalates, chemicals produced at high volumes for plastics, can damage DNA, trigger cell division and increase breast cancer risk or severity.
Most breast cancers occur in women 55 and older, as cells lose their ability to repair genetic damage and start dividing abnormally. Breast cancer rates have been rising in recent years for all women, with steeper increases among younger women. These trends cannot be explained by better screening or known risk factors like genetics, obesity or smoking, pointing to environmental factors as a cause.
Kay worked with her Silent Spring colleagues and University of California, Berkeley, researchers to build on her previous paper that linked more than 900 chemicals to increased breast cancer risk. Some of the chemicals cause mammary tumors in rodents, some interfere with hormones, many damage DNA and some do all three.
DNA damage that isn’t repaired before a cell divides can become a permanent mutation, a first step in tumor formation. Chemicals that trigger breast cell division—often by altering the hormones estrogen and progesterone—boost the chances of mutation.
If a premenopausal woman is exposed to gene-damaging chemicals during her normal hormonal cycle, then is exposed to hormone-altering chemicals, Kay said, “it’s just kind of hit upon hit” that sets the stage for cancer. Even after menopause, exposure to hormone-disrupting chemicals can activate cell division and increase breast cancer risk, especially if there is DNA damage, she said.
“Shocking” Number of Potential Breast Carcinogens
To understand how people might encounter chemicals with the potential to cause breast cancer, the team used more than a dozen U.S. government databases to gauge exposures.
They mapped their list of chemicals to production and import data to flag high-volume substances with potential for widespread exposure. They determined air emissions for each chemical from mobile sources like vehicles and stationary sources like factories, as well as releases into air, land and water near fenceline communities.

They also gathered information on known exposures from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey biomonitoring database. The NHANES measures only a small subset of chemicals in people, though, so the team filled in biomonitoring gaps with Environmental Protection Agency models that estimate daily exposure to chemicals. Finally, they compiled lists of chemicals used in everything from toothpaste to vinyl flooring.
The team found 500 chemicals linked to breast cancer in consumer products like cosmetics, plastic goods and detergents, and nearly as many in pesticides and dietary sources. Many of the potential breast carcinogens found in human blood and urine samples were detected in more than 90 percent of the population, but NHANES doesn’t monitor most of the chemicals.
It’s critically important to highlight the sheer ubiquity of these breast-cancer-related chemicals in the U.S. population, said Rashmi Joglekar, science policy director of Stanford University’s Health and Toxics Policy Lab, who was not involved in the research.
In 2019, the year with the most recent data available, manufacturers produced more than 5 billion pounds of potential breast carcinogens, including bisphenol A, used to make polycarbonate plastics and resins, and 10 chemicals that cause mammary tumors in rodents, including styrene, benzene and vinyl chloride.
It’s “really, really shocking” that some of the chemicals produced and released into the environment in the highest volumes are established mammary carcinogens or genotoxic chemicals, Joglekar said. Seeing millions of pounds of known carcinogens released into the environment in a single year highlights the failure of U.S. regulatory agencies to protect people, she said.
The study identifies chemicals the authors believe warrant additional research and potential regulatory attention, a spokesperson for the American Chemistry Council, which represents nearly 200 companies in the chemistry business, said in a statement. “The authors themselves note that many of the exposure estimates used in the analysis are based on predictive models that rely on limited data and assumptions and are subject to significant uncertainty.”
That uncertainty includes a universe of chemicals that aren’t being tracked. The authors flagged more than 340 potential breast carcinogens that aren’t included in EPA’s Toxics Release Inventory, even though a quarter of them were produced or imported in excess of 1 million pounds in 2019. And the study likely underestimates exposures, the authors noted, because their calculations are based on EPA models of average daily intake, rather than on estimates of the most exposed groups.
Some people could be exposed to certain chemicals at levels 10 to 100 times higher

South Sudan President Salva Kiir has dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country's first election since its independence in 2011.
The country has previously postponed elections twice and extended the transitional period several times.
Under the amended law, signed on Monday, Kiir removed the country's five vice-presidents and dissolved parliament, as well as national and state governments.
Kiir is the presidential candidate of his Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM). No prominent figures have announced plans to challenge him in the December poll. The main opposition leader Riek Machar was sacked as vice-president last year and charged with treason.
He is under house arrest.
Machar had been named vice-president as part of a 2018 peace deal to end a five-year civil war between forces loyal to the two men.
Kiir will remain in office with full constitutional powers until an elected president is sworn in. He also reappointed some ministers and governors in caretaker positions until the 22 December elections.
Ahead of Tuesday's announcement a heavy security presence was reported in the capital, Juba. Soldiers from the army and national security services blocked access to government ministries. Soldiers were also seen patrolling parts of the city.
A senior government official told the BBC that staff arriving for work were turned away and told to return the following Monday.
UN agencies in Juba also asked staff to work remotely while the situation was monitored.
Kiir last week dismissed the chairman of the national elections commission, Abednego Akok Kacuol, without giving a reason. He was replaced by the commission's secretary-general, Gabriel Bol Deng.
Akok had said in August that the commission needed $250m (Â£190m) to conduct the election but had received only $21m.
In June, the main opposition group, the Sudan People's Liberation Movement in Opposition (SPLM-IO), the party of Machar, warned people not to take part in poll preparations.
"Anyone coming to register voters and campaign in territories controlled by the mighty SPLM-IO, you will be a prisoner of war," Nathaniel Pierino, acting chairperson of the group, said in a post on Facebook.
The body which oversees implementation of the 2018 peace agreement, the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC), said South Sudan had entered a "critical phase".
It said several key talks under the agreement remained incomplete and urged the parties to agree on a path towards credible elections and a peaceful end to the transitional period, which has lasted since independence.
The latest 24-month extension was due to end on 22 February 2027.

READ MORE: Why Trump is rolling out the red carpet for Xi after years of slamming China Trump's decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington rather than receiving him at the executive residence shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China's leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade. First lady Melania Trump said her husband decided to personally greet Xi when he arrives in the Washington region because "they have a great relationship." "He's coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect," she said of Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, during an interview Wednesday on Fox News Channel's "Fox & Friends." READ MORE: As China and U.S. compete for AI dominance, both have shared concerns over safety The White House has not released many details about Wednesday's greeting, but Trump is expected to participate in an arrival ceremony at the base with Xi and his wife. The salutation will kick off a three-day visit that's expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump's May visit to China. But it also is a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan. Beyond using the visit to try to keep "strategic stability" between the two countries, Trump seems to be pulling out all the diplomatic stops to show off for Xi. Trump has lavished praise on Xi as a "great leader" and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend. That is all while he has given Xi a pass on many issues. Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticized the "lavish welcome." Wicker, R-Miss., said during a speech Tuesday in the Senate that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader "based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party." Wicker archly suggested a list of topics that Trump could discuss with Xi at the state dinner, such as "the purposes of China's massive military buildup, or about China's clear support for Iran," saying that "during every minute of dialogue" Trump should keep in mind that "his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America." Trump has made it clear he wants to wow Xi, telling reporters in recent weeks that he was delighted his new "work of art" helicopter landing pad would be ready for the visit while bemoaning that his massive White House ballroom would not. On Wednesday, Trump is expected to try to match the pageantry he was met with in China earlier this year. Xi was not at the airport to meet Trump — Chinese Vice President Han Zheng was there instead. But there a red carpet was rolled out to meet Air Force One in Beijing. A military honor guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, "Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!" also were present. The children wore white and light blue uniforms that mirrored the traditional paint colors of the presidential plane. Trump's airport ceremony for Xi will be followed on Thursday by more formalities, including an arrival ceremony at the White House and a review of troops. Before the black-tie dinner, which will feature tech industry leaders like Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk, the two leaders are expected to dive into the weighty issues behind closed doors, even as expectations are low that the trip will produce any major breakthroughs in the relationship. On Friday, Xi and Peng will be back at the White House for a private tea with the Trumps before joining them on a tour of the National Archives in Washington. The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the two countries. Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report. At a meeting of the group's board, the governors unveiled a 66-project blueprint to get things started while acknowledging enormous hurdles that must still be overcome. The projects include ambitious infrastructure, education and health initiatives that are designed to support Trump's 20-point plan to end the Israel-Hamas war. WATCH LIVE: Day 2 of the 2026 United Nations General Assembly "The need is immense," the board said, noting that full reconstruction from the physical damage across Gaza will cost roughly $35.2 billion over the medium term and another $71.4 billion in the next 10 years. Please check your inbox to confirm. The ceasefire, which took effect on Oct. 10, was meant to clear the way for a broader process to rebuild Gaza under the guidance of the Board of Peace. The plan included additional Israeli military withdrawals from Gaza, the disarmament of Hamas, the arrival of an international peacekeeping force and a new apolitical Palestinian government to administer the territory's day-to-day affairs. While the ceasefire halted the heaviest fighting and humanitarian conditions have improved, the Israeli military has expanded its control of Gaza and now occupies some 60% of the territory. This development could change poetry forever. Roses are red and now they’re also blue.
True blue roses were once thought impossible. Roses can make red and yellow pigments but don’t have an enzyme needed to make blue pigments. At least they didn’t until 2004, when researchers at the Suntory Global Innovation Center in Kyoto, Japan, genetically modified a rose to produce blue pigments. The team inserted the gene for an enzyme that can produce a blue pigment called delphinidin. But those roses were purplish, suggesting it takes more than blue pigment to make flowers blue.
Naturally blue flowers, such as irises, make blue pigments like delphinidin. But they also need almost colorless “co-pigment” molecules called flavone C-glycosides to create their blue hue. Those helper molecules stabilize pigments and make them appear deeper blue. Roses also lack genes for making the co-pigments.
This time, Suntory researchers inserted four genes from other blue flower species into a light pink rose. A gene from Canterbury bells (Campanula medium) allowed the engineered roses to produce multiple blue pigments. Two genes from wishbone flowers (Torenia x hybrida) and one from clustered gentian (Gentiana triflora) made enzymes that produce the colorless helper molecules. The combination of the blue pigment malvidin with a helper called isoorientin made bluer flowers than roses producing only delphinidin, the company announced August 25 at the 32nd International Horticultural Congress in Kyoto. The higher the level of co-pigments in the petals, the bluer the flowers, the researchers found.
Roses making the co-pigments are rated as violet blue based on a flower color chart. The rose bushes continued to produce blue flowers for seven years in greenhouse tests in Japan and three years growing in fields in Colombia.
The achievement is sweet. And the team hopes to further enhance the hue.

US President Donald Trump has disclosed millions of dollars' worth of stock market trades made during July, including in firms from Elon Musk's SpaceX to tech and AI giants such as Microsoft.
According to official documents, between $6.5m (Â£4.8m) and $31m worth of stock in Microsoft was sold on behalf of Trump, while they show purchases of between $165,000 and $400,000.
Across more than 1,000 trades, shares were bought and sold in AI company Nvidia and software firm Palantir, a contractor with the US defence department and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the filing shows.
A White House spokesperson said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties.
The spokesperson told the BBC: "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold.
"There are no conflicts of interest."
According to the filing, thousands of dollars' worth of stock was also bought and sold in SpaceX, the rocket, satellite and AI company led by Musk - who was once in charge of the US Department of Government Efficiency.
SpaceX listed its shares on the US-based Nasdaq stock market in June.
Its share price has fluctuated since then, sharply declining in July and August, but it is currently trading 14% higher than its stock market debut.
Shares were also bought and sold in Tesla, Musk's electric vehicle-maker, on behalf of Trump.
Trump has previously publicly disclosed thousands of stock market trades since he returned to the White House in January last year.

French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying.
His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov.
Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev.
However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe.
It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list.
Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns.
Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years.
Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing, external as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine".
The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans".
Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men.
Foreign Minister Baiba BraÅ¾e said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive". Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative".
French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations.
Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon.
Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government.
Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China.
"I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court.
Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev.

Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.
In a victim impact statement in court, his accuser, Miriam Haley, said the assault had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".
Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions".
Weinstein has already spent six years in prison as the cases against him play out, and he has a separate conviction for sex crimes in Los Angeles. He has faced three trials in New York over rape and abuse allegations.
He was originally convicted and sentenced in the Miriam Haley case in 2020. But in 2024, New York's highest court overturned the conviction, ruling Weinstein did not get a fair trial. He was retried and convicted again in the case last year.
Weinstein was a high-flying Hollywood producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, before reports in 2017 detailed allegations of sexual assault against him stretching back decades, sparking the #MeToo movement.

b6921a661b6e.text: By — Megan Janetsky, Associated Press Megan Janetsky, Associated Press By — James Brooks, Associated Press James Brooks, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/polo-off-mexican-coast-is-among-the-strongest-storms-ever Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Polo off Mexican coast is among 'the strongest storms ever' Nation Sep 23, 2026 12:11 PM EDT MEXICO CITY (AP) — Polo has grown into one of the most powerful Pacific cyclones in decades and was expected to skirt Mexico's southwestern coast as a major hurricane, while another Pacific system, Odalys, strengthened Wednesday from a tropical storm to a hurricane without threatening land. LIVE MAP: Track the path of Hurricane Polo The U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami has called Polo an "extremely dangerous" storm and forecast the system would turn sharply to the northwest before moving west-northwest over the next several days. Polo was about 165 miles (266 kilometers) south of Zihuatanejo and 320 miles (515 kilometers) southeast of Manzanillo, the center reported. It was moving slowly north with maximum sustained winds of 150 mph (241 kph). That put it at Category 4 strength, after earlier being a Category 5 storm. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Fluctuations in intensity are expected, but Polo is expected to remain a very powerful major hurricane during the next few days," the NHC said. Odalys was a Category 1 hurricane and was about 1,295 miles (2,085 kilometers) off the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula of Mexico, moving east-northeast at 9 mph (15 kph) with maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 kph), the hurricane center said. Waves, flooding and mudslides are all risks Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said experts indicated Polo was not likely to touch land. Still, hurricane-force winds extend up to 40 miles (65 kilometers) from the storm's center and tropical storm-force winds up to 105 miles (169 kilometers) from the eye, the U.S. center said. Tropical storm conditions were expected along the Pacific coast in Guerrero, Michoacan and Colima states Wednesday into Thursday. READ MORE: Polo has rapidly intensified to a hurricane and is expected to impact Mexico Polo on Tuesday became the third Category 5 hurricane of the Pacific season, following Genevieve and Lowell earlier this year. Category 5 is the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale, reflecting that a storm has maximum sustained winds exceeding 157 mph (253 kph). The hurricane set residents along Mexico's Pacific coast on edge once again after being walloped by a number of powerful cyclones in recent years. Beaches emptied and dark clouds swirled above choppy seas, while Mexican authorities temporarily suspended classes Tuesday in a number of areas. Mexico's navy shut down ports in the states of Guerrero and Michoacán and warned civilians and fishermen to take care. Concepción López Villegas was busily preparing her seaside restaurant for what may come. Strong waves were already lapping at the coastline of her city Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán. As men and children watched the stirring waters behind her, López Villegas said she feared powerful waves would destroy the small business she has worked decades to build. "We're worried and trying to protect our businesses," López Villegas said. "And of course, we're sad because it's our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed." U.S. National Hurricane Center data shows Polo's winds reached speeds comparable to only a few hurricanes in the region in recent decades, primarily Hurricane Patricia, which had winds that reached 215 mph (346 kph) in 2015. "This is one of the strongest storms ever in the (Pacific) Basin," said Kristen L. Corbosiero, professor at the University at Albany's Department of Atmospheric & Environmental Sciences. Heavy rain could produce flash flooding and mudslides. About 3 to 6 inches (8 to 15 centimeters) of rain was forecast for Guerrero and Michoacán states, with smaller amounts possible for coastal portions of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco states. El Nino fueled rapid intensification The U.S. Embassy in Mexico issued a weather alert, instructing citizens to avoid water and beaches and to heed warnings from Mexican authorities. "Even if the storm does not make direct landfall, heavy rain may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Hazardous ocean conditions — intensified by storms — may result in deadly rip currents and rogue waves," the embassy wrote in a statement. READ MORE: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns The rapid intensification of the storm has stunned scientists and authorities alike, with the NHC writing in a report that it was "truly remarkable" how quickly Polo gained strength in 24 hours. Philip Klotzbach, research scientist in the Department of Atmospheric Science at Colorado State University, attributed the intensification to the weather phenomenon known as El Nino, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region. In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes, he said. "There are all the ingredients that hurricanes need to get really strong really fast," Klotzbach said. No Atlantic hurricanes have formed yet this year, and this year has set a record for the longest start to a season without a hurricane. The effects of this year's El Nino crush storms before they get going. Brooks reported from Atlanta. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. de82f7ffcb75.text:
Yinkaâs view
For decades, the debate around Africaâs natural resources has largely been over who gets the value from what the continent digs up and ships out. But at Semaforâs The Next 3 Billion summit in New York this week, the recurring theme was more nuanced. The question was what economic ecosystems can African economies build around their resources before they leave the continent?
That means moving beyond extraction toward processing, manufacturing, infrastructure, energy, and the jobs that can come with them. It also reflects a changing approach to foreign capital. African governments increasingly want partnerships that build domestic capacity, rather than simply finance projects or provide an exit route for commodities.
Nigeriaâs trade minister Jumoke Oduwole put the ambition plainly when discussing the countryâs talks with US companies on critical minerals, saying her government is looking for âpartners that will make sure that the value chain development [and] the jobs are created on Nigerian soil.â
DR Congoâs Prime Minister Judith Suminwa described diversification of both the economy and its foreign partners as a priority, saying partnerships should âbring a plusâ to the country. The implication is that the choice is not necessarily between China, the US, Europe or the Gulf, but whether competition among them can be used to secure more lasting economic capacity.
There is a compelling logic to that strategy. Countries that remain primarily exporters of raw materials are vulnerable to commodity cycles and capture relatively little of the value created farther down the supply chain. More refining, processing, power generation and transport infrastructure could create wider economic spillovers.
But there is also a danger in making âvalue additionâ the answer to every development problem. Processing minerals or refining oil requires enormous amounts of reliable electricity, transport infrastructure, capital, and technical expertise. In some cases, importing finished products may still be cheaper than producing them locally. And building a factory does not automatically create a competitive industry.
The more interesting test, then, is whether Africa can turn its resource advantage into productive capacity without turning industrial policy into an expensive exercise in symbolism. The opportunity is real. The harder question is what African economies can build that will remain competitive after the foreign partners and commodity boom move on.
Notable
- Dangoteâs Lagos refinery is one of the starkest examples of the economic power of domestic production: It netted $1.8 billion in profit after tax in the first half of this year, more than its total revenue for 2025. The companyâs recent IPO was the largest in Africaâs history.

Millions of lettuces are set to be wasted as farmers are grappling with a record outbreak of aphids that has devastated the end of their growing season.
Growers are facing losses of Â£10m, as 30 million heads of lettuce will be rendered unusable, according to the British Leafy Salads Association (BLSA).
The organisation says that warm and dry weather has produced "ideal conditions" for the bugs, with as much as 30% of the UK crop between now and the end of October set to be wasted.
Homegrown lettuce dominates the market in the summer and early autumn weeks before a transition that sees more imports filling shop shelves.
But imported lettuces are now likely to be on the shelves in the UK a couple of weeks earlier than usual.
Farms in many parts of England - the Midlands, East Anglia, the south-east, south and north-west - have been impacted by the outbreak.
Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, BLSA spokesman Dieter Lloyd described the issue as "serious", while not affecting all of the UK crop.
He said people have been eating salads from UK products "all summer" but added: "The issue though is serious, the aphids bloom in June and again in August/September."
"What we're talking about here is the loss of the crop over the course of the last couple of weeks and the couple of weeks ahead."
He said that "this is not all of the heads in the UK, but it's a significant percentage of it" and producers are "looking at not using 30 million heads of lettuce at the cost of Â£10m to the growers".
Over the course of the season, UK growers produce around half a billion heads of lettuce.
Asked if weather is a factor that has contributed to the issues, Lloyd said that short-term weather patterns and regional variations do have an impact.
"We had a problem with aphids last year, we've had a mild winter which traditionally might affect the aphid populations and then they do like warm weather."
The National Farmers' Union said that they are looking to support growers and researchers amid the outbreak.
Martin Emmett, the organisation's horticulture chairman, said: "This summer's warm and dry weather created a number of challenges for growers and the effects are still being felt, with rising levels of pests and disease now adding further pressure to farming businesses following an already difficult period.
"While growers are working hard to tackle record high numbers of aphids, the NFU is supporting the work of grower groups, plant breeders and researchers."

The Scoop
UN agencies are putting a premium on diversifying where they source technology and computing power â away from solely American providers. Last yearâs US sanctions on the International Criminal Court, and Anthropicâs Mythos model cutoff earlier this year, provided a âwake-up callâ about relying on single â mostly American â companies, the chief information officer of the International Telecommunication Union said.
Some UN groups are exploring shared computing and data infrastructure, which could give them more control over their sensitive data, leaving them less dependent on US cloud and AI companies, Khuloud Odeh told Semafor. Agencies are also thinking about exit plans for tech agreements that could be upended. Odeh leads tech and AI strategy at the UN agency that sets international tech standards, giving her a unique vantage point into how the UN system is adopting AI.
One concern is that the Trump administration has shown a willingness to restrict access to chips and AI models as part of its foreign policy, potentially disrupting the UN agenciesâ or non-US companiesâ operations.
Countries around the world are increasingly discussing tech sovereignty â a broad term that generally means having control and choice over data and tech systems â but the UN is in a particularly precarious spot given Washingtonâs retreat from global bodies and disdain for some specific groups.
âWeâre all being asked, what is our game plan if something like this happened? What would be an exit plan?â Odeh said. That doesnât mean a âwhole radical moveâ away from all US technology, she added, but rather making backup plans, creating more choices, and sorting systems by sensitivity.
âItâs something I think about with every choice I make now,â she said, adding that itâs a âcoreâ consideration for CIOs across UN agencies, which each have their own tech budgets and vendor relationships.
At a meeting of the UN technology chiefs in Valencia in May, officials discussed âsanctions-driven service suspensionâ and âextraterritorial data accessâ as risks to the UNâs cloud arrangements, according to a report.
Know More
Much focus, especially during this weekâs UN General Assembly session, is on how the international community, including the UN, could set global rules around AI. The UN and its dozens of agencies, funds, and programs â which collectively employ some 120,000 people â arenât often thought of as major enterprise users of AI.
A UN registry counts more than 1,000 AI use cases, including projects aimed at reducing hunger and getting more schools connected to the internet. Odeh said the conversation is shifting from experimentation to determining where to put more resources.
âItâs not really about a proof of concept. Now it needs to be a proof of value,â she said.
Some of the UNâs data is especially sensitive, like refugee records and health information, raising the stakes of where it is stored and processed.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian has told the UN General Assembly that it will never "bend the knee" after almost seven months of war with the US and Israel, but is ready for a diplomatic solution to the conflict.
Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, Pezeshkian said: "He must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying."
He also insisted any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ships and ports.
"It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access," he said.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed since the start of the war in late February due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US blockade.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Witkoff said he hoped the discussions â the first since June â would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work.
But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

0ab941fd5e23.text: By — John Seewer, Associated Press John Seewer, Associated Press By — Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/harvey-weinstein-is-sentenced-to-15-years-in-prison-for-2006-sex-crime-in-new-york Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Harvey Weinstein is sentenced to 15 years in prison for 2006 sex crime in New York Nation Sep 23, 2026 11:57 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison in a #MeToo reckoning redux after the disgraced movie producer's original conviction was overturned and a retrial last year ended with a jury again finding him guilty of a serious sex crime. Weinstein's sentencing Wednesday for sexually assaulting one-time TV production assistant Miriam Haley followed a legal odyssey spanning more than six years after he was first convicted and sentenced in 2020. In 2024, New York's highest court erased Weinstein's conviction and ordered a new trial, ruling that Weinstein was prejudiced by testimony from other women whose allegations weren't part of the case. READ MORE: Harvey Weinstein's lawyers question accuser Miriam Haley at rape retrial Tried for a second time last year, Weinstein was again convicted of a first-degree criminal sex act for pushing Haley into a bedroom at his Manhattan apartment and sexually assaulting her in 2006. The charge carried a maximum penalty of 25 years in prison. Weinstein, first publicly accused of wrongdoing in 2017 and arrested in 2018, has already served more than six years in prison as his case has cycled again and again through the criminal justice system. He has repeatedly denied raping or sexually assaulting anyone. This is a breaking news update. AP's earlier story follows below. NEW YORK (AP) — The first time Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to prison, reporters, advocates and the curious public crammed the courtroom to witness the disgraced Hollywood honcho's #MeToo reckoning. Hours later, the world began shutting down as the COVID-19 pandemic raged. Now, after an overturned conviction and two retrials, Weinstein is set to be sentenced again on Wednesday for one of the same crimes — more than six years after his first sentencing in March 2020. Weinstein, 74, faces up to 25 years in prison for sexually assaulting a one-time TV production assistant, Miriam Haley, at his Manhattan apartment in 2006. He has already served more than six years as his case has cycled again and again through the criminal justice system. Haley gave her account of the assault at two trials and spoke again in court Wednesday just before Weinstein was to be sentenced. "Having been sexually assaulted by Harvey Weinstein has had a devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away. Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come," Haley said. "It's a life sentence for me." "I've been further traumatized in exercising my right to hold him accountable. All of this traces back to his actions," she said, adding that she thought about ending her pursuit of justice many times. Minutes later, Weinstein apologized in court to those he may have hurt. "I do have remorse for Miriam Haley's pain, but I have to reiterate my innocence," he told the judge while seated in a wheelchair. Why Weinstein is being sentenced a second time The Oscar-winning "Pulp Fiction" and "Shakespeare in Love" producer was originally sentenced to 23 years in prison after a jury convicted him of assaulting Haley and raping an aspiring actress, Jessica Mann, in 2013. But New York's highest court erased those guilty verdicts in 2024, ruling that Weinstein was prejudiced by testimony from other women whose allegations weren't part of the case. Tried for a second time last year, Weinstein was again convicted of a first-degree criminal sex act for assaulting Haley, who has also gone by the name Mimi Haleyi. In a messy split verdict, the jury acquitted him of forcibly performing oral sex on another woman, Kaja Sokola, and could not reach a verdict on a rape charge involving Mann. After another retrial ended in a hung jury in May, Manhattan prosecutors dropped the rape charge rather than pursue a fourth trial after Mann said she could not bear to testify again. That decision cleared the way for Weinstein's sentencing. Weinstein's health issues are central to the defense's plea for leniency Manhattan prosecutors asked for 20 years in prison — which would keep him behind bars until at least his late 80s. Defense lawyer Jacob Kaplan asked that Weinstein receive a sentence of three more years on top of the six years he's already served, saying a longer sentence would make it more likely that Weinstein dies in prison. Weinstein is in failing health and has been in the hospital six times since 2025, Kaplan said, while dealing with blood cancer, congestive heart failure, and kidney issues. He has used a wheelchair now for several years. Weinstein has denied raping or sexually assaulting anyone. Once he's sentenced, he can appeal. "I will be proven innocent. That I promise you," Weinstein told The Hollywood Reporter in a jailhouse interview in March. Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate rape case in Los Angeles. A California appeals court upheld the 2022 conviction but threw out his original 16-year sentence because the judge had considered his New York convictions that were later thrown out as an aggravating factor. After shuffling between state prison, where he tested positive for COVID-19 early in the pandemic, and New York City's notorious Rikers Island complex, the ailing Weinstein is now housed at a medical unit for jail inmates at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan. His health issues in recent years have included chronic myeloid leukemia, diabetes and walking difficulties that necessitate a wheelchair to get in and out of court, his lawyers said. Maymead, a company that plans to build a controversial asphalt plant south of Winston-Salem, North Carolina, is suing a consulting firm and one of its former employees, alleging they committed fraud, civil conspiracy and deceptive trade practices in spearheading opposition to the project.
The former employee, Chris Hopkins of Tennessee, used an alias, Chris Sanderson, to infiltrate a neighborhood group in Clemmons near the proposed plant, Inside Climate News reported in early September.
Although Hopkins told neighbors he opposed the plant for environmental reasons, Maymead alleged in court documents filed in Forsyth County Superior Court that he and then-employer Land Use Strategies were working on behalf of an unnamed competitor to thwart Maymead’s project.
“There was no legitimate business purpose in defendants’ attempts to manipulate citizens and to use them as agents to manipulate the market for asphalt,” the legal complaint reads.
The company alleged that Hopkins’ subterfuge was intended to “protect his client’s market position and competitive and pricing advantage,” and “to create opposition where opposition did not exist, to disseminate information known to be false, misleading, or inaccurate about asphalt plants.”
Hopkins did not respond to text messages from Inside Climate News seeking comment for this article; an email bounced back. In a brief interview last month, he denied that Sanderson was an alias but refused to provide identification to prove his identity.
At the time, Hopkins was a partner with Land Use Strategies, which specializes in “grassroots coalition building,” strategic communications and public affairs on behalf of mining interests, data centers, landfills and other industries, according to the firm’s website.
After Inside Climate News emailed documents to Land Use Strategies showing Hopkins’ dual identities, the firm responded that he was no longer an employee. The firm also told Inside Climate News in an email that it didn’t know about the situation in Clemmons.
Land Use Strategies did not respond to an email and a phone call seeking comment about the lawsuit.
Tom Terrell, an attorney representing Maymead, told Inside Climate News that Hopkins and Land Use Strategies were not engaged in “protected political speech.”
“It was an illegal attempt to manipulate supply and demand to control market prices,” Terrell said.
Maymead is asking the court to force Hopkins and Land Use Strategies to pay attorney’s fees and more than $25,000 in financial damages. With court approval, Maymead plans to identify the competitor it alleges Hopkins was aiding once the name is disclosed in the discovery phase of the litigation.
Maymead is under contract to buy land along Gun Club Road for the plant, but it needs county approval of its air permit application before constructing the project. The application is still under technical review; if the county approves a draft permit, the public can comment on it before the final version.
Residents are petitioning Forsyth County officials to deny Maymead’s application over concerns about air pollution, truck traffic and noise. Each year the plant would emit 7 tons of health-harming particulate matter, 4.8 tons of cancer-causing formaldehyde, a half ton of cancer-causing benzene and many other air pollutants, according to the application.
The plant would lie within 2 miles of eight elementary schools, several parks, churches, day cares and hundreds of residences, including a mobile home community.
Several Clemmons residents previously told Inside Climate News that they felt “invaded” and “betrayed” by Hopkins.
Few neighbors knew about the proposal until Hopkins, posing as Sanderson, formed an anti-asphalt-plant Facebook group and an online neighborhood discussion list. He visited neighbors in their homes and emailed and spoke with local government officials. He ordered and paid $700 for flyers, stickers and signs. A resident looking at the flyer metadata found “Christopher Hopkins” listed as the document creator.
Therese Vick is a long-time community organizer with the nonprofit Blue Ridge Environmental Defense League who lives in Johnston County, southeast of Raleigh. She said she encountered company operatives who were trying to disrupt local opposition when fighting a hazardous waste incinerator in Northampton County in the 1990s and during the rapid expansion of the hog industry in eastern North Carolina.
Industry moles often leave clues that they are not who they claim to be, she said. Impersonators might suggest or advocate for violence, interfere with a group’s strategy, make big promises or try to undermine an organization’s leadership.
Other tells include “someone new who shows up during a contentious issue, whom no one knows, and who has no verifiable local connections, is evasive about where they live, has a vague background, foments division and has unreasonable curiosity about leaders,” Vick said.
Hopkins gave differing accounts of where he lived, residents told Inside Climate News, and said he had experience dealing with mining and asphalt issues, but was vague about the details.
“Grassroots community organizing isn’t new to North Carolina,” Vick said, “and neither are the pressure tactics that come with high-stakes industrial development.”
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert.
Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo.
It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately.
Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.
By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.
In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar.
Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added.
A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato.
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said.
"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response".
Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
There have recently been a number of suspicious fires and blasts at defence facilities in a number of European Nato members from Italy to Bulgaria to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.
Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig airport - an accusation denied by Moscow as "absurd".
And earlier this week, Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC that his country had already made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they would "not surrender" if attacked.
Ukraine said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train", while the Russian military said only that it had struck "railway infrastructure".

The Scoop
Paramount, looking to firm up its financial picture as it digests Warner Bros. Discovery, is looking for fresh sources of cash. Executives at the company have discussed asking Elon Musk to become part of a syndicate of equity investors into Paramount, according to people familiar with the matter.
Muskâs name is one of a number of wealthy individuals that Paramount CEO David Ellison has considered tapping for the syndicate, the people said. Musk and David Ellisonâs father, Oracle founder Larry Ellison, have long been close, and it is in part the elder Ellisonâs money â and connections â that made Paramountâs takeover of Warner Bros. possible. Larry Ellison has personally guaranteed more than $40 billion of the equity financing for Paramountâs acquisition of Warner Bros.
Larry Ellison invested $1 billion in Muskâs 2022 deal to take X, formerly Twitter, private. He also invested in Tesla in 2018, and served on the companyâs board of directors for years.
The size of a potential Musk investment could not be determined. A spokesperson for Paramount declined comment. Musk did not return a request for comment.
Rohanâs view
An investment from Musk would be a significant vote of confidence in the combined Paramount Warner Bros. from a businessman who also has a devoted retail investor following. A check from Musk or other big financial backers would also give Paramount a more diversified investor base, and reduce Larry Ellisonâs financial burden.
But having Musk in this deal would also be politically fraught: Muskâs dollars and political influence were concerning to Democrats during the 2024 election, given his control of X. The possibility of him having even partial ownership in CNN and CBS would likely raise alarm bells in Washington, even though it is unlikely Musk would have formal input over the companyâs operations.

US President Donald Trump will host Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Washington, with AI, trade and Taiwan expected to be on the agenda for the leaders of the global superpowers.
Xi will be greeted personally by Trump at Andrews Air Force Base on the eve of a White House state dinner and a military flyover.
The three-day trip marks Xi's first state visit to the US since 2015 and his third meeting with Trump in the past year.
Adding to the high-stakes state visit, a US-China trade agreement reached last year is set to expire in November.
The trade truce - reached in October 2025 as Trump and Xi met in South Korea - saw Washington suspend steep tariff increases on Chinese goods while Beijing eased back from restricting rare earth exports critical for manufacturing.
Experts said they will be watching for some sort of announcement around an extension of this agreement during the forthcoming state visit.
Xi's trip to Washington, which ends on Friday, will have plenty of pomp and pageantry, and includes lavish dinners, private tours and performances.
He will be accompanied by First Lady Peng Liyuan who is expected to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art with US First Lady Melania Trump on Thursday.
David Sacks, a fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the planned extravagant welcome by Trump as "really unprecedented".
"From meeting Xi Jinping at Andrews Air Force Base to having a flyover for Xi as well, this is not something afforded to any US ally," Sacks said, "much less an adversary like China.
"It's quite, quite stunning," he continued.
Trump is expected to address several issues as he meets Xi, particularly on tariffs and trade.
The US president has long criticised his country's trade deficit with China, which stands at more than $91bn (Â£68.2bn), according to the latest US Census Bureau data, external.
Also, Chinese rare earth exports to the US are down, external despite the agreement last October.
US and Chinese officials held trade talks on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, but failed to make meaningful progress ahead of the Xi visit, multiple sources told the BBC.
The talks focused on finding areas of agreement around non-tariff trade issues and agricultural exports, according to sources familiar with White House thinking.
US negotiators were expected to continue talks with Chinese counterparts in Washington on Wednesday after Xi's arrival.
Another likely talking point between Trump and Xi is artificial intelligence, a topic that David Firestein from the Bush China Foundation said has "climbed rapidly toward the top of the agenda" ahead of this visit.
China and the US are competing in what has been described as an AI arms race. But after a series of recent high-profile security incidents involving the emergent technology, there has been growing pressure on the Trump administration to regulate AI and slow its development.
Senator Bernie Sanders wrote on X this week: "For the sake of all humanity, Trump and Xi must negotiate a treaty NOW to pause AI and ban superintelligence before it's too late."
Trump's former White House adviser Steve Bannon and some Republicans in Congress have also warned about dangers posed by AI.
The president, who views the technology as vital to the US economy and a battleground in a global struggle for power, has been reluctant.
He views defeating China in the AI race as a primary objective. "Whoever wins AI, wins," Trump has said.
Firestein told the BBC he expects Trump and Xi to discuss ways for AI collaboration.
On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, and said the two had "very successful" talks on trade and AI.
Several AI and tech industry titans will attend a White House state dinner on Thursday, according to US officials.
Open AI's CEO Sam Altman, Jensen Huang, whose company Nvidia makes chips that power AI, and X boss Elon Musk are some of the dinner attendees.
Experts who spoke to the BBC said any major breakthroughs on AI or other issues are unlikely to occur during the Trump-Xi meetings this week.
Then there is Taiwan, which remains a diplomatic thorn.
The US Congress has approved a multibillion-dollar arms sale to Taiwan that awaits Trump's signature. He has held off for now, viewing the move as a bargaining chip with China.
Beijing has long vowed to "reunify" with self-governing Taiwan and has not ruled out the use of force.
Firestein said he expects Xi will be looking for Trump to either commit to extending the delay of the arms sale or somehow avoiding the sale altogether.
Xi - like Trump - is also facing economic headwinds at home, and is expected to use this visit to discuss deepening US-China trade.
However, that presents a potential political problem for Trump. Some members of his cabinet and his supporters view China with deep suspicion.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued a letter, external to Ford Motor Company in September, urging the company to cut ties with China due to national security concerns and protection of American jobs.
Regardless of the clear hurdles that remain before any new US-China deals are inked, it is clear that Trump views personal contact with Xi as vital to the process.
"Trump has made a decision that no matter what, we need to not have a confrontational relationship with China," Stephen Orlins, president at the National Committee on US-China Relations, said.
"He believes that the more he and President Xi meet, the less confrontational that relationship will be," Orlins continued, "and he is right."
With additional reporting by Daniel Bush, Washington correspondent

c3264e8dabfc.text: Chicago could halt new data center development within city limits for a year. Why it matters: Data centers' growing demand for electricity and water could affect residents' utility bills and the environment, and city leaders want more time to study those impacts. The latest: Mayor Brandon Johnson, along with a group of alders, is pushing for a 12-month moratorium while the city develops a "comprehensive regulatory framework" for data centers. There are 39 active data centers in Chicago, according to the city. Details: The proposal would give Johnson's Data Centers Task Force time to study the industry's impacts on clean air, clean water and energy use. What they're saying: "Chicago is open for business, but we are not for sale," Johnson said in a statement. "We welcome innovation, investment, and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents." Context: The announcement comes as other alders, including Ald. Bill Conway (34th), push their own ordinance to regulate data centers. "The Mayor's proposal risks months if not years of debate and litigation, all while data centers keep building, polluting, and spiking utility bills with zero community input," Conway said in a statement. Conway's ordinance would immediately subject data centers to additional zoning requirements and community and environmental reviews. Zoom out: Chicago wouldn't be alone. At least a half-dozen major U.S. cities, including Seattle, Charlotte, Baltimore, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Oklahoma City, have temporarily halted or restricted new data center development while considering new regulations. At the state level, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has paused new tax incentives for data centers, but has said he doesn't have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on construction. Illinois cities like Bloomington, Carbondale, Effingham, West Chicago and Mattoon have already paused new data center development or expansion. The other side: "As the City of Chicago faces significant and continuing fiscal and budgetary challenges, it's important to recognize that data centers are net revenue generators that provide billions of dollars in economic investment," Data Center Coalition's Brad Tietz said in a statement. "Unfortunately, the Mayor's proposed moratorium sends another signal that Chicago is closed for business." Friction point: Communities across the country are pushing back against proposed data centers over concerns about electricity demand , water use, pollution and other impacts. President Trump has criticized efforts to restrict them, writing on social media: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign." What's next: Both proposals will now make their way through the City Council, setting up a debate over how the city should regulate new data center development.

September's full Moon will be visible in UK skies this weekend, just days after the autumn equinox.
Known as the Harvest Moon, it will reach its fullest point at 17:49 BST on Saturday 26 September.
At that time it will still be below the horizon for much of the UK, but it will rise shortly afterwards and appear almost completely full throughout Saturday evening.
It gets its name from being the full Moon closest to the autumn equinox, which this year took place on Wednesday.
Why is it called the Harvest Moon?
September's full Moon is traditionally associated with the harvest, because historically, the additional moonlight after sunset was useful to farmers gathering crops.
The Royal Observatory Greenwich also lists the Corn Moon as another common name, reflecting the crops traditionally harvested around this time of year.
However, it does not always fall in September and if October's full Moon is closer to the autumn equinox, it takes the title instead.
Why can the Harvest Moon look red?
If you catch the Moon as it rises it may appear yellow, orange or even reddish.
This is not a special feature of the Harvest Moon, but simply that when it lies low in the sky and is close to the horizon, its light has to travel through more of the Earth's atmosphere before reaching our eyes.
More of the shorter blue wavelengths of light are scattered, allowing the yellows, oranges and reds to become more prominent.
Will the weather be clear enough to see it?
The current forecast suggests Saturday could bring some drier and brighter weather, particularly across parts of England. However, there is some cloud further west and rain for parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland by the evening.
The best chance of clearer skies currently looks to be across some southern and eastern parts of the UK, while conditions are expected to be more changeable elsewhere.
The exact times of the moonrise will vary across the UK but will be shortly after it reaches its fullest point.
Keep up to date with the weather where you are online or on the BBC Weather app.

373965b7010b.text: In his first-ever meeting with Venezuela's new leader, President Trump emphasized the need to keep oil flowing, relations warm and that country's elections on the horizon, White House sources tell Axios. Why it matters: Trump did not insist on a future election date in his meeting with Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodriguez , but he emphasized their importance as a crucial final step in Venezuela's evolution into a full-fledged democracy, the sources said. "You have to have elections at the end of the day," Trump said to Rodriguez at one point, one of the sources briefed on the meeting said. Zoom in: Trump held the roughly 15-minute meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to thank Rodriguez for their good working relationship after the U.S. ousted her one-time socialist ally, Nicolas Maduro, on Jan. 3. Since then, the Trump administration has struck oil and gold-mining deals with Venezuela, which had been a U.S. adversary for more than a quarter-century. Venezuela has one of the world's largest sovereign debt problems of $300 billion — larger than its gross domestic product — which needs to be restructured before the country holds elections, U.S. officials say. "The country can't succeed until that is solved," a White House official said. What they're saying: "We held a historic meeting with the president of the United States, Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security," Rodriguez posted Tuesday night on X. The post included a photo of Rodriguez holding up two fingers in a "V" (for Venezuela) and Trump giving his characteristic thumbs-up. Friction point: The photo outraged the small but vocal Venezuelan diaspora community in the U.S., where critics want to hear more about Venezuela elections and less about deals. On the same day Trump and Rodriguez met, allies of Venezuela opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Marina Corina Machado went public to complain that she has been blocked from re-entering the country. In the Miami area, home to both Secretary of State Marco Rubio and a sizable population of Venezuelan exiles and expats, Rubio's 2024 U.S. Senate opponent, former Democratic Rep. Debbie Mucarsel Powell, posted the image on X and urged people to register to vote. "Tell every single member of the South Florida delegation that you are done with the lies and the blatant corruption. No Mas!" she wrote . Between the lines: The U.S. wants Venezuela's elections to be called by Venezuelans via the country's new National Reconciliation Council, which represents various political parties in the country. It's a three-step plan: Change the composition of the Venezuelan Supreme Court to make it more representative of the country. The opposition is going to get to nominate justices, an official said. Reform the National Electoral Commission to ensure there's not a repeat of 2024, when it manipulated the vote count and stole the election from Edmundo González on Maduro's behalf. Announce an election date. Trump, however, pointedly did not say when he wants that to be. Inside the room : Trump and Rodriguez were joined by two Venezuelan officials as well as Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. Trump did most of the talking and also regaled Rodriguez with a description of the precision U.S. military operation that ousted Maduro. "It was warm. It was friendly. But it was also direct," one of the sources said about Trump's discussion of the importance of future elections. "She acknowledged it. She said she wants elections too," the source said. Zoom out: The multiple challenges Venezuela is facing from the legacy of socialist mismanagement to the earthquakes that damaged the country this summer make calling an election date even more complicated, U.S. officials say. "We don't want to have an election, have a democratically elected government take over and inherit an economic catastrophe within six months," said one. "A democratic government is going to be facing massive street protests over inflation, the economy. It could threaten the entire thing." The intrigue : By process of elimination, insiders say a Venezuelan election in the summer or fall of 2028 makes more sense because it would give the country more time to repair its finances and electoral system. Trump also would like to leave office with the legacy of removing a dictator, fixing a country and fostering democracy — but he might want to wait until the final months in office so the U.S. could still exert outsized influence on Rodriguez's government. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) has called for Venezuela to hold elections on July 24, 2027, but Trump administration officials and allies say that might be too early. "If can be in '27, that would be great. We would like that," an official said, cautioning that Venezuelans need to lead and need to fix their debt problem first. "Whether the date for those conditions to be met are 2027 versus 2028 is still up in the air," the official said. "It certainly can't go on indefinitely."

But it offers a window into how the progressive wing of the Democratic Party is approaching AI regulation ahead of November's midterms and a 2028 presidential campaign in which the technology is expected to be an increasingly prominent issue. (AP) — Police in Mississippi have arrested a second man in the death of a Black woman found hanging from a tree and have issued an arrest warrant for a third suspect. Jackson police said late Tuesday that they arrested 25-year-old Earnest Lloyd Jr. in the death of 29-year-old Tasia Fortune, whose body was found hanging behind an abandoned home in the city on Aug. 3. READ MORE: Man pleads not guilty in the hanging death of Tasia Fortune in Mississippi Like Fortune and the first man arrested, 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff, Lloyd is Black. He appeared at a brief hearing Wednesday in Jackson. Fortune's mother Christy Spivey, who attended the hearing, said afterward that she was ecstatic to see arrests made in her daughter's death. She said that neither she nor several of her daughter's friends knew Lloyd, and she cautioned that everyone is innocent until proven guilty. "My family is not the only family that this is affecting," Spivey said of the defendants' families. "I feel for them as well. The only difference is that mine can never come back. At least they can have telephone visits." "I'll never truly have peace," she said Ratliff was arrested in September on murder charges. He pleaded not guilty and remains jailed without bond. Police said in a statement that they issued an arrest warrant for a third suspect, but gave no details about that person's identity or alleged link to Fortune's death. They also said they expect to issue additional warrants. READ MORE: What we know about the death of Tasia Fortune in Mississippi After Ratliff's arrest, Jackson's police chief, RaShall Brackney, said Ratliff had an "association" with Fortune, but she didn't elaborate. Although police haven't suggested a possible motive for the killing or said whether they think race played a role, the case has attracted widespread attention because the manner of death recalled lynchings in the Southern state. A Kentucky native, Fortune had four children and had been living in Jackson for about a decade, relatives said. Spivey previously said her daughter struggled with homelessness in recent years, and that she wasn't sure where her daughter was living at the time of her death. She said that before her death, her daughter had talked about starting a cleaning business and was trying to get her life in order. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
