“Michigan’s lawsuit was part of a coordinated campaign against an industry that is vital to everyday life and serves as the engine of America’s economy. Climate policy is a federal, not state, issue, and we are pleased with the court’s decision,” Ryan Meyers, API senior vice president and general counsel, said in a statement.
BP declined to comment, while Chevron, ExxonMobil, and Shell did not respond to a request for comment.
Michigan has not yet announced whether it will try to appeal.
“The Attorney General disagrees with the opinion and order issued on the energy affordability antitrust case the Department brought on behalf of the People of the State of Michigan,” Danny Wimmer, press secretary for the Michigan attorney general office, said in an emailed statement. “Our office is reviewing the opinion in full and considering our options.”
The ruling comes after the same judge dismissed a lawsuit brought by the Trump administration last year to try to preemptively block Michigan from suing Big Oil over climate harm. Since that lawsuit was filed before Michigan had brought any sort of case, the alleged harm was too speculative, Beckering ruled.
The dismissal of Michigan’s antitrust case is the latest legal win for major oil and gas companies that are facing mounting demands for climate accountability through state laws and lawsuits. A federal court in Syracuse, New York, recently struck down New York’s landmark Climate Change Superfund Act that sought to make large fossil fuel producers pay for a portion of the staggering hundreds of billions of dollars the state is expected to incur to adapt to climate change. In March, the Maryland Supreme Court sided with fossil fuel companies in upholding a lower court ruling dismissing climate tort lawsuits brought by the cities of Baltimore and Annapolis and Anne Arundel County..
The U.S. Supreme Court, meanwhile, is slated to take up a climate tort case filed by Boulder, Colorado, against oil companies Suncor and ExxonMobil, in a hearing on Oct.5 that legal experts say could be “incredibly consequential” for the more than two dozen other climate lawsuits pending against the fossil fuel industry. If the court rules in favor of Suncor and Exxon on the question of whether federal law preempts state climate lawsuits, it could put an end to many of these cases.
“With the [climate] tort cases [the fossil fuel industry] has won some and lost some,” said Michael Gerrard, founder and faculty director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University.

e919428e4bc4.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/fbi-investigates-hackers-claim-to-have-stolen-employee-data-compromised-jobs-website Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FBI investigates hackers' claim to have stolen employee data, compromised jobs website Nation Sep 23, 2026 5:37 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI said Wednesday it was investigating a criminal hacking group's claims that it had stolen "very sensitive data" belonging to thousands of agents and applicants and that it had compromised the bureau's jobs website. "The FBI is aware of a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information," the FBI said in a statement. It said that while the "point of breach" was undetermined, "we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk." WATCH: Patel explains why FBI no longer considers bestiality an automatic hiring disqualifier A message that circulated online from a hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the hack. The jobs website, the main portal for prospective employees to learn about the FBI and initiate the application process, remained offline as of Wednesday afternoon. "We have compromised the FBI. We hold very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job," said the ShinyHunters message, which was directed to FBI Director Kash Patel and Brett Leatherman, the assistant director in charge of the bureau's cyber division. The claims could not immediately be verified. An email to an address associated with ShinyHunters was not immediately returned. In its message, ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations contained in an FBI public advisory from May that described the organization as a "cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion." That public service announcement characterized ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims," commonly harass or threaten victims and "may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist." ShinyHunters said in its message to the FBI that it was "offended" by those characterizations and demanded that the FBI remove those claims. It did not say what would happen if the FBI did not do so within a week. "This is not a ransom, coercion, or extortion. Your federal policies do not apply here. This PSA is NOT financially motivated," the hacking group's message said. The FBI, the nation's premier federal law enforcement agency, has been a common hacking target. In March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating "suspicious activities" on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of Patel's and posted online what appear to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work resume and other personal documents dating back more than a decade. The FBI described the compromised information as "historical in nature" and said it involved "no government information." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 21c29e036c8f.text: By — Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ai-firm-leaders-tell-un-security-council-that-it-could-be-a-risk-to-all-humanity Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AI firm leaders tell UN Security Council that it could be a risk to all humanity World Sep 23, 2026 5:23 PM EDT UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to set controls over the burgeoning technology they are designing in order to save the world — or, at least, its people. WATCH: Trump dismisses concerns about AI risks at UN, says he won't rein it in "If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," said Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of Anthropic. "We could lose control of the future to AI," said his competitor, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI. Both said the countries of the world, though the U.N. Security Council, where they testified Wednesday afternoon, have to set safeguards, which would be actual controls to prevent the technology from getting too powerful to rein in. They also called for the world to make sure that the power of AI isn't concentrated in one company or country. For world leaders, one key question about AI is this: Who should control life-and-death decisions — human or machine? The United Nations Security Council on Wednesday huddled with top technology leaders to figure out if the increasing abilities and pervasiveness of artificial intelligence should be controlled and, if so, by who. Other lingering questions: How could it be done? When might it be just too late? The day before, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of "killer robots." Experts and European leaders said that's not hyperbole but something that's already a reality or at least perilously close. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. âThereâs a sense of urgency. Candidates have got to start talking about it now. Theyâve got to talk about it in â28, and we have to act immediately when Congress returns,â Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., told reporters on Wednesday.

1b9ca9079822.text: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian forcefully rejected President Trump's portrayal of Iran as a source of terrorism at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, insisting instead that Iranians are "victims of terrorism." Why it matters: Pezeshkian used one of the world's biggest diplomatic stages to directly challenge Trump on U.S. soil — as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran rages on. What he's saying: "The United States president described us as terrorists," Pezeshkian said in a roughly 18-minute speech. "We have been the victims of terrorism… Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists." "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength," he said. "We live in a world in which the powerful, instead of thinking about humanity, justice, fairness, and democracy, they seem to be the protectors and creators of instability and destruction." Zoom in: Pezeshkian cited attacks that he blamed on the U.S., including strikes that killed children. He pointed to the deaths of more than 150 Iranians at an elementary school in Minab, including more than 120 children. A recent UN report found "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. committed a war crime in the strike. While the U.S. has not released findings of an investigation related to the attack, the AP has found evidence that at least one U.S. missile struck the school. Pezeshkian also mentioned the alleged deaths of children playing at a sports hall and an adjacent school after they were struck by a U.S.-made ballistic missile. Between the lines: The same UN report found that Iran's crackdown on protesters likely constituted "crimes against humanity." The report cited tactics including "murder, imprisonment, torture and other inhumane acts" as "part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians." What to watch: U.S. and Iranian officials held three hours of indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN on Tuesday, with Trump calling the meeting "very productive" and suggestions a deal remains possible. Iran has downplayed the breakthrough, saying its negotiating position has not changed — underscoring how far apart the two sides remain even as diplomacy continues. Go deeper: UN report: U.S. may have committed war crimes in Iran

216d3036e739.text: A district judge tossed an election interference lawsuit by President Trump against the Des Moines Register, parent company USA Today Co. (formerly Gannett) and pollster Ann Selzer , rejecting claims that its inaccurate pre-election poll amounted to consumer fraud. Why it matters : The dismissal is an early court test of Trump's broader push to use litigation against media organizations over coverage he disputes. Zoom in : In his ruling, Judge Scott Beatle said the plaintiff's attempt to use fraud law to allege liability on the poll was not a valid legal argument because political speech is protected by the First Amendment . "As such, the only question before the Court is whether the Petition states a claim the law recognizes," Beatle wrote. "At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability." "After considering the parties' arguments, the Court must conclude that the protection is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed," he wrote. What they're saying : "Today is a victory for the First Amendment—and for the essential role of a free press in American democracy. We are gratified that the Court recognized what this meritless lawsuit sought to obscure: that claims of "fake news" are little more than an attempt to punish news outlets for coverage those in power do not like," said Polly Grunfeld Sack, USA TODAY Co, Chief Legal Counsel. "A free press is fundamental to an informed public and a vibrant democracy. This decision reaffirms the enduring First Amendment principles that empower journalists and sends a message to those who think they can intimidate the press through legal action." The big picture : The lawsuit is part of a broader effort by Trump and his Administration to target media companies with legal action for what they believe is unfair coverage. To date, the courts have mostly sided with media companies, citing the strength of the First Amendment. What we're watching: The White House referred Axios to Trump's personal lawyers, who did not respond when asked whether they plan to appeal.

696e1d6a5988.text: The president of Iran told the United Nations General Assembly his country won’t bend to U.S. intimidation. Masoud Pezeshkian spoke one day after President Trump threatened to escalate the war from the same stage. On the sidelines, U.S. and Iranian officials signaled no breakthroughs in mediated talks. Nick Schifrin reports. Amna Nawaz: The president of Iran told the United Nations General Assembly his country won't bend to U.S. intimidation just a day after President Trump threatened to escalate the war from the very same stage. Geoff Bennett: On the sidelines, U.S. and Iranian officials signaled no major breakthroughs in mediated talks. Nick Schifrin has the latest after another busy day in New York. Nick Schifrin: It is a building on U.S. soil, an organization dedicated to peace, and never before has it hosted the leader of a country at war with its host until today. Masoud Pezeshkian, Iranian President (through interpreter): Yesterday, the United States president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism. Nick Schifrin: And on the same dais where President Trump yesterday delivered this threat... President Donald Trump: Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Nick Schifrin: ... Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian delivered his own defiance. Masoud Pezeshkian (through interpreter): We will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force. Nick Schifrin: Within minutes, the sole member of the U.S. delegation had heard enough and walked out of the room. But, inside Iran, Pezeshkian leads the faction that advocates for negotiation and economic integration with the West. He's losing that argument to hard-liners, who today threatened Iran's neighbors after they cooperated with U.S. sanctions banning Iranian airlines. Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iranian Supreme National Security Council (through interpreter): If any country joins the United States in this adventure, its airports will no longer be able to operate flights. The choice is yours. Marco Rubio, U.S. Secretary of State: Do they want to be a country or do they want to be a revolution? Nick Schifrin: Speaking right after Pezeshkian, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called yesterday's indirect talks between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and American mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner significant. But he said Pezeshkian's speech was the pot calling the kettle black. Marco Rubio: Slaughtering 10,000 of your own people in protests is a violation of the U.N. I hope it's a violation of the U.N. principles. I think sponsoring terrorist organizations in the region to attack your neighbors, attack energy infrastructure, attack civilian sites is a violation of the U.N. system. So I don't know what standing Iran has to lecture anyone on human rights or the international system when they habitually violate it. Nick Schifrin: But Rubio acknowledged that another violator of the international system, Russian President Vladimir Putin, is invited to Florida in December, when President Trump hosts the G20 in his Doral resort. Marco Rubio: We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president, but with other world leaders. We hope that's an invitation he will accept. Nick Schifrin: But, today, Kyiv was filled with the sound of Russian drone strikes. Authorities said at least two people were killed and dozens injured... Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: De-escalation steps are important, are needed before winter, now. Nick Schifrin: ... as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned the war could escalate. And as Ukraine begins to rely on autonomous weapons, Zelenskyy warned the AI future could become the present. Volodymyr Zelenskyy: As early as next year, there is already a real possibility that AI, not only people, will begin -- will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield. And we need peace before we reach that point. Dario Amodei, CEO and Co-Founder, Anthropic: That AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole. Nick Schifrin: Today, the Security Council held its first ever U.N. General Assembly AI meeting, including warnings from American AI leaders. Sam Altman, CEO, OpenAI: No one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their world view on everyone else. Nick Schifrin: But, in this chamber, the flawed but still only international body whose resolutions are legally binding, it fell to the co-chair of the U.N.'s independent AI panel, Yoshua Bengio, to warn the world it must police AI companies and issue a clarion call for collaboration. Yoshua Bengio, Co-Chair, U.N. Independent International Panel on AI: Today, a handful of companies and countries are acting in their self-interest by taking reckless risks with humanity's fate. Our future, all of us, our future is at stake. Decisions that affect us all should be made by us all. The choice is still ours, but we must act now to correct the trajectory. Nick Schifrin: This year's U.N. General Assembly theme is Restoring Trust, a U.N. that delivers for all. This week, that sentiment has been fleeting, as many here are worried the future feels fractured and uncertain. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Nick Schifrin.

c915484c7943.text: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. At the same time, a federal judge heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning the outlets from the White House. Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington this evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. And at the same time, a federal judge today heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning them from the White House. Our Liz Landers is at the White House covering both stories, and she joins us now. So, Liz, we will start with this state visit. What is the focus of it? Liz Landers: Yes, Geoff, President Trump is greeting leader Xi right now at Joint Base Andrews here in Washington for an arrival ceremony that has all the pomp and circumstance of this major state visit. This is the first time that Xi has been to the White House since 2015. And President Trump visited China back in May and was not awarded this same kind of pomp, circumstance and arrival. In particular, Xi did not greet him when he landed there in China back in May. You're seeing some of those images now. I will remind our viewers that those images are from several months ago because the White House TV pool is still not covering the president's events today. We believe that there are going to be a number of issues that will be addressed during this visit. A senior administration official told us earlier that AI, artificial intelligence, of course, will be on the top of the list, also some of these export controls that the United States has on our computing chips and selling those to China. The possibility of reducing tariffs on some goods is apparently going to come up, and also political prisoners. Several China watchers and experts that I have spoken with don't really think that this meeting is going to be so much about deliverables as it is about continuing to forge that personal relationship that President Trump has with leader Xi. I spoke earlier today with Kyle Chan. He's a fellow at the Brookings institute. And he was actually talking about these export controls, saying that matters less and less for the Chinese government because they are going all out to build their own AI chips themselves. And when it comes to artificial intelligence in particular, you heard some of that addressed from the U.N. today in Nick's story. China is not interested in a joint slowdown of AI development, according to Chan. He says that they're more worried about cyber risks, hacking companies, and they don't share, China does not share the same concerns that we have heard from U.S. AI companies and leaders recently that robots, AI may kill us all in the near future. Geoff, one more thing I want to add. Not everybody is happy about this visit and all of the accoutrements that are being laid out for President Xi. Republican Senator Wicker, he's the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, says that he would have advised against this lavish welcome to what he calls a brutal dictator. Geoff Bennett: And, Liz, there's a state dinner tomorrow evening. Who is expected to be in attendance? Liz Landers: Well, Geoff, as you would imagine, with all of this talk of AI and technology, there are leaders from several major business companies and AI companies that are going to be at the White House tomorrow. A senior administration official says that Jeff Bezos will be there, as well as Elon Musk, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, a chipmaker, and Sam Altman of OpenAI. The first lady, Melania Trump, said in a FOX News interview today that President Trump wanted to have the state dinner because they have a great relationship. She said that she's been involved in every detail of the planning for the state dinner tomorrow night. And she also -- and I'd also just add that this is only the second state dinner that President Trump has now had in his second term in office, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: All right, Liz, in the minute we have left, bring us up to speed on this lawsuit involving the three news organizations that were banned from the White House by President Trump. Liz Landers: There was a hearing on this, this afternoon, and the judge in this case, a district judge here in Washington, said right off the bat that he was skeptical of the argument that the Trump administration, that the Trump White House is making here on due process grounds. It sounds like the judge believes that the due process of these news organizations was violated. The government is arguing in a filing that they issued late last night that news organizations failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House. This has now turned into a conversation about national security. That is what the president and the administration are arguing is at stake here, that these news organizations somehow violated national security there. The judge also seemed skeptical of that, Geoff. We still do not have an answer from the judge as to whether the ban on Politico, CNN, and MS NOW will be lifted. Geoff Bennett: Liz Landers outside the West Wing at the White House for us tonight. Liz, thanks so much. Liz Landers: Of course.

f69192fcdb5a.text: By — Geoff Bennett Geoff Bennett By — Doug Adams Doug Adams Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/former-kansas-gop-governor-explains-why-hes-backing-democrat-adam-hamilton-for-senate Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Audio Former Kansas Gov. An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI "infiltrated" an Australian government website in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said.
The agent gained unauthorised accessed to a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive Medicare information", Albanese told a news conference at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Medicare refers to Australia's universal healthcare scheme. The breach is among the first publicly reported AI-led hacks of a government website in the world.
OpenAI said it only became aware of the incident in August "during an ongoing review of OpenAI misaligned model activity", and informed Australian officials on 10 September.
While the review is ongoing, a spokesperson for the AI firm said that it is not believed that any patient records were accessed.
Albanese said the breach occurred in June this year, but OpenAI only informed government officials via email on 10 September.
The prime minister said he spoke directly to CEO of OpenAI Sam Altman to say that it had taken "too long" to inform authorities and "to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident".
He said the agent accessed both public and non-public files and a "forensic investigation" is under way to find out if other government systems were affected.
The investigation will be led by the Australian Signals Directorate, the country's cybersecurity agency.
The public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal is administered by Services Australia, the main hub to redirect users to government services.
He told reporters: "No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing.
"Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable."
Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firm named Hugging Face.

8f0099869568.text: Meta on Wednesday debuted "Muse Charm," a new, keychain-sized AI handheld device it will use to bring its viral Muse assistant to the masses. Why it matters: Meta's has raced ahead of OpenAI , Apple and other companies that are racing to build a new crop of small AI devices, revving up the massive market interest that Muse has generated in the market. Driving the news: The Muse Charm will be available for purchase by December, and the company is the first tech giant to unveil its plans for an entirely new category of device. OpenAI has spent billions to build a hardware division, so Meta's advance on the category is likely to stun many analysts and investors. Meta has also poured billions into hardware, most notably VR, an effort that most analysts have written off as a waste. Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has long held that a convergence of those investments with AI could make that bet pay off. Catch up quick : In addition to Charm, Meta announced new Muse capabilities including live video chat, real-time voice conversations with custom voice options and an e-mail address for each person's agent. Meta announced new retail partners, including Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Wayfair and more, a growing list that makes Amazon's decision not to allow Muse stand out. Muse has prompted a stock selloff in recent days as investors fear an end to stickiness between brands and customers. Meta said Muse is coming soon to its AI glasses, though it declined to be more specific than "in the coming months." "I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives," CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during his Meta Connect keynote on Wednesday. Zuckerberg said that Meta's business model behind Muse is a novel one. "We believe that Muse will make you money, and we're standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions," he said. Beyond Muse, Meta used the event to debut a range of new hardware along with new privacy options that could make the gear more palatable to the mainstream. Meta's first audio-only glasses aim to appeal to those who want the benefit of open-air sound and an always available AI assistant without the cost and potential creepiness that comes from the camera-equipped version. The new models, which will be available later in October, start at $349. Meta is also updating its Meta Ray-Ban and Meta Glasses lines with modest improvements and new designs. The more radical shift is coming on the VR side of things . Meta previewed a much slimmer, $1,299 headset due out next spring. The Meta VR glasses shift the computing, battery and storage to a separate, wired puck, allowing for a 5K display in glasses that weigh just 100 grams. The headset relies entirely on voice, hand gestures and eye gaze to control a range of apps across games, entertainment and productivity. The big picture: Meta has invested heavily in glasses and AI over the last several years. Now it sees those giant bets converging. "It just feels really clear that [AI]'s what's going to enable the next big platform," said Alex Himmel, Meta's vice president of wearables. "You're really starting to see that vision of VR and AR converging into glasses, starting to happen sooner." Between the lines: Meta is continuing a big shift on the privacy front. The company had already said it is working on a confidential virtual machine option for the Muse assistant. On Wednesday, Meta added that it is also readying "Private Processing" for AI glasses, a system designed to keep data protected even while it is being processed in the cloud, similar to Apple's Private Cloud Compute.

"Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off.
She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water.
Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well.
They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities.
They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September.
Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety.
Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days.
Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.
It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes after the collapse of Nova Khakova Dam in 2023, flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.
Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education.
Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.
Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city.
Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive.
"There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May.
"I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it."
Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains.
Which weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food.
No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago.
While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger.
Warning: Distressing and graphic descriptions of dead bodies below.
Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, external - about 24km to the east.
Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher.
Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army.
She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information.
"I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth â I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine."
While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones.
Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety.
"They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said.
Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder.
They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana.
Russia's occupation authorities demand those deaths are confirmed by post mortem examination carried out by a Russian doctor, the BBC has been told. That is not possible in Oleshky.
Only those who die of natural causes could be buried, she added, and as a result, "some bodies have been on the streets since December".
Bodies are "either getting piled" up in the local hospital morgue, "where there's been no power since winter", says volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova, or "stray dogs eat them".
That detail has been verified by the BBC based on numerous pictures obtained from residents. They are all too graphic to publish.

93bf3c30c625.text: Meta's new virtual reality glasses take a big step toward being something an average person might be willing to wear, ditching much of the bulk as well as the need for handheld controllers. Why it matters: Unlike Meta's Ray-Bans, its VR devices have struggled to break out of their gamer niche and into the mainstream. Yes, but: In order to slim down the size, the new Meta VR glasses require a wired "puck" that can be held or clipped onto a belt. It contains much of the device's computing horsepower, including its processor, battery and storage. Zoom in: I spent about half an hour on Tuesday getting to use a prototype of the new specs, which are controlled through a combination of eye-tracking, hand gestures and voice commands. Magnetic prescription inserts attach easily, similar to the approach Apple took with Vision Pro. Zoom out: The glasses are designed to serve a range of purposes from watching a movie or immersive concert to playing games and getting work done. I played a re-imagined version of Beat Saber that cleverly re-maps the music game for control via hand motions. I watched a clip from last year's NBA finals. I used a trio of virtual monitors to do some "vibe coding" on a website, with one display showing the Muse terminal and another previewing the site itself. Meta sees these VR glasses as a "general device," Meta VP of product Angela Chang told Axios. "It's not built for any specific use case per se." My thought bubble: It's the most practical combination I've seen of an Apple Vision Pro-class device in a headset I'd be willing to wear outside of the house. The big picture: Google is working on a similar device, known as Project Aura, set to debut later this year and built in partnership with Xreal. Meta touts its wider field of view and higher optical quality, among other advantages over Aura. Between the lines : As for why it won't arrive until next spring, Meta executives say they want to be sure it makes a good first impression, especially inside a VR ecosystem. "We really are trying to strive for a very high bar on the software quality and experience side," Chang said. Bottom line : Meta said it has modest expectations for unit sales, but says success will look like attracting folks beyond gamers, Chang said. "Are we bringing in new people into VR who, you know, maybe in the past would have looked at the Quest and said, 'Nah, that's not for me?'"

Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.
Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".
European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental.
"Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame".
"It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.
'Sex positivity'
Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change".
Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming.
The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations.
Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine.
But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen.
Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaam haar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaam been" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaam lice" for pubic lice.
However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives.
The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda WindmÃ¼ller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change "Shamlippen" to "Vulvalippen".
WindmÃ¼ller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations.
When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame.
"Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but WindmÃ¼ller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines.
Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home.
'Virginity membrane'
Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign.
The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mÃ¶domshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity.
The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once.
"With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says.
Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs".
In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy".
She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria, external - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion."
The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them."
'Judgmental words'
Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first.
"Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?"
New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion.
Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss.
One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue.
"Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen, external.
Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected.
"Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen."
In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases.
But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress.
"I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact."

07aac6328164.text: Senate Majority Leader John Thune plans to run for another term as GOP leader, even if Republicans lose the chamber's majority, he told Axios in an exclusive interview Wednesday in his Capitol office. Why it matters: Thune (R-S.D.) is giving his senators broad leeway and tons of cash to preserve GOP control of the Senate. "I do see the Senate as a firewall in a lot of ways," Thune told Axios. "We will spend probably the next two years — if the House flips — trying to do impeachment or investigations, etc.," he said. Otherwise, the chamber will focus on judicial and executive nominations. Zoom out: Thune has three ways to help in the "tough environment" for Republicans in 2026. 🪧 1. Run against Washington: Thune said he understands if GOP candidates need to rhetorically distance themselves from Congress or even fellow Republicans in D.C., including himself. And when it comes to distancing from President Trump: "In some places the president's coming in, some places he isn't." Candidates can draw their own conclusions, Thune said. Republican candidates are increasingly concluding that to win their races, they need to break with Trump on some issues. 🗳️ 2. Vote for your state: Thune's policy with senators is " don't surprise us and when you can, stay with the team," but "do what's in the best interest of you and your state." That could lead to a rebuke of Trump when Democrats force another vote on an Iran war powers resolution, expected before the Senate breaks for October. People's views have "evolved and changed" as the war has dragged on, he said. Many senators are "responding to what they're hearing back home." "That's a really hard vote," Thune acknowledged. " Any time you are committing your country to putting young men and women in harm's way — those are the hardest votes you'll make." He hopes Republicans will stick together to win the vote. What to watch: Thune wants to give Republicans more votes before the break to champion back home. He sees an opportunity with permitting reform legislation, which is being negotiated behind the scenes. Thune said it's possible he sets up a procedural vote on it after the final vote on the Protect College Sports bill. Thune is also floating a vote on the House-passed legislation targeting data center energy costs if the Senate remains in town next week. 💰 3. Spend cash like crazy: The Thune-linked Senate Leadership Fund is set to spend nearly $280 million in video advertising this year — more than any other group, according to AdImpact. Texas PAC, which is affiliated with SLF, is on track to spend another $112 million. " Texas is expensive ," Thune said, but "we're doing everything we can to help. We can't afford to lose Texas." The bottom line: "That's ultimately up to the conference," Thune emphasized when asked if he'd run again if the GOP lost the majority, but "that's the plan." "The elections are going to be really important — I think – in how we view what happens next." Thune said you can't "rule anything in or out" when asked if he could face a challenger for the position. "But I think we worked really hard to create an environment here that is conducive to individual senators being able to achieve their objectives," he said. "I think, in this job, you have to be a good listener."

You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.
You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.
Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen.
"Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."
Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June.
It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.
FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.
The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel.
What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?
The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.
Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.
Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.
He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".
What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared.
"Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.
Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.
Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.
Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.
Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.
Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience".
"Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.
Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction.
"To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."
What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.
Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'".
But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.
Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve.
"While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.
But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace.
Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate".
"The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission

d632fdebcd72.text: By — Jeffrey Brown Jeffrey Brown By — Anne Azzi Davenport Anne Azzi Davenport By — Courtney Norris Courtney Norris Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/marlon-james-explores-how-homophobia-shaped-life-in-jamaica-in-the-disappearers Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Audio Marlon James’ new novel, "The Disappearers," was shortlisted for the Booker Prize. It tells the story of a group of gay men trying to make their way, and stay alive, in the homophobic culture of Jamaica in the 1980s and 90s. It’s raw, violent and sexually explicit, while also leavened with wit and humor. Jeffrey Brown spoke with James for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Listen to this Segment Watch Watch the Full Episode PBS NewsHour from Sep 23, 2026 By — Jeffrey Brown Jeffrey Brown In his more than 30-year career with the News Hour, Brown has served as co-anchor, studio moderator, and field reporter on a wide range of national and international issues, with work taking him around the country and to many parts of the globe. As arts correspondent he has profiled many of the world's leading writers, musicians, actors and other artists. Among his signature works at the News Hour: a multi-year series, “Culture at Risk,” about threatened cultural heritage in the United States and abroad; the creation of the NewsHour’s online “Art Beat”; and hosting the monthly book club, “Now Read This,” a collaboration with The New York Times. When Meta first launched its AI-powered smart glasses in 2023, in collaboration with the trendy sunglasses brand Ray-Ban, it unleashed a storm of controversy.
There have been multiple reports of the devices being used to harass women and girls in particular, filming them without their consent, then sharing the footage.
The image problem doesn't seem to have been cured by Meta's enlistment this summer of Kylie Jenner, Kim Kardashian's sister, as their prime model. The devices have been dubbed "pervert" or "creepy" glasses. In the UK, JD Wetherspoon pubs, a handful of major theatres, Comic-Con, some schools, and Faslane, home of the UK's nuclear submarines, have all chosen to ban them.
On Thursday, Meta is unveiling a new version which does not contain a camera at all, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. They will have the audio functions of the original glasses - including the ability to make phone calls or play music, with the sound funnelled directly into your ear - but with fewer implications for privacy.
To some in the industry, it looks like an interesting pivot - a response, perhaps, to the backlash over privacy.
The tech giant denies that the new glasses have been rushed out in response to public anger. They say the product has been in development for two years. The audio-only version is cheaper than its camera-enabled cousins, and Meta says it has a lighter frame and better battery life.
When I put it to Meta Glasses' head of product Ankit Brahmbhatt that I thought they might overtake the original camera-enabled glasses in sales, there was a pregnant pause.
"We have, I think, something for everyone," he said, choosing his words very carefully.
Does the release of a camera-free option represent a shift in how tech companies see the future of smart glasses? And is Meta's original vision getting further away?
Or should we see camera-free glasses as a niche side-product that serves a small market - a bit like how some mobile manufacturers are now releasing internet-disabled "brick" phones for people who are tired of social media?
Music, maps, and washing cars
There's no doubt that smart glasses have become controversial.
I was lent a pair of Meta Ray-Bans â with cameras - to try out. I was initially nervous about wearing them in public, in case someone got physical: I have heard of people knocking them off wearers' heads and smashing them in the street.
The reality was that I wore them on public transport and on foot in several cities including London, Glasgow and Portsmouth, and nobody batted an eyelid. It made me wonder whether awareness of them is really as high as both Meta and anti-glasses campaigners believe.
That said, some people quietly told me they would not be confident enough to approach someone wearing them even if they did spot them, for fear of the interaction being filmed and uploaded.
The glasses are designed to work as an extension of your phone. They use Bluetooth to sync with a handset via Meta's AI app. They are voice-activated, with open speakers in the arms funnelling sound into your ears. The result is a bit like wearing headphones without the addition of noise-cancelling features, so you can still hear the world around you.
My potentially cancellable opinion is that I found many of the glasses' features useful. Interestingly, none of them included the camera.
Listening to music and podcasts on the move without having earbuds stuffed into my ears felt safer. I felt more confident about avoiding the gamut of e-bike-riding phone thieves in central London without my phone physically in my hand.
And as someone with a pitiful sense of direction, I rely a lot on map apps. It was handy to have the directions spoken in my ears. The pay-off for this, however, was having to accept allowing the Meta AI app to know exactly where I was at all times. Meta is notorious for its hunger for personal data.
When I posted about using the Meta Ray-Bans on social media, I got a bit of a hard time. Less so when I showed them to people in my everyday life.
My hairdresser loved the idea of using them to record her clients' hair transformations. A builder I chatted to at the gym reckoned they would be useful on sites for recording what he was doing, either in the event of an accident or even to teach others new skills. My friend who runs said he would like to wear them on a jog.
Plenty of content creators are big fans. My son borrowed them to wash my car, and was proud of his film showing me how he delicately chipped away at a stubborn bit of bird poo without damaging the paintwork (I was pleased, and happy to take his word for it).
More broadly, smart glasses have been welcomed by the blind community. One user described them to the BBC as a "game-changer" because they can give audio descriptions of current locations and read out visible text like restaurant menu options. Earlier this year Meta donated 15,000 pairs to a charity for the blind in Ireland.
Calls for regulation
But still, anger over privacy has grown.
The glasses have a blinking white LED that switches on when the camera is active, but a whole industry has sprung up around finding technical workarounds to disable that light, some of which involve taking the glasses apart.
Meta says less than 0.1% of the frames it has sold worldwide have been physically tampered with. Exact sales figures are unknown, but Ray-Ban's parent company EssilorLuxottica has reported that it sold seven million last year.
Liz Hunter, a tech founder and parent who has set up a petition calling for urgent new regulation of smart glasses, is furious.
"They should never, ever have left the lab at Meta," she told me. "It's a real travesty of public trust, and of women's equality, and it's rolled back our privacy rights right before our very eyes."
Hunter thinks smart glasses should remain available for blind people, but not for the general population.
"We don't need them, we don't want them," she says.

- Published
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during their lengthy deployment.
The disclosure was made in a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York on Tuesday in response to questions from the Democrat on the well-being of sailors onboard following mounting concerns.
Family members of sailors had raised alarm about deteriorating mental health and grim conditions during a prolonged mission in the Middle East as part of the US war in Iran.
The carrier, which had been deployed since last November, is now returning to the US. The BBC has contacted the US Navy for comment.
In his letter, Cao said that there were five chaplains and multiple mental health professionals available on board to meet the "spiritual and emotional needs of the crew".
He said the eight sailors included "the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons".
While the US Navy has previously acknowledged supply challenges on the carrier, it denied that a mental health crisis was taking place on the Lincoln, which had some 5,000 crew aboard.
Cao's letter also denied widespread concerns about broken plumbing and shortages of fresh food, but acknowledged temporary "localized piping failures" and problems with the reverse osmosis desalination units, and some meal options were reduced for a "short time".
Senator Gillibrand, a member of the Senate's armed services committee, criticised the Trump administration's previous responses to reports of grim conditions, calling the treatment of service members "completely unacceptable".
"What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," she said in a statement to the BBC on Wednesday.
"Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect," she added.
The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February. The deployment, which was originally set to end in May, was repeatedly extended.
In August, the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier, was sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln following a nine-month deployment.
US sailors stopped in Thailand on their way home, hitting bars, malls and beach areas in their first time on land before continuing on to the US.
Suicide remains a leading cause of death in the US Navy and Marines, according to an analysis of military data by USNI News, while veterans have higher rates of suicide than Americans who have not served in the military, according to the Veterans Administration.
A study, external of 956 sailors released in January 2025 found that troops aboard US Navy ships suffer the highest rates of "serious psychological distress" compared to other branches of the US military.
The study cited "unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest".
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line or you can call the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline on 988.

For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.
As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.
Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table.
"A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department.
"When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."
The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.
The state health department told the BBC it has administered nearly 4,300 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines at pop-up clinics near the epicentre of the outbreak since it began in late April.
But even as health officials see success in their vaccine programmes, the state has reported four deaths from measles complications, marking the most deadly outbreak the US has seen since 1992.
The infections have led to tensions between state and federal health officials, including vaccine-skeptic Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
Those politics are back of mind in the Amish community, where people are growing fearful of more deaths as they watch their friends and family fall sick with the disease, which for decades has been eliminated in the US.
"They're not a community that's as easy to reach - we can't just put up a social media post," Weiser said. "They are suffering at the moment, and we're trying to reach out and make connections."
Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.
About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.
There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said.
"A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.
Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated.
"Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."
He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials.
Boots on the ground
Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.
Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.
Since the outbreak started, the county has given 538 MMR vaccines, 340 of which they administered in private settings.
"People have called up and said, 'I can't get to your clinic, or, I don't want people to know I've changed my mind," Franklin said. "'If you can come to us, that's a lot easier.'"
The boots-on-the-ground approach has helped the health department dispel misinformation and build trust with the community, local health officials said.
In recent years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across the country as false theories about the safety of the measles vaccine have proliferated on social media.
Those theories have found roots even in an insulated community with limited access to computers, Weiser said. She has heard people ask if there are heavy metals in the vaccine that could make them magnetic, or if the shot has a computer chip in it.
"You're clearly getting information from that hard-core group that is promoting that misinformation and disinformation," she said.
People in this "hard-core group", who are staunchly against vaccines, are unlikely to be swayed, experts and officials themselves said.
But now, local health officials said, many affected by the Pennsylvania outbreak are seeing their neighbours fall seriously ill and asking thoughtful questions. Weiser said many are parents who are unfamiliar with the shots and are scared to make the wrong choice for their children.
"There is the classically-defined anti-vaxer, versus people who are unaware or their culture feels differently," Franklin said. "The thinking and the willingness to discuss and possibly change your mind is different between those two bookends."

887b865fc202.text: The Trump administration is pushing for three immediate steps in its effort to de-escalate the war in Ukraine and restart diplomacy with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview on Wednesday: A ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Reopening the Black Sea grain corridor. A trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting, possibly in Abu Dhabi. Why it matters: President Trump is engaged in a renewed effort to revive a diplomatic track to end the war, but his immediate priority is a deal to halt Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel fuel — which have contributed to punishing prices in the U.S. and globally. But after several days of diplomacy and meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week, an energy ceasefire looks elusive. It's unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin even wants it. Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev will arrive in New York on Thursday for a meeting with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to discuss the latest U.S. proposals, according to a source with direct knowledge. Driving the news: Zelensky spoke with Trump on Tuesday in New York about efforts to end the war and a possible energy ceasefire. Later on Tuesday, Witkoff and Kushner met with Ukraine's negotiations team and the national security advisers of France, the UK and Germany. Zelensky told Axios the proposal for a mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure came from the U.S. and that Ukraine is ready to agree. "On the table now there is a proposition: energy ceasefire. We are ready," he said. Zelensky added that the U.S. is also seeking to reopen the grain corridor and convene a trilateral meeting between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia. Zoom in: The last U.S.-Ukraine-Russia meeting took place in February before the war with Iran. Since then, negotiations have gone into a deep freeze. Zelensky said he told Trump he would prefer to hold a trilateral meeting and make an energy ceasefire one of its first concrete outcomes. The U.S. raised the possibility of first holding a meeting between technical teams, as opposed to a meeting at the leaders level. It floated Abu Dhabi as a possible venue, Zelensky said. "We are open — any country, any format," he said. The Ukrainian president said he told Trump during their meeting that December's G20 summit in Miami could also be an opportunity for a leader-level trilateral summit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that Trump invited Putin to attend the summit. Zelensky also said simply getting the three sides into the same room would itself be a significant step toward de-escalation. Catch up quick: The current push for resuming negotiations started three weeks ago when CIA director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow. It was followed by Witkoff and Kushner traveling to Moscow and Kyiv. They met Putin for three hours in Moscow on Sept. 5 and then traveled to Kyiv to meet Zelensky. After they returned, Trump had a long phone call with Putin. Behind the scenes: Zelensky said Witkoff and Kushner were very optimistic when they briefed him after meeting with Putin. "They said, 'We think that Putin is ready.' I said, 'Look, I'm not sure,'" Zelensky recalled. According to Zelensky, the U.S. envoys responded: "No, we are close." Zelensky said he told them he was ready to discuss an energy ceasefire and other de-escalation steps but remained skeptical Putin would follow through. Yes, but: Zelensky said he continues to doubt Putin's intentions and believes the Russian leader could find reasons to avoid a trilateral meeting with leaders present. On Wednesday, the Kremlin said the conditions aren't ready for resuming peace talks with Ukraine and that there is no prospect at the moment for high-level meetings between the parties. Minutes before Zelensky spoke to Axios, Russia launched multiple ballistic missiles toward Kyiv. Zelensky received several updates on his phone about the additional missile attacks throughout the interview. What they're saying: Zelensky said Trump was "very positive" about the diplomatic push during their meeting Tuesday. Trump told him, "We will try," Zelensky said. "I said, 'Great, and really wish you not only to try [but] to succeed,'" Zelensky recalled. Zelensky stressed that Kyiv wants progress before winter sets in, regardless of the U.S. political calendar. Between the lines: The U.S. has its own economic interest in an energy ceasefire. Zelensky said American officials told him that reducing attacks on energy infrastructure was important because of the impact on energy prices. State of play: Zelensky said he spoke Tuesday with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and officials from India, the UAE and Egypt about the ceasefire effort and reopening the grain corridor. Those countries are also talking to Russia, he said. "Everybody wants [a] ceasefire. The corridor has to work again. We support [it]. They speak with Russians, I know. We will see," Zelensky said. What's next: Zelensky said Witkoff, Kushner and his team held follow-up talks after his meeting with Trump and agreed to continue working on the proposals and convey messages to Moscow. Ukrainian officials said some elements still need to be developed over the next two weeks before the Americans take them back to the Russians. Zelensky said he expects Trump to focus first on trying to secure the energy ceasefire.
