The Scene
Greg Brown became chief executive of what was then Motorola in 2008. But itâs only in the last decade that he thinks he has become âa reasonably good CEO.â And he credits a series of career-threatening encounters with activist and private equity investors for getting him there.
Motorola invented the mobile phone, but by the time Brown was handed the reins, its cellphone business had been outpaced by Nokia and Samsung. Apple had introduced the iPhone just two months earlier, and Brown concluded that his company had no future in smartphones, which were losing hundreds of millions of dollars a quarter.
âWe were a year and a half to two years away from bankruptcy, extrapolating out,â he recalls in an interview for The CEO Signal.
Brown resolved to spin off the mobility business for which his brand was best known, and says now that âthere wouldnât be a firmâ if he had not done so in 2011. That let him start to build the new Motorola Solutions, an overlooked âjewelâ¦ buried in the bowelsâ of the parent company, as a leader in critical public-safety technologies. It now provides police forces, school districts, and hospitals with tools ranging from communications networks and AI-assisted video analysis to drones and defense equipment.
But the separation that set Brownâs company on a path to todayâs $75 billion valuation nearly didnât happen. As directors wobbled at the eleventh hour, debating whether to keep the company together and âget rid of Brown,â he confronted them with a back-me-or-sack-me ultimatum.
âI said, âI donât care what you do with me, but youâre out of your minds if you donât separate and exit cellphones. You want to shoot me? Shoot me. But youâre crazy if you do anything differently.ââ
He prevailed, but it was not his last test. In 2014, under pressure from the activist investor ValueAct, Motorola Solutions board members debated whether to sell the whole company. Brown, who had already examined and rejected the idea, thought it would be âdumbâ to distract the business with an auction process and risk selling at a depressed price.
âI said, âBullsh*t, weâre not doing that,ââ he recalls, âAnd if you want to fire me, go ahead and fire me.â He drafted a resignation letter, only for his wife to convince him late one night that quitting made no sense. He later apologized to the board for his âemotionalâ delivery, but not for the substance of his argument.
Those standoffs speak to the uncommon amount of pressure under which Brown has operated: For each of his 18 years as CEO, he has had an activist or a private equity investor on his board. Carl Icahn, ValueAct, and Silver Lake have each brought a level of extended scrutiny that few of his peers have faced.
How to turn the toughest investors into strategic allies
Motorola was already under siege from Icahn when Brown started. The veteran activist had launched a proxy battle and was calling for the company to split itself up. Brown admits to feeling intimidated by Icahn at first, but he decided to engage, even as his board objected to settling. âI also knew I had no choice,â he explains: âCarl was coming one way or the other.â
The two men reached a point of mutual respect, he says, where Icahn âknew I would do what I said I would do,â and Brown felt that the âendurance testâ of answering Icahnâs frequent calls had made him a âtougher and strongerâ CEO.
ValueActâs 2014 challenge was scarring, but even as Brown rejected its push for a full-blown sale, he listened and ultimately agreed when it challenged him to unwind the largest acquisition he had made up to that point. âI am a believer in a meritocracy of ideas,â he explains. âCheck your ego at the door [and ask], âWhatâs the right thing to do now?â And that decision today might be different than what you would have decided three or four years ago.â
Despite his outburst to the board, he also agreed to test whether any buyer wanted the whole of Motorola Solutions. The process confirmed his belief that none did, but it caught the attention of Silver Lake. When the tech-focused private equity firm proposed investing $1 billion in exchange for two board seats, Brown saw a chance to bring in fresh capital and expertise. Bringing Silver Lakeâs Egon Durbin and Greg Mondre onto his board was âone of the best decisions I ever made,â he says now.
Motorola Solutions bought out Silver Lakeâs convertible notes in 2024, and Durbin and Mondre have since left its board, but Brown says his experience with them, ValueAct, and Icahn made him a better, more accountable leader.
âIt made me transition as a CEO that thinks like a manager to thinking like an owner,â he says. The difference is that, now, when deploying capital, he asks himself: âWould you do that with your own money?â
There were âdark momentsâ in the process, Brown admits, but it taught him lessons that he now teaches to people who report to him, including on the importance of candor. âShare your mistakes. Share your indecision. Share your vulnerability. Just tell the truth,â he says. âDonât bullsh*t around.â
How to put your best people on your biggest problems
Brown describes himself as a consummate learner who is not embarrassed to ask âdumb questions.â But he realized several years ago that he was doing a poor job of prioritizing the information he consumed and managing his time.
âEarly on, I was more doer than delegator,â he says. So he stepped back and asked what information he really needs to run the company, and how often he needs to see it. He now carries an iPad packed with financial, operational, and competitive data â and very detailed org charts.
He spends the largest share of his time playing the role of âchief people officer and leadership officer,â he says. That means that heâs constantly tracking people in the top four levels of the company, on his iPad and in one-on-one meetings, to assess their performance, potential, and âreplaceability.â
Itâs a practice informed by a moment when he asked his team to list the company

9340d9ba037e.text: Debates in political campaigns used to be a given. Today, candidates increasingly view them as optional — or a political liability to be avoided. Why it matters: In a midterm cycle dominated by unprecedented spending on contrast ads, the candidates themselves are remarkably reluctant to challenge each other face-to-face. It's a sign of how campaigns have evolved, and an erosion of norms: Candidates — fueled by their parties and super PACs — still try to tear apart the opposition, they just do it from a distance. In the age of short, shareable video clips, TV debates offer candidates equal parts opportunity and risk: An electric moment can travel far and wide, but so can an unforced error. By the numbers: In 10 of the most closely watched races for governor, there are no agreed-upon debates between the major-party nominees in half of them — Arizona, Florida, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, according to an Axios review of scheduled debates. Four years ago, just two of those 10 gubernatorial contests went without a debate. In 10 tight Senate races this year, there are no debates scheduled in three states — North Carolina, Ohio and Texas. That's up from one debate-free race in the same seats last time around. Some campaigns are still dickering over possible venues and moderators, and more debates could be added closer to the Nov. 3 election. Driving the news: Florida's Democratic nominee for governor, David Jolly, became the latest official no-show when he said Sunday that he wouldn't debate Republican Rep. Byron Donalds. "I think he's acting with bad faith and continues to peddle lies," Jolly said. "You can't debate a liar." Donalds called Jolly "scared." This is would be the first time since 1974 that Florida hasn't had a debate among contenders for governor. Neither Jolly not Donalds debated their primary opponents. Zoom out: Jolly's debate dodge — unexpected for a financially outgunned Democrat running in a red state— is part of a broader pattern in which challengers and incumbents are making strategic decisions not to debate. In some cases, they enumerate their reasons. In others, they aren't offering much of an explanation. In Ohio , Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton is refusing to debate Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, citing personal attacks against her and her family. "I will not be giving a platform to someone who I think is not just out of touch and not right, for I think he is a danger," Acton said. In Texas , Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who debated Democratic challenger Beto O'Rourke in 2022, hasn't agreed to debate Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa this year. No explanation given. In Nevada , Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford says he's accepted two invitations to debate Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. But Lombardo hasn't publicly committed to them — or commented about it. Yes, but: One state stands out from the rest, Iowa. It had one gubernatorial debate in 2022, but has four scheduled this fall, a sign of how hotly contested the Republican-led state has become as support for Trump and his policies has cratered in farm country. The intrigue: Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs is one of the few candidates who's declined to debate this year and also declined to debate her opponent four years ago. But she's tweaked her rationale. In 2022, when she faced Republican Kari Lake, Hobbs argued that Lake, a Trump loyalist, would turn a debate into a spectacle, with "constant interruptions, pointless distractions, and childish name-calling." This year, Hobbs is refusing to debate Republican Rep. Andy Biggs, offering a new explanation: Her campaign says engaging directly with Arizonans is more effective than a debate stage built for "short soundbites and political theater." Zoom in: Even the Senate — an institution built around debate — isn't immune. In Texas, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has accepted invitations to three televised debates against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Paxton's campaign says he'll debate Talarico but hasn't committed to any of the proposed events. (On Thursday, Talarico challenged Paxton to debate on Fox News, which he called "Ken Paxton's safe space.") In North Carolina, neither former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) nor Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair, have accepted any of at least three debate invitations, although both have indicated they're open to debating. In Ohio, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) said he assumes he'll debate Republican Sen. Jon Husted, but nothing has been scheduled. What they're saying: Brett O'Donnell, a veteran GOP debate-prep consultant, said the disappearance of debates is bad for democracy, but it's a sign of how the campaign and media landscape are changing. "There's so much more money in campaigns now, and a way to get messages out on social media," he said. "We live in a world where people get impatient after watching something for 15 seconds online," O'Donnell added. "How many people will actually watch an hour-long debate?"

2bf82178d3e1.text: Meta is seeking to make privacy protections a centerpiece of new products including its viral assistant Muse , marking a major shift for a company built on extensive use of customer data. Why it matters: The radical turnaround is an acknowledgment that the winner of AI's new assistant race will have to reassure users that they can turn over their emails, finances, health data and other sensitive information. Without that, a super-intelligent personal agent is essentially useless. Driving the news: Meta, whose privacy policy once allowed it nearly unfettered access to use almost everything people did with Meta AI (in almost any way it wanted), has made a significant shift in recent months to put privacy at the center of its AI strategy. In a 6,500-word August manifesto , CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a broad promise. " We believe that people should have a fully private mode for personal agents where even Meta or any other service provider cannot see or grant access to your information." With Muse, which appears to be on a path to becoming one of the most popular AI hits since ChatGPT, the company is offering all customers their own personal virtual machine. A soon-to-be-available option would ensure that even Meta won't have access to the data. Meta is also readying a similar "private processing" option for interactions with its AI glasses. Small efforts have been underway for more than a year, starting with the addition of incognito chats and private processing , which arrived first in WhatsApp, where Meta also provides end-to-end encryption. More recently, the options have spread to other Meta apps. Yes, but: Customers still have to pay close attention if they want to minimize the amount of data shared with Meta. In Muse, for example, the default setting allows interactions to be used for training the company's AI models, though that can be turned off. And not all of the privacy changes being offered to Muse users apply to those accessing Meta AI in other ways, such as through the Facebook, Instagram or Meta AI apps. Plus, Meta devices continue to spur other types of privacy concerns. "Meta's products that embed microphones and cameras in everyday devices pose serious privacy risks to people just trying to live their lives and go about their day without being recorded or surveilled," Electronic Privacy Information Center executive director Alan Butler told Axios. "Confidential processing doesn't solve the problem of pushing embedded surveillance systems out into the world." The big picture: Meta has spent years building a thriving business based on tapping extensive knowledge about its customers to serve up content and ads that it knows will be right up their alley. Its practices have also drawn lawsuits from a wide range of entities that say Meta designed social media to be addictive and caused harm. How it works: Meta is betting on a new business model to fund Muse, which won't provide the same data for targeted advertising that supports most of the company's services. Muse has $20- and $100-per-month paid tiers for heavy users, but Meta expects the free tier to account for most usage. "We believe that Muse will make you money, and we're standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens, with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions," Zuckerberg said. Our thought bubble : There's still a trust gap based on Meta's years of gobbling up nearly all the data it could. That can't be addressed with words, but requires establishing a new track record.

Abortion Is on the Ballot Again as Post-Roe Policies Continue To Evolve
MAPLEWOOD, Mo. — After Missouri voters added abortion protections to the state constitution in 2024, Kelly McCoomb decided to keep her yard sign supporting the measure in the basement of her suburban St. Louis home.
Abortion access is important to McCoomb. She wants her daughter to grow up in a state where the option is available if needed, and the sign was a keepsake from the day Missourians voted to reverse the state’s near-total ban. McCoomb also couldn’t shake the feeling that she’d need to display the sign in her yard again soon.
“I have little faith in our Missouri government,” McCoomb said, sitting on her front porch.
Sure enough, just two years later, the state’s Republican-dominated legislature is asking Missouri voters to overturn the abortion protections they recently supported. The conflicting measures even have the same title: Amendment 3. But while a “yes” vote in 2024 supported adding protections to the state constitution, a “no” vote in 2026 would keep them. McCoomb covered the “YES” on her yard sign with a “NO” made from black duct tape before placing the sign back in her yard.
Voters will weigh in on abortion in Missouri, and three other states, in the November general election. Missouri is also one of two states voting on it for the second time since 2024. Nevada will vote again, too.
The spate of referenda comes after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned federal abortion protections with its 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, leaving each state to make its own abortion policy. The result has been a patchwork of state rules with varying degrees of bans or limitations, and even a series of “shield laws” in states where abortion remains legal that aim to protect providers from prosecution in states where it’s not.
“I just think there’s a constitutional crisis that’s coming,” said Kristi Hamrick, vice president of media and policy for the anti-abortion organization Students for Life Action.
“Can you have 50 state standards on whether or not a human being is a human being? Can you have 50 state standards on whether human beings have legal protection?” Hamrick said.
Advocacy Groups Work To Clarify Ballot Measures
That patchwork of abortion protections is the reason Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom introduced the 2024 ballot measure to enshrine the state’s law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception into the state constitution, said Denise Lopez, president of the coalition.
The measure received strong support two years ago, with 64% of voters in favor. Nevada law requires two majority votes to enshrine constitutional amendments, so voters will need to support the expanded protection again in November for it to be enacted.
The Nevada ballot measure wouldn’t change the state’s existing law allowing abortions up to 24 weeks after conception. But the proposal would make it more difficult to overturn abortion access, requiring voter approval of any new ban in two elections.
Lopez said Nevadans for Reproductive Freedom has been campaigning to ensure voters are still mobilized.
“Folks care about it,” she said. “They’re seeing what’s happening at the national level, and they want to make sure that whatever’s happening in our neighboring states, like Idaho and Utah, doesn’t happen here in Nevada.”
Idaho, where a ballot measure establishing abortion rights recently qualified to go before voters in November, has one of the strictest abortion bans in the country. Voters will decide whether state statute should allow abortion through fetal viability, the point when a fetus can survive after birth, which is generally considered to be around 24 weeks.
In Utah, abortion is allowed up to 18 weeks while legal challenges to the state’s ban continue.
In Virginia, where abortion is already allowed through two trimesters of pregnancy, until 28 weeks, voters will decide whether to amend their state constitution to codify those rights.
Missouri is the only state voting this year on removing abortion protections already on the books. The measure would repeal the 2024 amendment that guaranteed abortion access through fetal viability in the state and replace it with a ban on abortions with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, and pregnancies resulting from rape or incest. Abortions for rape and incest would have to occur before 12 weeks of pregnancy.
Missouri was the first state to ban abortion after the Dobbs decision in 2022. At that time, abortions had already mostly ceased in the state after three decades of state regulations targeting the practice, including a 72-hour waiting period, minimum dimensions for procedure rooms and hallways in clinics that provide abortions, and a mandate that the clinicians have admitting privileges at nearby hospitals, among others. Only 150 abortions were performed in Missouri in 2021, down from 5,772 in 2011, state records show.
Even though Missouri voters backed the abortion amendment in 2024, it took nearly two years for medication abortions to resume in the state.
A Second Vote Causes Confusion
Margot Riphagen-Dunn, CEO of St. Louis-based Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, said the whiplash of a second statewide vote on abortion mirrors the confusion that patients have experienced about whether abortion is available in the state.
“Chaos is kind of the point here,” Riphagen-Dunn said, “and it is absolutely a tactic that gets in the way of being able to provide.”
The confusion has presented problems for abortion opponents in the state as well.
“I think it’s unfortunate,” said Reagan Barklage, who is a vice president of Students for Life of America and the treasurer of the Missouri Students for Life Ballot Committee. “People need to be very clear on what they’re voting for.”
Barklage said she has had to correct anti-abortion voters while out canvassing to remind them that they are voting “yes” on Amendment 3 this year even though they voted “no

NY-17: Second in a series on the environmental stakes of one of the nation’s most fiercely contested congressional races.
Nancy Vann’s resolve has become the subject of a local jingle. Its chorus goes: “If she can do it, so can we.”
Vann, 78, moved to Peekskill, 40 miles north of New York City, after September 11, 2001. Brown & Wood, the law firm at which she worked, occupied five floors of the World Trade Center. She watched both towers fall before her 10:30 a.m. call-in.
Over the next 10 years, her dawn and sunset hours were spent on the Metro-North, a commuter railroad, the Hudson River unspooled alongside.
Vann was no stranger to the Hudson Valley; since the late ‘90s, she had owned a summer cabin in a co-op community in neighbouring Buchanan. Her cabin lay just half a mile from Indian Point Energy Center, a nuclear power plant on the river’s eastern bank. Indian Point, she later learned, had possibly been considered as a target by the 9/11 hijackers.
The nuclear plant, formerly owned by Louisiana-based Entergy, and since acquired by Holtec International, is presently being decommissioned, the years-long process of permanently retiring a facility. How that process is going and what, exactly, it might lead to are points of contention as the Trump administration aggressively pushes a rebirth for America’s nuclear industry.
That debate has become particularly fraught in New York’s 17th Congressional District, where the plant’s future could become an issue in one of the most closely contested House races this November.
Susan Shapiro, an environmental attorney and resident of the district, called Indian Point “the elephant in the room in our region.”
Candidates have opposing views on what should become of the site. Cait Conley, the Democratic challenger, wishes to see the decommissioning progress, while incumbent Republican Mike Lawler, a veteran party official in New York, has advocated for Indian Point’s reopening, and recently took Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright to the site.
“The fact is, there’s no better-positioned site for energy generation in the Hudson Valley than Indian Point,” he told the New York Post in a recent interview.
Nuclear energy sits firmly under Lawler’s “all-of-the-above” energy strategy to improve grid reliability and lower utility costs. Conley, meanwhile, is not decidedly anti-nuclear, but calls the site “broken and decrepit” on her campaign website, which lists “Stopping Mike Lawler’s drive to reopen Indian Point” as a policy priority. A decorated combat veteran and national security official in the Biden administration, she has not publicly taken a position on the plant’s decommissioning.
“I really wanted the Democrats to weigh in on this, but they seemed to be avoiding it,” said Erik Lindberg, a resident of Peekskill.
With Republicans controlling the House by a narrow 218-213 margin, Democrats’ chances for retaking the chamber are considered good—and this district, in the affluent suburbs of New York City, is considered one of their best chances for picking up a Republican-held seat. Whether nuclear power becomes a decisive issue may depend on how voters weigh its potential benefits for energy costs against concerns about public health.
Vann had never paid close attention to Indian Point, or the nuclear issue, until 2014, when she read that Enbridge, a major Calgary-based pipeline company, planned to build a 42-inch gas pipeline beneath her property. It was also within roughly 100 feet of the nuclear plant’s emergency backup generators and switchyard. It was then that she became involved, first in the pipeline fight, then in the battle over Indian Point.
Today, she sits in on six to seven weekly calls about nuclear sites in various stages of transition. There are plants undergoing decommissioning, like Indian Point and San Onofre, in California; others, once slated for closure, that remain in operation, like California’s Diablo Canyon; and “zombie nukes,” like Michigan’s Palisades and Pennsylvania’s Three Mile Island, that are today being brought back online following permanent shutdown. In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul ordered the construction of an “advanced nuclear power plant,” the first in decades.
Indian Point occupies one of the most densely populated nuclear sites in the United States, with roughly 20 million people within a 50-mile radius. The reactors sit near the Ramapo Fault, a minor seismic zone. They used the Hudson River for cooling water and the controlled release of wastewater.
The strong activist base in the community has long made for an activist versus industry dynamic. In turn, they have been blamed for the plant’s closure.
Ultimately, Indian Point’s unsustainable operating costs led to its shutdown in 2021. Entergy also faced years of litigation over the plant’s license renewal, including lawsuits brought by New York State and environmental groups like Riverkeeper.
Over the years, the plant leaked radioactive waste into groundwater, vented an estimated 600,000 gallons of radioactive steam into the atmosphere, spilled some 3,000 gallons of dielectric fluid and 100 gallons of oil into the river and on occasion raised nearby water temperatures by 15 degrees, killing fish and triggering environmental concerns.
A recent study led by Harvard University’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health found higher cancer mortality rates in counties near operating nuclear plants.
Seven years after moving to Peekskill, Vann was diagnosed with duodenal cancer, a rare and aggressive disease; doctors discovered a grapefruit-sized tumor in her small intestine. She has also had seven cats die, each from cancer.
“It doesn’t prove anything,” Vann said. “But it leaves a bad feeling.”
Then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo pushed to shutdown Indian Point despite the plant providing high-paying, unionized jobs, 400 of which were lost when it closed. Unions today form a key part of Lawler’s political base, in a district where a third of residents live in a union household.

Nitin Nohria spent a decade as dean of Harvard Business School, and taught his first workshop there for new CEOs in 1997. Many of todayâs business leaders think of that era as an easier one to navigate, but he rejects the idea that todayâs technological and geopolitical upheavals have changed what companies need from their leaders.
The demands of the job have been âmore constant than different,â he says: The people who respond well to the conditions of their time âend up writing a great chapter, and the people who respond to it poorly donât.â
Nohria has distilled such insights into a new book, The CEO: The Role, the Reality, the Responsibility. Its most important message, he says, is that the CEOâs job is ânot to make all the decisions, but to create the conditions that allow other people to make decisions well.â Leaders should invest their time âto multiply impact rather than to answer demands.â
Nohria also chairs Thrive Capital, whose founder and managing partner, Josh Kushner, recently backtracked on a plan with FIFA to commercialize the World Cup, after it generated a fierce backlash. Kushner has invested in OpenAI and SpaceX, and his former HBS teacher sees AI as the defining challenge for this generation of CEOs â even if it also offers an answer for those who find it lonely at the top.
The technology heralds a new era of decentralization, he believes, and that will make the people CEOs have surrounded themselves with feel threatened. But the leaderâs job is âeven more compellingâ in a decentralized organization, Nohria argues. âVision, alignment, purpose, culture â these things will become even more important in the future of these organizations, and that is uniquely the job of the CEO.â
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: AI is a transformational technology. What do you think it changes about the CEOâs role?
Nitin Nohria: We donât have visibility yet into all the ways in which AI is going to play out in the lives of a Fortune 500 CEO, how much AI will rearchitect firmsâ business processes and workforces, or where we will see opportunities for new revenue. But Iâm sure that any CEO who comes of age today, if they havenât come up with an answer to that by the end of the decade, will not be [a] great [CEO].
The second part, though, is that AI provides opportunities for CEOs to have a virtual board of directors, a new person on the team, and a way of interrogating their own thinking which may reduce the loneliness of being a CEO. If you end up using it as a substitution, I think youâll probably end up making a mistake. But if you say, âIt would be nice to have, out of the eight people in my executive team, two people who bring to us a superintelligence on an ongoing basis that informs our discussions, interrogates our discussions, causes us to think differently, and forces us to make judgment calls better,â that could be a plus.
To what extent does AI change the structure of the modern corporation? Companies have organized themselves in functional silos, and this is a cross-functional technology.
As a student of organization structure, itâs been striking to see the pendulum swing between decentralization and centralization over time. I think that this will be a moment of decentralization again. Because what was the reason to have a large headquarters? Itâs because we could not hire enough CFOs or general counsels to put into every business. [Companies] say, âThese are precious forms of expertise. We want to keep them in the center.â But now you could bring all of that intelligence to the edge. I think this is going to be another decentralizing moment in which we can bring the expertise that resided in the headquarters back out to the front lines.
Is that threatening for the central power of the CEO?
Some of the current friction in the adoption of AI comes from the fact that it does restructure power in an organization. When power changes in organizations, companies end up having friction to adapt to that power. Because thereâs one thing that is eternally true about human beings: that nobody gives [up] power easily. Iâm not sure that it makes the CEO necessarily less powerful. I think it makes the corporate infrastructure that CEOs have usually surrounded themselves with feel more threatened.
The subtitle of your book is The Role, the Reality, the Responsibility. Are we entering a new realm of CEO responsibility when some CEOs are overseeing technologies they say could end humanity?
AI will create yet another set of profound responsibilities to make sure that businessesâ relationship with society is not one in which society says business is harmful. All these CEOs will have an added [responsibility to] navigate AI so that people feel that this moment was to the benefit, in the end, of society, even though there are often some dislocations along the way. You do have to, as CEOs, be responsive to the fact that your license to operate comes from society.
How do you apply these principles in your role as chairman of Thrive?
My role at Thrive is at its core to remain a teacher. Josh [Kushner] and others knew me as a teacher, and the job of the teacher, in my experience, is much more to ask the right questions than say that I have the right answers, and to ask questions that interrogate our thinking, that force us to think more deeply.
What was your role in Thriveâs recent discussions with FIFA, and how does the way that investment idea played out map to the themes of your book?
A central part of my role as chairman of Thrive is to work with the leadership team, asking questions and helping them think through the choices they face. This story was originally published by Yale Environment 360.
In a modern five-story building in the center of Hamburg, Germany, technicians are preparing to install several new “racks”—gray metal casings that hold computing hardware—alongside the scores that already line the narrow, dimly lit corridors of the German Climate Computing Center (DKRZ), one of the world’s largest repositories for climate simulation data. The new equipment will add about 5 petabytes of storage capacity to the 254 petabytes of data already stored here. One petabyte of data is equivalent to the storage space needed for roughly 200 million high-resolution images.
Under normal circumstances, the DKRZ’s mission is to provide computing power and storage to the German climate science community. But these new racks will serve a different and highly sensitive purpose: They will store backup versions of climate simulations from the other side of the Atlantic. The operation aims to ensure that essential work performed by U.S. scientists for the next major United Nations climate assessment, due in 2029, cannot be meddled with or compromised by the administration of President Donald Trump, which has slashed funding for climate research, buried scientific reports, removed references to human-caused warming from dozens of government websites and sought to prevent satellites from collecting key climate data.
Leaders of German science organizations publicly cite these actions as their primary motivation for creating backups. The German Research Foundation, the country’s main science funding body, believes that the Trump administration could block European access to data and research findings stored in the U.S. “The deletion of data has also become a possibility,” says the foundation’s program manager, Kathrin Winkler, “and there is a risk that [data] could be manipulated to skew findings in a desired direction.”
Trust in U.S. science policy has fallen to a low point in Europe, and fears of losing scientific data are mounting. The U.S. government quit both the U.N. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change in January, though U.S. researchers are still contributing to global climate science. To support them, the German Research Foundation in late 2025 set up a program, with a budget of $35 million, to provide a safe haven for permanently storing copies of U.S. data from public and open sources.
The DKRZ project is called “CMIP7-ark”—a lifeboat for the U.S. contribution to the seventh IPCC assessment. Six other projects for U.S. science datasets, with names like “SHIELD” and “SEND” (Secure Endangered Earth Data), have also received funding. Christopher Kadow, head of the data analysis division at the DKRZ, says, “We cannot simply accept that important contributions might be lost for technical or political reasons.”
Data collections form the foundation of all empirical science. Climate, environmental and biodiversity research relies on countless historical and contemporary datasets. Some of these collections, such as the iconic time series of atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations made at Hawaii’s Mauna Loa Observatory, have been ongoing for decades and are critical for tracking environmental change. (In 2025, the Trump administration tried to defund and close the observatory, but later Congress rejected its proposed cuts.)
While detailed datasets are essential for research, it is not standard procedure to back them up in alternate locations. Most scientific datasets are physically stored on hard drives or magnetic tapes at the universities or institutions where they are generated. One simple reason for this is that, until recently, the world seemed safe enough that scientists saw no need for offsite backups. Another reason is that transferring and storing such large amounts of information is complicated. Sending petabytes of data through the internet takes months, and renting faster fiber optic cables can be extremely costly. Often, the most cost-effective way to transfer large volumes of data is to put them on hard drives or far cheaper magnetic tapes and send them through the “sneakernet,” which means they are physically transported by car, plane, or ship.
Still, the process is expensive and arduous, so most datasets have been kept in just one place. But in a world where political upheaval, cyberattacks and armed conflicts are becoming more frequent, this practice is increasingly considered to be precarious. “If data is stored at only one site, there is a much greater risk of loss from events such as extreme weather or infrastructure failure,” says Eleanor O’Rourke, the U.K.-based director of the International Project Office of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, which coordinates global climate models for the IPCC’s assessments. Climate simulations for the IPCC are now considered so critical that overseas repositories are thought necessary for all contributions.
Until recently, the idea that the U.S. science community would have to track or rescue lost datasets was unthinkable. After all, environmental data generated or funded by U.S. government agencies was paid for by taxpayers and generally remains in the public domain. Yet these datasets exist in physical forms at specific locations and require dedicated experts to maintain them, which makes them vulnerable to human interference, as well as natural disasters, technical problems like short circuits or battery explosions and neglect. “The data repositories, digital asset management services, and preservation systems that ensure research data remains open and accessible are often overlooked—until they disappear,” data experts Jennifer Gibson and Kaitlin Thaney warned recently.

The Signal Insight
Brian McNamara spent six years running the group behind Advil, Centrum, and Sensodyne before GSK spun off its consumer health division in 2022. Perhaps a fifth of that job is comparable to what his role is now, as CEO of Haleon, he estimates, such was the difference in responsibilities.
As CEO of a standalone company with its own London listing, he needed to educate a new board, manage a debt overhang, and make capital allocation decisions across a far bigger strategic playing field than the one that had been open to him under his former parent company.
McNamara also wanted to create a performance-focused, consumer-centric drive in a business that had grown up under the umbrella of a more cautious pharmaceutical company. But he discovered that âthe organization was quite tiredâ after its efforts to separate the company from GSK, and before that, to integrate two large mergers.
âThe team that took us through separation did a phenomenal job,â McNamara says, but he concluded that he needed to bring in new skills and energy. His response was to change 13 members of his 15-strong leadership team, bringing in fresh talent from leading consumer brand companies like Procter & Gamble, EstÃ©e Lauder, Unilever, and LâOrÃ©al.
With the initial sprint to define a new company and strategy behind him, hereâs how he describes the lessons from its spin-off, and why you shouldnât see such a milestone as a finish line.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: The split from GSK was four years ago. How do you think about this moment in the story?
Brian McNamara: I think about the journey of the company in phases. Phase one was to separate, build all the corporate functions, and deal with our leverage. At about the two-year mark, we got through all that. Then the next phase was laying out the new strategy, with our ambitions of reaching a billion more consumers and delivering industry-leading shareholder returns. Now, the last phase for me is to create a truly agile, performance-focused, consumer-centric company.
What was the culture you inherited? And what are you trying to do with it?
GSK was a great owner, but it was a pharma company, and the speed of a consumer business is very different. I joined GSK in 2015 through its Novartis joint venture, but we spent three years integrating that business. Then we announced the next deal, with Pfizer, and spent two years integrating that business. Then we spent a year separating [from GSK], and then we had to stand up [Haleon as a new] company. These are all incredibly internally focused things. So we needed to step back from that and create the right external focus and the right growth mindset and the right performance culture.Â
Whatâs changed in your own leadership role?
I ran this business for six years as a division of GSK. I think there was maybe 20% of that role that was the same. Itâs that big a difference. [Other CEOs] would talk to me about what itâs like to be a listed company CEO. And to a person, they said, âListen, Brian, logically, we can tell you. But until youâre in the seat, you really wonât understand it.â And they were absolutely right.
I had a fantastic board, but they were relatively new to the business, so they needed to be educated on it. Despite all our efforts to separate and have everything set up the way we wanted to, these things are hard and theyâre a little messy, so we needed to make some changes.
The other change was my external role, ensuring that Iâm staying current on technology changes and whatâs happening geopolitically, and talking with other CEOs on how theyâre navigating these situations. I found people are extremely generous with their time. When youâre in that kind of role, itâs a unique place to be, and you need a different kind of support and advice.
You said the organization was quite tired. What have you learned about injecting energy at those moments?
As we moved to separation, I think a lot of people viewed it as the end, like we were getting to the finish line. And, by the way, they probably had an unrealistic view of how great it was going to be as our own company. I was the division head for 21 quarters, and I got maybe 10 questions [on GSK analyst calls] over those 21 quarters, so we were a bit protected by the umbrella of GSK. The News
The diesel export ban that President Donald Trump is mulling in a bid to bring down record-high prices would backfire in two ways â further dividing Hill Republicans while risking even pricier gasoline.
Itâs not clear that the Trump administration will impose diesel export limits, which the president said this week that heâd explore as average national prices push past $6.50 per gallon. If Trump does push ahead, his main cheerleaders will be GOP candidates in tight races this fall who are eager to market more ideas to lower costs before the midterms.
But most congressional Republicans want nothing to do with the idea, no matter how close they are with the administration.
âThe better policy would be for states like California to lift the restrictions that theyâre imposing on the exploitation and the refining of diesel,â Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., told Semafor. âTaking down domestic barriers that have been exerted by states â that, to me, is a far better approach.â
US oil executives have fought hard against a ban, warning it would push prices higher worldwide; the European Union recently echoed their concerns, as its own diesel costs climbed following Trumpâs remarks. Energy analysts are just as critical, describing it as a Band-Aid at best â even if the constraints are nonbinding, as Energy Secretary Chris Wright suggested they could be in Pennsylvania on Thursday afternoon.
âThe diesel export ban, even if in a strong-armed âvoluntaryâ form, is a desperate idea that promotes inefficiency and ultimately higher prices,â said Skanda Amarnath, a former Federal Reserve economist who now helms the left-leaning organization Employ America.
The frosty response from Trumpâs own party is particularly notable after a year that began with Republicans stiff-arming his earliest ideas to lower the cost of living. Soon after, Trump pursued an Iran war that has since dragged on past the seven-month mark, straining the global economy and leaving voters increasingly pessimistic.
GOP lawmakers instead proposed alternatives like cutting gas taxes or tapping oil reserves: âWe should be looking at multiple solutions,â Hagerty said.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., lamented that âwe always keep skating to where the puck is at the expense of getting to where the puckâs going to be,â calling the ban âjust another example where, even in the White House, I think thereâs disagreements about the pros and cons.â
âThe president always makes the decision that is best for the American people,â a White House official told Semafor, adding that he âis evaluating all the options on the table.â
Know More
GOP Senate candidates like Ashley Hinson in Iowa and Mike Rogers in Michigan say a ban is necessary to bolster their statesâ struggling agricultural producers.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who also faces a tough race, said she hasnât âhad the chance to look atâ the proposal. Like Hagerty, she proffered a different solution: releasing heating oil from a federal reserve ahead of the winter.
Oil-state Republicans are harshest of all in their criticism: Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, derided it as âa gimmickâ that âwonât work.â
As plummeting consumer sentiment emboldens Democrats to push farther into GOP-held territory despite a cash deficit in some key races, they see the export ban as proof of the GOPâs desperation this late in the cycle.
âRepublicans can try one gimmick after the other, but they refuse to deal with the source of the problem,â House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters this week. âGo tell Donald Trump to end that war in Iran that no one in America asked for in the first place.â
While there is already legislation that would restrict diesel exports, the Trump administration doesnât need Congress to act, legal experts told Semafor. Trump can impose a ban unilaterally thanks to sweeping authorities provided by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act â the same law that provided his initial authority for tariffs since struck down by the Supreme Court.
âThis would be a very straightforward thing to do under IEEPA,â said Georgetown Lawâs Peter Harrell, a former State Department official who later oversaw supply chains on former President Joe Bidenâs National Security Council and National Economic Council.
Trump needs to declare oil shortages a national emergency, Harrell said, and sign an executive order restricting diesel exports. The order could allow the Energy Department to make some exemptions âin case there is some unforeseen adverse consequence,â he added.
Trump also has the option of wielding the Defense Production Act, as he did to crack down on exports of critical minerals and protective equipment. âBut that would be more complex,â Harrell said.
Room for Disagreement
The small group of Republicans who have called for a ban to tamp down prices say itâs a necessary step to shield farmers and consumers from the Iran warâs economic fallout.
Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, said on the Senate floor this week Trump should impose the embargo by executive order to âhelp family farmers who feed and fuel the world.â
Eleanor and Nickâs View
Democrats see the response to Trumpâs latest idea as proof that Republicans are flailing, but we see the clearest sign yet of what our colleague Burgess identified earlier this week: A GOP long in this presidentâs thrall is suddenly moving past him at an increasingly fast clip.
The degree of blunt talk we heard from Trumpâs party about the economic and political downsides of a ban â at least, on the record â would have been unimaginable last year.

e939e712fa60.text:
Ashleyâs view
The White House and its allies are lonely in their insistence that AI development in America must accelerate without governments setting ground rules.
At the UN General Assembly in New York City, as well as in meetings with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington this week, President Donald Trumpâs team was clear: US companies are the leaders in AI; they plan to keep it that way; and they reject any international attempts to rein in the technology.
Trump, with his call to leave AI âexactly where it isâ contrasts with Xi, who said responsible AI development is necessary â as other Chinese officials said this week that they support a global governance framework.
Without official support from the US, however, any such agreement will be difficult to execute. White House science and tech adviser Michael Kratsios rejected global efforts in a UN address that he called an âintervention.â
As a result, nations may be left setting nonbinding rules and best practices without the buy-in of the biggest companiesâ home country. Meanwhile, frontier labs are pushing forward with their own self-regulatory schemes, which will ask them to agree on testing standards in a highly competitive environment.
Yet even AI CEOs are more aligned with the UN than with Trump. Companies are pushing for coordinated âAI pacing,â saying they support global efforts to coordinate on safety and affirming that they cannot set the standards for responsible AI use on their own.
âThe international community will need to establish a common framework to manage the risks associated with frontier AI models,â said Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot, the French official who chaired the UN National Security meeting on AI featuring the CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face.
Polling shows Americans are largely skeptical of claims that the US must beat China at AI development, and that people are generally worried the technology is moving fast enough to pose a risk to their jobs and livelihood. Those surveys show worries about AI acceleration across party lines.
Trumpâs AI isolation from the world, and much of the electorate, puts congressional Republicans in a strange position, too. Theyâre advocating for AI safety and slowdowns and sponsoring bipartisan legislation to regulate AI, while their party leader presses the gas.
As Semafor first reported on Thursday, Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., has asked Secretary of State Marco Rubio to convene National Security Council meetings with cyber experts and AI developers about potential national security threats, including possible AI-enabled attacks on critical infrastructure.
âThe United States should continue to lead the world in the development and deployment of artificial intelligence,â Young wrote to Rubio. âMaintaining that leadership also requires ensuring that our government keeps pace with emerging capabilities and understands the risks they may present.â
Room for Disagreement
Trumpâs allies often see ulterior motives behind much of the current advocacy for stricter AI safety rules. Some argue that companies as big as OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic are seeking âregulatory captureâ by trying to shape legislation that only their companies will have the means to comply with, therefore giving themselves a leg up.
Others decry âdoomerism,â or the belief that AI could kill off humanity or eliminate jobs, as hysterical and speculative. Criticizing the effective altruism community, which many AI safety groups have connections to, is another burgeoning White House tactic.
But the core of the presidentâs message is simple: The US should do nothing that might give China, with its cheaper open-source models, an advantage in the AI race.

Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has announced that he is helping to fund a new $660m (Â£500m) fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and Djibouti
The project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres.
It is expected to begin operations within 18 months.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline would reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one.
The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol.
Speaking at the ground-breaking ceremony, Dangote, Africa's richest man, said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient.
Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction.
Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues.
The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa.
Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day.
The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (Â£1.2bn).
In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu.

1c298c9e5509.text: With midterms 39 days away and the outlook for President Trump 's party looking increasingly bleak, top Republicans say they're focused on three big questions for the final stretch: Are their attack ads working? Republicans expect a wave of private polling in early October to reveal whether their massive financial advantage is cutting into Democrats' leads. GOP groups had spent more than $450 million through Sept. 23, more than twice what Democrats had spent, according to campaign finance expert Rob Pyers. But Republican strategists say they aren't sure yet whether the barrage is working amid voter anger over high prices, data centers and Trump's war in Iran. Trump's political operation didn't begin pouring its $416 million war chest into attack ads until around Labor Day, and Republicans argue the ads need time to sink in. Strategists are particularly watching the Texas Senate race, where national GOP groups have sunk more than $100 million into helping Ken Paxton against Democrat James Talarico. Several polls have shown Paxton — whom GOP leaders have long viewed as a problematic nominee — trailing Talarico. "September tests whether your messaging moves the needle in races — and early October is when the map locks in," a Republican strategist told Axios. 2. Who gets cut loose? Republicans concede they'll have to make painful spending decisions by early October. That could complicate things for GOP Senate contenders Mike Collins in Georgia and Michael Whatley in North Carolina, who have consistently trailed Democrats Jon Ossoff and Roy Cooper despite millions in Republicans' spending. If Collins and Whatley's numbers don't improve, Republicans say they could redirect money to Michigan and New Hampshire, where the party is playing offense. Republicans also may have to spend more in traditionally red states such as Kansas, where polls show GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in a tight race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Hamilton would be the first Kansas Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1932. The race is tight enough to have drawn Vice President Vance to the state for a recent visit to try to give Marshall a boost. Trump's political operation, meanwhile, has begun spending to defend a South Carolina House district that Trump carried by 13 points in 2024. 3. What does Trump do? The president and his political team remain one of the midterms' biggest question marks. Trump's team said early this year that he'd campaign weekly for GOP candidates. That didn't happen. Trump now says he'll spend the final 30 days campaigning for candidates in 35 key Senate and House races. By early October, Republican strategists expect to see whether he'll follow through — and, if he does, where he goes. Where Trump doesn't go could be just as telling. Some Republicans in competitive races are keeping their distance from the unpopular administration . When Vance visited Iowa last week, GOP Senate candidate Ashley Hinson didn't appear, citing previously scheduled events. Then there's the question of how much Trump's willing to spend. Strategists say that should become clear in early October.

fa0bc73d38bb.text: A new analysis of the AI buildout shows its staggering scale: $10.3 trillion in estimated AI infrastructure investment through 2032. That amounts to 3.6% of GDP a year, dwarfing the investment booms that built America's railroads , highways, electric grid and telecom networks. Why it matters: The AI boom has become far too big and too costly for even the largest tech companies to finance alone. This has resulted in trillions of dollars in demand for outside capital — and the potential risks that come along with that, according to new research being presented Friday at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity. Financing the buildout will require tapping bond markets, banks and private credit on a massive scale, adding to the flood of debt competing for investors' money at a time when borrowing costs are already surging. So far, those higher costs appear to be doing little to curb the industry's appetite to build. The knock-on effect: The more capital the buildout absorbs, the greater the potential pressure on borrowing costs elsewhere in the economy. In effect, any other entity that needs capital — from the U.S. government financing its $2 trillion per year deficit to an individual seeking a home mortgage or car loan — is in competition for funds with these hyperscalers. What they're saying: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia Business School professor behind the new paper on how the AI infrastructure boom is being financed, says the industry's appetite for investment remains remarkably resilient to higher rates. "They are so gung-ho to build these things" that even recent rate hikes and historically high long-term yields won't "deter too much of that development," Van Nieuwerburgh told reporters recently. Morgan Stanley estimates that Big Tech will need roughly $2.9 trillion to expand its computing capacity through 2028 — with more than half coming from outside investors, according to the paper. Case in point: Facebook parent Meta chose to finance most of its $30 billion Hyperion data center through outside investors, even though doing so meant paying substantially more to borrow. The project's debt carries an interest rate at least 1 percentage point higher than Meta likely would have paid on its own debt, adding more than $5 billion in costs over the life of the deal, the paper estimates. Threat level: The surge of outside money — much of it from private credit — allows the AI boom to keep scaling. But it spreads possible risks across the financial system, often through financing structures that are harder for investors and regulators to track. The infrastructure would need to generate $3.7 trillion in annual revenue in the next six years to earn a 10% return — roughly 9% of GDP. "The risks have been spreading throughout the financial system," Van Nieuwerburgh said, as the industry taps pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, private credit and other sources of outside capital. "With that expansion comes more complexity, more opacity, and it's becoming difficult to track where the risks are being distributed," he said. "These risks are coming to a pension fund near you, so to speak." What to watch: Van Nieuwerburgh says the influx of outside capital risks allowing the buildout to race ahead of actual demand. "Sooner or later, we're going to have oversupply, just like we do in every real estate cycle, and then the prices will collapse," he said. "I don't see why this time is different." The bottom line: The AI investment boom is now a major force in the broader economy, boosting growth while putting new pressure on capital markets and the financial system. " This AI buildout is by far the largest ... it's 50% larger than the second-largest, which was the railroad buildout," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

More tree planting, wetland restoration and drainage work could take place in parts of Northamptonshire to "safeguard nature for generations to come".
West Northamptonshire Council has approved its first Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) which was required by the Environment Act 2021 and is the responsibility of all authorities.
It said the area was one of England's "most nature-depleted areas" and its wildlife sites "are often small, in poor condition, and isolated from one another".
Working with a range of partners the council hopes to improve landscapes that are "under unprecedented pressure" with some species in decline.
A spokesperson for the council said: "A healthy natural environment is essential for tackling climate change and wider environmental challenges.
"The diversity of habitats and species provide essentials such as clean and plentiful water, food, clean air, productive soil, flood protection, shading and cooling, as well as benefits like space for recreation, exercise and wellbeing."
Nigel Stansfield, Reform UK's cabinet member for environment, recycling and waste, said: "Our aim is to safeguard nature for generations to come, and create cleaner, greener spaces that meet the needs of local communities and offer them an opportunity to connect with nature."
He said it was vital to have a workable strategy that sets out "how we intend to safeguard nature for generations to come."
Stansfield added he hoped the strategy would get organisations, landowners and local people to take action "to ensure our natural environment becomes more robust and resilient to provide the benefits we often take for granted".

A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has formally said her allegation was untrue.
The unnamed woman filed a lawsuit in 2024 claiming she had been drugged and raped by Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, and Sean "Diddy" Combs at a party after the MTV Video Music Awards in 2000.
The stars denied the allegation and she dropped the lawsuit last year. Carter then sued her and her lawyers.
In a statement filed in that case on Thursday, she wrote: "Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever."
The woman, known in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, also said: "My claims that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me while a third celebrity, [name redacted] watched are false. There is no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter.
"I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone."
Jay-Z and family's 'trauma'
Carter had vehemently denied the accusations, saying they were a "blackmail attempt" and describing them as "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations".
When the accuser dropped her case in February 2025, the rapper, who is married to singer BeyoncÃ©, said: "The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed."
The woman, from Alabama, has now been removed from Carter's lawsuit.
She said she had not received any money from the rap superstar or anyone acting on his behalf, and had not been paid to make her latest declaration.
The rapper is still suing the woman's former lawyers, led by Tony Buzbee.
In a statement to Rolling Stone, external, which first reported Jane Doe's new declaration, Buzbee said he had not seen it.
He said: "We have multiple lawyers (at least four) who dealt with Ms Doe long before she met me. She gave the exact same story to each. If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that's new information."
When Carter filed his lawsuit against the woman and her lawyers in February 2025, Buzbee claimed at the time that Carter's investigators had "repeatedly harassed, threatened and harangued this poor woman for weeks, trying to intimidate her and make her recant her story".
In her new declaration, the woman said: "I never received any threat from Mr Carter or anyone acting on his behalf."
'No due diligence'
Setting out the events that led to her allegation, the woman said she saw an advert on Facebook in September or October 2024 looking for people who might have sexual assault claims against Combs. "The ad triggered memories of being raped when I was 13 years old," she said.
She was contacted by a law firm but was not provided with a draft of the lawsuit containing her allegations and did not authorise it before it was filed in October 2024, she said.
She also said Buzbee and other lawyers acting on her behalf filed it "without conducting any independent investigation, background inquiry, or due diligence, and without obtaining any corroboration of the allegations".
She said: "The October Complaint alleges that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me when I was a minor while an unnamed celebrity watched. As discussed above, these allegations were false."
Buzbee also represents numerous other people who have made allegations against Combs.
Combs denied Jane Doe's claims, which his lawyer described at the time as one of a number of civil cases "pushed forward by an attorney more focused on media headlines than legal merit".
In July 2025, Combs was convicted by a criminal court on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends, and is currently serving a four-year prison sentence.
The BBC has contacted Mr Combs for comment.

Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray after fighting broke out this week between regional forces and the national army.
Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the much smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray.
"Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme.
The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.
Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody".
Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services.
Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting fears of a return to a full scale civil war and reports of panic buying.
During the two-year conflict which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world.
Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - with estimates that some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Sunday, the party in control of Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government.
On Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police.
There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Additional reporting by Peter Mwai, BBC Verify

One of the three attendees who was shot at Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has passed away from complications stemming from his injuries, according to the Pennsylvania attorney general.
Jim Copenhaver, 76, was struck twice when a gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop. Another attendee, Corey Comperatore, was killed in the shooting and Trump's ear was grazed by a bullet.
Copenhaver died on Wednesday at a hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner shared with local media.
The gunman, 20-year-old Thomas Crooks, was killed by Secret Service after he opened fire.
In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot".
"More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice," Trump said. "Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne."
An attorney for Copenhaver's family said his dedication to the US was a "defining part of his life".
"As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered," the lawyer said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
In an interview with CBS a year after the Butler rally, Copenhaver and David Dutch, the third attendee who was shot, said they had been through infections and surgeries after being wounded.
Copenhaver was shot in the arm and the abdomen. A year later, the bullet was still lodged in his body next to his spine, he told CBS, causing him to walk with a cane.
Both Dutch and Copenhaver sued the federal government for damages in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries.
Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."

1091afd5ed7d.text: By — James Pollard, Associated Press James Pollard, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-live-day-4-of-the-2026-united-nations-general-assembly Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Day 4 of the 2026 United Nations General Assembly World Sep 25, 2026 9:17 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — New players hit the United Nations General Assembly sidelines this week as humanitarian groups searched for a counterweight to foreign aid cuts that have hampered global fights against disease, malnutrition and poverty. Watch the UN General Assembly live in the video player above. Nonprofits, foundations and corporations pack Manhattan ballrooms and closed-door meetings each September to direct some sliver of the world's attention — and funding — to their missions. Timed annually to the U.N. General Assembly's high-level meetings, the scramble is even more urgent after recent sharp declines in funding sent by some of the richest countries to poorer ones. Across the many conferences, forums and roundtables, the week exposed the gulf between the biggest aid organizations, who have the money and connections to weather this period of public aid retrenchment, and others grappling with their role in the changing landscape for humanitarian funding. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Big movers still made big pledges. The Gates Foundation touted its $1 billion commitment to AI-powered tools for farmers, educators and health workers. Bill Clinton called on Clinton Global Initiative attendees to "step into the void created by retreating governments." There, former USAID administrator Samantha Power highlighted the ways her coalition to end childhood lead poisoning adapted when U.S. President Donald Trump's administration dismantled her former agency, USAID. "Philanthropies took risks. Governments took ownership. Multilateral institutions invested and the coalition kept moving," Power, a Harvard professor, said Wednesday at CGI. "That is the story of optimism I want to leave you with today." Other mid-sized actors described a mixed mood. Major foundations are still in "soul-searching mode," according to Global Fund for Children co-CEO John Hecklinger. His fund serves as an intermediary between well-endowed foundations and more grassroots nonprofits. Funders, he finds, understandably can't fill every gap but are also hesitant to maintain the previous status quo. "There's not this forced, strategic approach. The vision is disjointed," said Ann Lee, the co-founder and CEO of Community Organized Relief Effort. "It's very, very sort of ad hoc." Nonprofits turn to new donor countries Still, the U.N. sidelines brought out new nonprofits and funders eager for impact. Eleanor Crook Foundation CEO William Moore spent the week garnering support for his fledgling nonprofit to eradicate child deaths from acute malnutrition. Operation End Starvation launched this summer with a $100 million, two-year commitment from the U.S. State Department. But Moore anticipates needing 17 times more every year to purchase enough therapeutic foods such as peanut butter paste and get them into starving children's mouths. On Wednesday, OES announced a $5 million grant from the Gates Foundation. The goal is to eventually become for malnutrition what vaccines alliance Gavi is for immunizations or what The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria is for the deadliest infections. His pitch: OES will pay for overhead and match one-third of government money through philanthropy if countries cover the costs of the foods and delivery. Moore noted one lunch he had scheduled with Nigeria's health minister — part of a sector-wide shift to partner with the high-burden countries where aid organizations work. "They've said, 'We're ready for this. We're ready to take on this additional responsibility. We want to own the systems that are needed to improve the livelihoods of our people,'" Moore said. "We're really excited as philanthropy also to be of service to that." Moore's nonprofit is among a growing number turning to Arab Gulf nations. Moore said Operation End Starvation is having good conversations with official state donor entities and the philanthropies affiliated with their royal families. The region's leaders have recognized a need "to fund and to bridge the gap" created by aid cuts, according to Hammam bin Nasser bin Juraied, executive director of the Arab Gulf Programme for Development. An 'openness to collaboration' Other aid groups are working more closely with local partners in hopes of reducing overhead costs and increasing their impact. The News
Zambia is close to resolving a months-long dispute with the US over a proposed health agreement, the African nationâs foreign minister told Semafor. Mulambo Haimbe said Washington had agreed to remove contentious data-sharing provisions. The US State Department has not publicly confirmed the change.
The US has struck health agreements with African nations that involve sharing data with Washington about pathogens that could spark epidemics in their countries as a condition of getting the funding.
Haimbe said the two sides had also agreed to drop a disputed linkage between the health agreement and a separate critical-minerals deal, another point of contention that Zambia had raised publicly earlier this year.
âI believe that it has now been agreed that those provisions be replaced completely,â Haimbe said of the data terms. âThe linking, the coupling of the critical minerals agreement with the health assistance â¦ has also been set aside.â
Haimbe said the revised agreement was now at a stage where the two sides could sign it. The comments come after Haimbe met US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Chris Kulukundis in New York this week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. A statement from Zambia said the two countries had reaffirmed their strategic partnership and agreed to deepen cooperation in health, investment and critical minerals, but did not mention the disputed provisions or confirm that they had been removed.
The proposed agreement would provide US health assistance to Zambia over five years for a proposed grant valued around at $1.5 billion, with the US contributing just over $1 billion.
Know More
The dispute became public earlier this year as Washington sought to negotiate new health agreements with African governments that tied US assistance to commitments on health systems, data and other areas.
Zambia objected to provisions covering the use of health data and also resisted Washingtonâs effort to link the health agreement to cooperation on critical minerals. Haimbe said in May that the two agreements should be treated separately.
The disagreement came as Zambia was seeking to attract more investment into its copper and other critical-minerals industries while maintaining longstanding economic ties with China and developing closer commercial relations with the US.
Haimbe told Semafor that Zambia wants to work with both countries without giving either preferential treatment. âMe being in Beijing does not mean that Iâm against Washington and vice versa,â he said.

3596e243df95.text: Bill Gates will warn on this weekend's "Meet the Press" that he can see a future where AI wipes out humanity . Driving the news: "AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths," he will tell Kristen Welker on "Meet the Press" on Sunday, per excerpts NBC released Friday. "Even though it's pretty hard to get to 100%, there's never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools." Zoom out: Gates released a memo in August that defined AI as a technology more consequential than virtually any other in history. In the essay, he argued that "AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice." "On the current course and speed, there's a very high chance of a net negative outcome," he said. What's next: Gates says that government and political parties need to work together now to find ways to keep AI from spiraling out of control.
